live-002: The New Jersey Supreme Court's unanimous opinion in Township of Jackson v. Getzel Bee draws a bright line around a maneuver some municipalities have used to unlock preferred parcels: condemning land not for the taking itself, but to trade it away for a different tract the town actually wants. Jackson Township condemned two privately held parcels with the intent of swapping them to a developer in exchange for a separate tract slated for open-space preservation. The Court found the condemned parcels were never destined for public use in their own right, and that the township's disclosures to the affected owners shifted over the course of the proceeding in a way that failed condemnation law's good-faith requirement. The ruling is being read as a 'Kelo'-adjacent guardrail: public-benefit framing alone won't save a condemnation used as a private trading chip. Developers and REITs whose entitlement strategy in New Jersey — or jurisdictions likely to follow this reasoning — depends on a municipal land swap should revisit those structures before relying on them further.
live-003: Wilmington Savings Fund Society, FSB, as trustee for the Benchmark 2026-B43 CMBS trust, sued Milton 90 Pleasant Valley Street LLC and Development Associates of Benton Harbor LLC on July 28, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, Mortgage Professional America reported. According to the article, Barclays Capital Real Estate made the $34.4 million loan around April 14, 2026 at a 6.4% fixed rate, maturing May 6, 2036, and it was assigned to the trust effective May 20, 2026. CWCapital Asset Management is the special servicer. The loan is secured by about 46 acres at 90 Pleasant Valley Street in Methuen, Massachusetts and the Fairplain Plaza shopping center in Benton Township, Michigan. The trustee alleges two guarantors filed Chapter 11 in New Jersey around June 4, 2026, and the borrowers then missed the first payment due June 6, raising the rate to an 11.4% default rate. A default letter followed on June 16 and an acceleration letter on July 15. The borrowers leased nearly all of each property to affiliated companies under 99-year leases, and those affiliates have also filed Chapter 11. The trustee alleges the borrowers are not enforcing those leases, conduct the filing calls "affiliate atrophy," and that collecting from the affiliates would cover the loan payments. The complaint seeks foreclosure of the mortgages, foreclosure on personal-property collateral under the UCC, and appointment of a receiver to take possession, collect rents and step into the affiliate leases and the related bankruptcy cases. One guarantor is named as a defendant to pursue any shortfall after a sale; the other two are not, because the bankruptcy stay bars joining them. The allegations have not been tested, and no court has ruled on them.
live-004: FitFactariDC LLC, a commercial tenant, sued CoStar Group and five large brokerages, CBRE, Colliers, Cushman & Wakefield, JLL and Newmark, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois on June 12, 2026. The proposed class action says CoStar gathered and passed along sensitive lease data, while the brokerages supplied that data and got access to competitors' information in return. The tenant says the arrangement made it pay "artificially inflated" rent on a lease in Denver, The Real Deal reported, citing Bisnow. According to the complaint, seeing rivals' final lease terms almost as soon as they were signed let the defendants keep asking rents in step, give smaller concessions and hold firm in negotiations with tenants. CoStar general counsel Gene Boxer called the lawsuit "frivolous" and said the company expected a "swift and complete victory," according to the report. The other defendants declined to comment or did not respond. The court docket shows the tenant voluntarily dropped Colliers International Group Inc. on Aug. 7, 2026; its U.S. unit, Colliers International USA, LLC, remains a defendant. Judge Joan H. Lefkow set a briefing schedule on Aug. 13, and CoStar and the brokerages filed separate motions to dismiss on Aug. 17. The tenant's response was due Oct. 1 and replies Nov. 2, and the court canceled the Aug. 19 initial status hearing. The case follows years of litigation against RealPage and apartment landlords over rent-setting software, including a Justice Department suit that RealPage settled in November 2025 without paying penalties or admitting wrongdoing, in exchange for changes to its platform and independent oversight, The Real Deal noted. This suit applies a similar theory to commercial lease data.
live-005: The SEC's complaint against Tampa-based non-traded REIT RAD Diversified REIT, its co-founders Brandon 'Dutch' Mendenhall and Amy Vaughn, and affiliated entity The Seminar Solution, LLC alleges a five-year, $152M offering that was never registered and was fraudulent from the start — raised from more than 5,500 retail investors between 2019 and 2024. Roughly $54M of that capital was allegedly diverted to an affiliated entity to cover personal expenses, even as the REIT continued marketing itself to investors using representations about profitability and liquidity the SEC says didn't match its actual financial condition. The enforcement theory leans heavily on related-party fund flows and continued capital-raising after internal warning signs — a declined credit line, a rising rate of foreclosures in the portfolio, and frozen investor redemptions are all cited. Sponsors and boards of retail-facing, non-traded REITs should treat this as a preview of what the SEC is looking for when it examines related-party transaction controls and disclosure practices.
live-006: Silver Star Properties REIT filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on May 28, 2026, Bisnow reported, citing a June 5 shareholder update filed with the SEC. The Houston-based REIT said it aims to reorganize its obligations and preserve "tangible and intangible assets." It reported $75 million in liabilities and $100 million in assets, warned shareholders that the proceedings might cancel their equity, and said four loans are in default, along with a $5.75 million promissory note on a self-storage property that moved to foreclosure on June 2. The company previously filed for Chapter 11 in September 2023, with a plan to liquidate legacy office assets, reposition others into a new entity and resolve $217 million in outstanding debt. It planned to sell its retail, office and industrial holdings and move fully into self-storage, and bought nine properties in 2023 through an acquisition of Southern Star Self-Storage. According to the shareholder update, ongoing litigation, tight finances and lending constraints led to a review of strategic alternatives. Bisnow reported that the pivot was slowed by an SEC investigation, litigation and blocked deals to sell properties. In a 2023 lawsuit, Silver Star accused founder and former CEO Allen Hartman, who left in October 2022, of fraud, breach of fiduciary duty and interfering with asset sales; that case is still ongoing. Bisnow corrected its article on June 11 to clarify the status of that case and the date of Hartman's departure.
live-007: Via Mizner Lender 1 LLC, the administrative agent for a group of lenders, sued in Palm Beach County Circuit Court on July 17, 2026 to foreclose a mortgage on the Mandarin Oriental condominium project under construction on Federal Highway in Boca Raton, according to The Coastal Star. The borrower is Via Mizner Owner III, the Penn-Florida Companies affiliate building the condos, which gave the mortgage in August 2023. The lenders seek $417.7 million to repay the original $270 million loan plus interest, advances and fees, and allege Penn-Florida stopped making interest payments in June 2024 and failed to pay the full amount in September 2025 as promised. The complaint seeks to cut off claims by what it calls 'purported junior lienholders,' including construction manager Strategic Group Builders, and 'purported contract purchasers' of condo units, arguing that the mortgage is superior to other interests arising from the borrower. Strategic Group filed its own suit on July 6, seeking $24.1 million it says it was not paid, plus interest, costs and fees, and seeking to foreclose a lien it recorded against the property. It named Via Mizner Owner III and four project lenders, which it says stopped making monthly payments to it without notice. The Coastal Star also reported that unit buyers have pursued their deposits in separate cases, and that at least nine have settled. Separately, in a case concerning the adjoining Mandarin Oriental hotel, Penn-Florida affiliates Via Mizner Owner II and Via Mizner Pledgor II filed for Chapter 11 in December 2025 after failing to repay about $210 million to lenders at maturity, The Coastal Star reported. The auction of that property was moved to August 14, 2026, with a sale hearing set for August 21. The Coastal Star did not report a response from Penn-Florida to the foreclosure complaint.
live-008: CommunityAmerica Federal Credit Union filed two lawsuits in Hennepin County District Court against the owners of two office buildings in the Metropoint business park in St. Louis Park, Minnesota, the Minneapolis/St. Paul Business Journal reported, according to Connect CRE's July 23, 2026 roundup. The buildings are Metropoint 300, at 300 Highway 169 S., and Metropoint 400, at 400 Highway 169 S. The credit union is seeking to recover roughly $46 million in loans tied to the properties. Both buildings were scheduled to be sold at a foreclosure auction in September 2026. The report did not name the owners or say why the loans went into default.
live-009: U.S. District Judge Melissa R. DuBose on July 28, 2026 granted the landowners partial summary judgment on one count of their suit against the Town of Johnston, a ruling the Rhode Island Current described as finding the town's attempted seizure of a 31-acre property for a proposed apartment complex unlawful. The owners' companies planned a 252-unit affordable housing complex on the site on George Waterman Road. The dispute dates to December 2024, when Mayor Joseph Polisena Jr. issued a public letter opposing the project and warned the town would 'fight back' using 'all the power of government' available, the Current reported. Polisena said he wanted the land for a new public safety complex and town hall. On March 10, 2025, after an appraisal valued the property at $775,000, the Town Council voted 5-0 to begin condemning the site, and the owners sued the same night, arguing the taking was pretextual. DuBose issued a temporary restraining order on March 19, 2025, followed by a preliminary injunction. On August 4, 2026, the owners moved for contempt, arguing that two resolutions passed at a July 31 special council meeting, one putting a charter amendment on the November ballot to expand the town's condemnation authority and one creating a Municipal Public Building Authority, violated the injunction. DuBose ordered the town to show cause and to produce the meeting's agenda, minutes and resolutions; a town spokesperson told the Current that 'motions cannot be ignored.' On August 11, after reviewing the town's response, DuBose found the town's actions on and around July 31 did not violate the April 2, 2025 injunction and canceled the show-cause hearing, according to the docket. On August 28 she denied the town's request for a separate final judgment on the count it lost, and the case is in discovery.
live-010: New York's highest court reinstated an implied-covenant-of-good-faith claim brought by 111 West 57th Investment LLC against Apollo-affiliated mezzanine lenders, centered on the 2017 sale of a $25M junior mezzanine loan secured by the plaintiff's equity in the Steinway Tower project. The loan was sold to Spruce Capital Partners at par value even though internal models reportedly showed roughly $600M in underlying equity value, and Spruce initiated a UCC Article 9 strict foreclosure just two days after acquiring the loan, wiping out the plaintiff's equity position entirely. The Court of Appeals held that Apollo's contractual right to assign the loan at its 'sole discretion' does not, on its own, exculpate the lender from good-faith-and-fair-dealing claims when the discretion is alleged to have been exercised as part of a scheme to strip a joint-venture partner's equity. The ruling remits the case to Supreme Court, New York County for further proceedings, while affirming dismissal of the plaintiff's related tortious interference claims. The decision resolves a split among the Appellate Division's departments and brings New York in line with Delaware law on this question. Mezzanine lenders, sponsors, and equity investors operating under New York-governed capital stacks should expect a lower pleading bar going forward for bad-faith challenges to loan assignments and strict foreclosures, even in deals where assignment rights were drafted as facially unqualified.
live-013: A federal judge in New Jersey has allowed investors to pursue a putative class action alleging that the directors and advisers of three non-traded Lightstone Value Plus REITs did not disclose their chairman's conflict of interest before shareholders voted to remove the funds' liquidation deadlines, AltsWire reported. U.S. District Judge Michael A. Shipp ruled on August 5, 2026 that the plaintiffs adequately alleged that the proxy statements and related solicitor calls omitted a material conflict involving David Lichtenstein, the REITs' chairman and chief executive, who through affiliated entities owns the funds' external advisers. According to the complaint, Lichtenstein held subordinated participation interests through three special-purpose entities, potentially worth more than $59.8 million, that would have had no value if REIT II and REIT III had liquidated by the deadlines in their original charters, September 2024 and March 2025. The plaintiffs allege the 2022 proxies disclosed that the interests existed but not that they depended on extending the REITs' lives, which the court found could have significantly changed how a reasonable shareholder viewed the vote. The court also found that phone solicitors made misleading statements between a December 2022 meeting, where the amendments failed, and a January 2023 reconvened meeting, where they passed; investors allege solicitors called a "yes" vote "the most likely path to liquidity." The charter amendments, presented as a single item, also eliminated board fiduciary duties to shareholders, cut quorum requirements to as little as 33% of votes entitled to be cast, restricted shareholder access to investor lists and expanded indemnification for officers and directors, according to AltsWire. All four counts survive, including breach of fiduciary duty claims against the director defendants and the advisory entities. Lightstone did not respond to AltsWire's request for comment. The case, filed in November 2024, is now in initial scheduling before Magistrate Judge Tonianne J. Bongiovanni.
live-014: Former tenant Jacob Keller filed a putative class action against UDR, Inc. — a Highlands Ranch, Colorado-based, NYSE-listed multifamily REIT — on July 2, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California. The complaint, Keller v. UDR, Inc., No. 3:26-cv-03865 (S.D. Cal.), alleges UDR used a RealPage algorithmic pricing device to set rents and occupancy levels at a UDR-managed San Diego property, in violation of San Diego Municipal Code § 98.1103, which bars landlords from using software that generates rent or occupancy recommendations from non-public competitor data. Unlike the antitrust conspiracy theory driving the federal RealPage MDL, San Diego's ordinance requires no proof of coordination among competitors — it simply prohibits use of a covered algorithmic device outright and authorizes a private right of action with per-violation statutory penalties of up to $1,000, in addition to damages, injunctive relief, and attorneys' fees. The complaint notably relies on UDR's own acknowledged use of RealPage software in the District of Columbia Attorney General's separate November 2023 antitrust suit against RealPage and roughly a dozen large landlords. The case underscores that algorithmic-pricing exposure has split into two tracks: the federal MDL, where RealPage's landlord-customers have paid roughly $360M combined in settlements, and a fast-growing patchwork of municipal bans — now including San Diego, Philadelphia, and New York State — that impose standalone statutory liability regardless of any conspiracy, and that can reach large public REITs as readily as private operators.
live-015: The New Jersey Supreme Court on July 13, 2026 unanimously modified the test, set in its 1992 decision in Sica v. Board of Adjustment of Wall, that governs use variances for 'inherently beneficial' uses such as hospitals, senior housing, schools and child care centers, the New Jersey Globe reported. Justice Anne M. Patterson wrote for the Court. The case arose from Monarch Communities' proposal for a 165-unit senior living facility on residentially zoned property in Montville Township. Senior housing is an inherently beneficial use under state law, but the township's zoning board denied the application, finding that it conflicted with the zoning plan and would have significant negative impacts, according to the Globe. The trial court and the Appellate Division both reversed the board. The Court held that Sica no longer fully reflects a 1997 amendment to the Municipal Land Use Law that requires inherently beneficial use applicants to satisfy both of the statute's 'negative criteria.' Under the revised fourth step, a board must first decide whether the applicant has shown that the variance would not substantially impair the intent and purpose of the zone plan and zoning ordinance; if not, the variance must be denied before any balancing of public benefits against detriments. These applicants remain exempt from the heightened Medici proof standard that applies to ordinary use variances. The Court reversed the Appellate Division and remanded to the zoning board to reconsider under the new standard, expressing no view on whether the project should be approved.
live-017: Travelers Property Casualty Company of America and St. Paul Fire and Marine Insurance Company, which issued excess policies under Travelers, filed a declaratory judgment action in Marion Superior Court on Nov. 26, 2025 against Washington Shoppes LP and The Broadbent Company, Inc. (No. 49D01-2511-CE-056363), The Indiana Lawyer reported. The insurers ask the court to declare that they owe no defense or indemnity coverage for cleanup at the shopping center at 10021 E. Washington St. in Indianapolis. Washington Shoppes has owned the site since 1998; The Indiana Lawyer describes Broadbent as owning the retail area that Washington Shoppes operates. Sunrise Dry Cleaners operated at or around the address from 1987 to 1996. A 2023 site investigation requested by the shopping center found tetrachloroethylene (PCE) and its degradation products in the soil and groundwater. The Indiana Department of Environmental Management later identified the property owner as potentially responsible for the contamination, and the center sought coverage for defense and cleanup costs. The insurers say each of their primary and excess policies excludes coverage for pollutants such as tetrachloroethylene. They also argue that, even if Washington Shoppes shows it qualifies as an insured, coverage may be barred if it knew of actual or potential contamination before acquiring the site or before the policies were issued. Attorneys for both sides did not respond to The Indiana Lawyer's requests for comment.
live-019: The EPA and Columbia Falls Aluminum Company, LLC (CFAC) lodged a 647-page consent decree in the U.S. District Court for the District of Montana in Missoula, resolving CERCLA and Montana state Superfund claims tied to the company's former aluminum reduction plant in Columbia Falls, Montana. Under the agreement, CFAC will pay $57.6 million toward cleanup of arsenic, cyanide, fluoride, and polyaromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) contamination in soil and groundwater at the shuttered smelter site, including construction of a groundwater slurry wall around the main contaminant source area to halt migration toward the Flathead River and low-permeability caps over onsite landfills. The consent decree remains subject to a 30-day public comment period running from July 7 to August 6, 2026, and further review by the U.S. District Court in Missoula before formal entry. EPA and the Montana Department of Environmental Quality will jointly oversee design and implementation of the remedial work, which the agency estimates could take two to three years to complete once a final remediation design is set.
live-022: RealPage, which licenses revenue-management software to owners and managers of residential rental properties, sued Attorney General Letitia James in the Southern District of New York in November 2025 (No. 1:25-cv-09847), challenging General Business Law § 340-B, which New York enacted on October 16, 2025 as an amendment to its antitrust law, the Donnelly Act. Section 2 of the law bars facilitating agreements between competing landlords not to compete, including by operating software that performs a "coordinating function," which the law defines as collecting pricing and lease data from two or more unaffiliated landlords, analyzing it by computer, and recommending rents or lease terms. Section 3 makes it unlawful for landlords to set or adjust rents based on such software's recommendations. RealPage moved for a preliminary injunction, the state agreed not to enforce the law until that motion was decided, and the attorney general moved to dismiss. While the motions were pending, RealPage filed notices of supplemental authority, including, on August 10, 2026, the Second Circuit's August 5 decision in DoorDash, Inc. v. City of New York, which held that a New York City rule requiring delivery platforms to share customer information with restaurants violated the First Amendment. In an August 13 letter, reported by Law360, the attorney general's office said that case involved a compelled disclosure of customer data, while the New York statute regulates anticompetitive conduct. In her September 29 opinion, Judge Caproni found that RealPage's recommendations, which it now generates mostly from customer-supplied and public data under its consent decree with the U.S. Department of Justice, are commercial speech subject to intermediate scrutiny, and that Section 3, as drafted, "probably does not" survive that review. She found that Section 2 targets conduct that is already illegal and does not restrict protected speech. She denied the motion to dismiss on both jurisdictional and pleading grounds. The attorney general answered the complaint and moved for reconsideration on October 13, 2026, and briefing on that motion closed on November 3. Under an October 23 scheduling order, fact discovery is due by February 22, 2027, and the case will be tried without a jury.
live-023: U.S. Bank National Association filed a complaint in Denver District Court on Monday, August 10, 2026, on behalf of lenders, seeking appointment of a receiver for Republic Plaza after a loan default in March, the Denver Gazette reported. A receiver would protect and maintain the property to ensure the lender's debt is repaid. The complaint says the defendant, "being a sophisticated commercial borrower, has failed to make payments as required by the Loan Documents," and that the plaintiff has "reasonable concern" that the property will not be properly operated or maintained. The 56-story tower at 370 17th St. is owned and managed by Brookfield Properties, which recently rebranded as BGRE, and MetLife Investment Management is also an owner. Brookfield declined to comment to the Gazette. The building narrowly avoided foreclosure in 2023 under a deal that gave its owners until March 2026, 9News reported at the time, according to the Gazette, which also reported that Bank of America's Colorado office was set to move out of the building in October. Reported loan figures differ. Connect CRE, citing the Denver Business Journal, described an approximately $130 million defaulted loan, while a later Connect CRE roundup citing Morningstar Credit listed the loan at $230.1 million, held in two CMBS trusts. That roundup said Trigild has been appointed receiver and plans to sell the property in 2027, that the loan moved to special servicing ahead of its March maturity, and that the property was appraised at $136.0 million after the transfer.
live-024: U.S. Bank, acting for two lender groups, has sued to foreclose on the retail portion of Brightline's MiamiCentral station, The Real Deal reported, citing the South Florida Business Journal. The defendants are Brightline Investment Holdings, the Brightline-affiliated owner of the 124,000 square feet of retail at 600 Northwest First Avenue, one of its subsidiaries, and property manager FECI Realty. The case does not involve the train station, the rail company or the station's office buildings, which Blackstone-managed funds bought in 2021 for $230 million, and the retail space and station remain open. The retail property was financed in 2022 with a $128.5 million loan split into two pieces. The $65 million senior piece is held by XYQ Cayman Ltd., which the lawsuit identifies as an affiliate of Boston-based Bracebridge Capital; four EB-5 funds for foreign investors seeking U.S. green cards hold the remaining $63 million. The senior piece is paid first, and the foreclosure suit concerns only that piece. The lender alleges the borrower failed to make a $16 million principal payment due Dec. 26, 2025 and a $6 million payment due March 15, 2026, and stopped making quarterly interest payments in December 2025. It says the full $65 million senior balance is now due and asks the court to foreclose, enforce guarantees from Brightline Investment Holdings and its subsidiary, and appoint a receiver to oversee the property. The report did not include a response from Brightline. The retail space is 65 percent leased, with 41,000 square feet available, according to an online listing cited by The Real Deal. Tenants include AT&T, Starbucks, Chick-fil-A, Rosetta Bakery, Joe & The Juice and Wolf of Tacos. The suit follows Fitch's July downgrade of bonds issued by the separately owned rail operator, Brightline Trains Florida; the rating agency cited a "very high probability" that the operator will miss coming debt payments.
live-026: Acres Loan Origination LLC, an affiliate of commercial mortgage lender Acres Capital, has filed a foreclosure complaint in New York state Supreme Court against the Auden Buffalo student housing community at 2915-2949 N. Forest Road in Amherst, Buffalo Business First reported, according to Connect CRE's roundup for the week of August 13, 2026. The defendant is an affiliate of DMG Investments, a New York City real estate developer. In the complaint, Acres says it made two loans totaling $32.5 million in early 2021 to finance construction of Auden Buffalo, and that the loan matured in January 2024 with all of the principal still unpaid. The filing came days after a group of lenders represented by Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. began foreclosure proceedings against Air Buffalo, an apartment building at 1265 Sweet Home Rd. that is also owned by a DMG affiliate, according to the same report. Connect CRE's summary did not include a response from DMG.
live-028: The Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project is a planned 67-mile transmission line through rural parts of Baltimore, Carroll and Frederick counties that New Jersey-based PSEG is building at the behest of grid officials, according to Maryland Matters. To complete its application for a certificate of public convenience and necessity, PSEG needed field surveys: the Fourth Circuit's opinion says Maryland's Power Plant Research Program deemed the application incomplete until certain field-based studies were done. PSEG sued in the District of Maryland on April 15, 2025 against landowners who refused access, invoking Real Property Section 12-111(a), which lets a 'body politic or corporate having the power of eminent domain' enter private land for surveys after a bona fide effort to notify the owner in writing. Judge Adam B. Abelson granted a preliminary injunction on June 20, 2025. On appeal, 117 parties argued that letting PSEG survey would amount to exercising eminent domain before it holds a certificate. The panel disagreed. If that were required, Judge Berner wrote, PSEG would have 'no viable path' to obtaining a certificate, and delaying the permitting process 'could exacerbate the very energy crisis' the project was meant to address. The panel found no abuse of discretion in the injunction, agreed with the district court that the brief access the statute allows is not a taking under the federal or Maryland constitutions, and rejected the argument that PSEG's in-service deadline could not be met. Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III joined the opinion; Judge Julius N. Richardson concurred. PSEG said it appreciated the court's 'careful consideration' and would keep engaging with property owners. The president of the opposition group Stop MPRP said she was 'deeply disappointed' and noted the ruling does not approve the line or let PSEG acquire land, questions still before the Public Service Commission. Maryland Matters reported that Abelson had held one resident in contempt in July for obstructing surveyors and had allowed U.S. marshals to accompany surveyors onto a handful of properties. On November 4, 2026, 60 landowners, represented by a public interest law firm, asked the U.S. Supreme Court to hear the case, arguing the Fourth Circuit allowed entry without first establishing that PSEG holds the eminent domain power its right of entry depends on, Maryland Matters reported.
live-029: The developer of the Mandarin Oriental-branded Residences in Boca Raton has sued its lender, an affiliate of Madison Realty Capital, in New York state court, days before a scheduled UCC foreclosure auction of the developer's ownership interests, The Real Deal reported. Via Mizner Owner III LLC and Via Mizner Pledgor III LLC, led by Penn-Florida Companies president and CEO Mark Gensheimer, filed the suit on Aug. 13, 2026 against Via Mizner Lender 1 and Via Mizner Lender 2 LLC and seek more than $500 million in damages. They ask for declaratory judgments on the parties' relationship and on alleged violations of New York's Uniform Commercial Code, and for an order stopping the sale. On Aug. 17, Justice Andrew Borrok signed an order temporarily halting the auction and set a hearing for Oct. 1. According to the complaint, Madison led more than $300 million in financing for the project in 2023 and, months later, stopped funding, saying the loans "were out of balance." The developer says it then could not pay vendors, and that Madison took control of construction, replaced the project manager with Straticon LLC, began paying vendors directly and put a lawyer without construction experience in charge of decisions. The complaint also alleges Madison told a consultant's employee to go "scorched Earth" on the project, and that all work stopped once Madison stopped paying vendors. It accuses Madison of "gross mismanagement and gross negligence" and of manufacturing the defaults behind its enforcement. Madison did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In July 2026 the lender filed a nearly $418 million foreclosure suit against the developer, alleging missed payments beginning in 2024 and a failure to repay the loan when it matured. By late 2024 the two sides had signed restructuring agreements confirming Madison's control over the condo portion of the project, including its completion, according to the report. The 1.5-acre site at 105 East Camino Real is planned for a 164-key Mandarin Oriental-branded hotel and an 88-unit condo, linked by a sky bridge, which remain unfinished after years of delays; the project was first announced in 2015. Buyers, contractors and subcontractors have also sued the developer in separate cases over the years.
live-031: U.S. Bank National Association, as trustee for the registered holders of the Morgan Stanley Bank of America Merrill Lynch Trust 2016-C28, filed suit on August 12, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey against Lenox Drive Office Park LLC, a Delaware company that owns office buildings on Lenox Drive in Mercer County, Mortgage Professional America reported. Greystone Servicing Company handles the loan. Lenox Drive Office Park LLC bought Princeton Pike Corporate Center in Lawrenceville in early 2016, NJB Magazine reported at the time. According to the complaint as reported, Morgan Stanley Bank, N.A. made a $130 million loan to the borrower in December 2015, split across several promissory notes and secured by a mortgage on the office park along with cash-management agreements and UCC filings on rents and fixtures. The loan matured on January 1, 2026, and the trust says it was not repaid. As of July 1, 2026, the trust says $141,767,219.75 was owed, including principal, interest at the note and default rates, late fees and servicing charges, with interest still accruing. The trust seeks an order foreclosing and selling the property and the appointment of a receiver to run the office park during the case and conduct the sale. The federal docket shows a clerk's entry of default on October 8, 2026, an amended complaint on October 29, and an entry titled "Appoint Receiver" on November 6. No court has ruled on the merits.
live-035: The developer and 9 New York Ave LLC filed the suit in the Circuit Court of Cook County, where JLL is headquartered, Law360 and Bisnow reported. Bisnow reported that the developer, a Maryland-based investor who had put money into multifamily deals before but is not a specialist in the sector, delivered the 115-unit Pinnacle in the NoMa neighborhood in 2024 and sold it in April 2026 to July Residential for $30.5 million. The complaint asserts breach of contract, fraud, fraudulent inducement, negligent misrepresentation and breach of fiduciary duty. According to Bisnow's account of the complaint, JLL projected stabilized NOI of $1.65 million in March 2021 and said construction lenders would require a minimum 8.5% debt yield, which that figure did not meet. JLL allegedly raised its projection to $1.94 million in December 2021 despite what the suit calls no material change in the property, then to $2.04 million in January 2022 and $2.07 million in the model given to the lender's appraiser, a level that cleared the threshold and implied a $51 million stabilized value. The suit attributes the increases to higher assumed rents, lower payroll, lower vacancy and no rent concessions. The appraisal for the lender, Hingham Institution for Savings, projected NOI of $1.85 million, and an appraisal the developer obtained in December 2020, before hiring JLL, projected $1.4 million. The suit says the developer invested more than $13.3 million and lost more than $7.4 million; the damages claim adds fees, interest and $4.3 million in lost opportunity. Hingham made a $23.7 million construction loan in May 2022, according to D.C. land records cited by Bisnow. The suit also says the developer tried in June to arbitrate under an April 2021 project management agreement, but JLL declined, arguing the claims did not fall under that agreement. JLL did not respond to Bisnow's requests for comment.
live-036: Wilmington Trust, a Delaware-based affiliate of M&T Bank Corp., sued Philadelphia-based Rubenstein Partners on June 7, 2024 in the Hamilton County Court of Common Pleas to foreclose on the office tower at 312 Elm St. in downtown Cincinnati, the Cincinnati Business Courier reported in an article republished by Colliers. The complaint said Rubenstein owed $39.6 million in principal, interest, late charges and fees on a $46.1 million note executed in 2015, when Rubenstein bought the building. In an answer filed August 12, 2024, Rubenstein admitted each of the allegations, including that it had defaulted. Judge Lisa Allen appointed a managing director of Colliers Real Estate Management Services as receiver on July 30, 2024, with authority to collect rents, lease vacant space with the lender's consent and, with court approval, sell the building. The Business Courier said 312 Elm was the third office building in Cincinnati's central business district to go into receivership; the Netherland Plaza Hotel and the tower at 600 Vine St. were also in receivership. The tower, completed in 1992, has more than 378,000 square feet and was about 45.7% occupied. On December 30, 2024, Wilmington Trust filed a similar foreclosure suit against Rubenstein over 312 Plum St., a nearby office tower that Rubenstein bought in a deal that closed the same day as its 312 Elm purchase, the Business Courier reported. That complaint alleged Rubenstein owed $16.2 million on an $18.4 million mortgage loan and was delinquent on debts to vendors, and said the lender terminated a June 2024 discounted payoff agreement in October 2024 after Rubenstein allegedly failed to comply with it. live-039: The owner of 148 State St., a Financial District office building, sued the City of Boston in Suffolk Superior Court on December 17, 2025, in a proposed class action alleging that the Assessing Department retaliated against commercial owners who appealed their assessments to the state Appellate Tax Board. live-040: The New Jersey Supreme Court ruled on August 10, 2026 that a municipality condemning property does not have to state, in the ordinance authorizing the taking, the public use it intends. The 6-1 decision in Borough of Seaside Park v. Shree Jyoti, LLC (A-2-25) resolves the borough's effort to acquire the Desert Palm Inn, a motel it moved to condemn in April 2022, the New Jersey Monitor reported. According to the opinion, the borough council passed a resolution authorizing an appraisal and acquisition by eminent domain on November 15, 2021, and on April 14, 2022 passed an ordinance saying the taking would 'promote and protect the health, safety and welfare' of residents. The opinion notes that the record documented extensive code violations and a history of police incidents at the property. The borough's first condemnation complaint, filed July 19, 2022, was dismissed without prejudice because the ordinance did not specify a public use; its amended complaint identified a public parking lot with electric vehicle charging, and the borough later added a public drinking water well. The trial court and Appellate Division ruled for the borough. 'No law requires a municipality to articulate the intended public use in the ordinance itself,' Justice Michael Noriega wrote for the majority. The court also observed that the matter 'likely could have been resolved by simply disclosing the intended public use at the earliest reasonable point,' the Monitor reported. Justice John Hoffman agreed the statutes do not require a stated public use but would have blocked the acquisition under the 'square corners' doctrine, which requires government to deal forthrightly with the public. He wrote that Seaside Park knew its plans at least a month before moving to condemn but declined to tell the owner when asked, and that 'the majority degrades the square corners doctrine.' He contrasted the ruling with a recent decision blocking Jackson Township's use of eminent domain where its stated public purpose was found false.
live-041: A commercial landlord's stumble on the first attempt to evict a nonpaying tenant did not cost him nearly $200,000 in back rent, the Massachusetts Appeals Court ruled on August 24, 2026, resolving a dispute that had turned into an unplanned tutorial on the interaction between summary process practice and claim-preclusion doctrine. The case began in the Roxbury Division of the Boston Municipal Court, where trustee Paul Eng filed a summary process action against tenant Chen's Food Enterprise, Inc. for nonpayment of rent. That first case was dismissed because Eng had not served the written notice to quit the lease required before litigation could begin, a common and generally fixable defect under Massachusetts practice. Eng served a corrected termination notice and filed a second summary process action. Following a three-day bench trial before Judge Kenneth J. Fiandaca, the trial court rejected the tenant's argument that the first dismissal barred the second suit and entered judgment for Eng on both possession and $198,000 in unpaid rent. Chen's Food Enterprise appealed to the Appellate Division of the District Court and Boston Municipal Court departments and won a reversal: the Appellate Division held that the first case's dismissal operated as an adjudication on the merits for claim-preclusion purposes, meaning the second, corrected suit should never have gone forward at all. Had that ruling stood, it would have handed commercial tenants a powerful and largely accidental tool — any landlord who missed a notice requirement in an initial filing could have been permanently barred from ever recovering rent through summary process, no matter how quickly or completely the defect was later cured. Writing for a unanimous panel that also included Justices Ditkoff and Tan, Justice Sookyoung Shin rejected that reading, holding that the Appellate Division's application of claim preclusion could not be reconciled with the plain language of G. L. c. 239, § 7, the statute governing summary process for nonpayment of rent. The court concluded the statute affirmatively authorizes a landlord to bring a second action once the underlying notice defect has been fixed, because a dismissal grounded purely in a failure to satisfy a notice precondition is not the kind of merits determination claim-preclusion doctrine is meant to protect — the unpaid-rent question had never actually been tried in the first case. The decision restores what most Massachusetts landlord-tenant practitioners had long assumed was the governing rule: a procedural dismissal for a curable notice defect leaves the underlying rent claim intact so long as the landlord actually fixes the problem before refiling. Tenants' counsel lose a defense that functioned less like an argument on the merits and more like a windfall keyed to a landlord's paperwork error, but the ruling leaves fully intact their ability to contest notice compliance, lease termination, and the amount of rent owed in whatever action actually proceeds to trial, exactly as Chen's Food Enterprise did across three days before Judge Fiandaca. For commercial landlords and their counsel, the practical lesson cuts in two directions. A dismissal for a defective or missing notice to quit should be treated as correctable rather than fatal, and a landlord who promptly serves a proper termination notice and refiles should not assume the underlying rent claim has been lost — though building in the time and cost of doing it twice, as Eng ultimately had to, is itself a reason to get lease notice provisions right before filing the first time. Property managers and in-house counsel would do well to audit notice-to-quit requirements against both the governing statute and the specific lease before any nonpayment summary process action goes out the door, since the defect here was entirely avoidable and added more than two years of delay before the landlord actually collected. Tenants' counsel, meanwhile, should not bank on an early notice-based dismissal as a permanent shield against a rent claim and should focus litigation strategy on the merits of the nonpayment dispute itself, since this decision is specific to notice-based dismissals under G. L. c. 239, § 7 and does not disturb ordinary claim-preclusion principles where a dismissal actually resolves a case's merits.

live-046: On Monday, Aug. 17, 2026, Judge Kimberly Fitzpatrick of the 342nd District Court in Tarrant County signed a temporary restraining order barring the Town of Westlake from "holding a vote on, approving, adopting, or taking any action to implement Resolution 26-25 concerning the Circle T Data Center," including at a special meeting set for that day, The Dallas Express reported. live-047: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit affirmed a district court judgment holding a hotel-loan guarantor personally liable for $3,954,244.04 after his borrower entities defaulted on a loan secured by three Texas hospitality properties and then, on the eve of a scheduled foreclosure sale, transferred ownership without lender consent and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. The decision in Access Point Financial, LLC v. Everhardt, No. 26-11169, is unpublished and therefore non-precedential, but it offers a clean, closely reasoned illustration of how far federal courts will go to enforce the bad boy, or non-recourse carve-out, provisions that are now standard in nearly every institutional commercial real estate loan. Access Point Financial, a Florida-based hospitality lender, loaned $56.33 million secured by hotel properties in the Houston, Austin, and Dallas-area submarkets to entities controlled by Charles Everhardt, who also signed a personal guaranty. When the borrowers fell behind, Access Point issued a notice of default and scheduled a foreclosure sale of the Houston and Dallas collateral for September 5, 2023. According to the record, the day before that sale, the entity holding the Houston property transferred 100% of its membership interests to 3 Big MMM, LLC, an entity affiliated with Ted Doukas, without seeking or obtaining Access Point's consent, a step the loan documents required before any change in ownership or control. That same day, under the newly installed management, the Houston borrower filed a voluntary Chapter 11 petition, which automatically stayed the scheduled foreclosure. Access Point sued in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia on September 18, 2023, alleging three independent full-recourse events under the guaranty: the Houston borrower's voluntary Chapter 11 petition, the unconsented replacement of Everhardt by DDI Equities as the borrowers' manager, and the unconsented transfer to 3 Big MMM. After foreclosure sales of the Dallas and Houston properties and an earlier sale of the Austin property, the borrowers still owed about $3 million plus interest. The district court granted summary judgment on the bankruptcy filing and the manager change and calculated that Everhardt owed $3,954,244.04. Everhardt appealed, arguing among other things that 3 Big MMM was not authorized to file the petition, so the Houston borrower had not 'filed' a voluntary petition within the meaning of the guaranty. A panel of Circuit Judges Newsom, Lagoa, and Brasher rejected that argument. Applying Georgia law, which construes guaranties strongly against the guarantor, the panel held that the guaranty did not require an 'authorized' or 'successful' petition, and that it was undisputed the Houston borrower had filed a voluntary Chapter 11 petition, which by itself triggered full recourse. Having resolved the appeal on the bankruptcy filing, the court did not decide whether the transfers to DDI or 3 Big MMM were also full-recourse events. It affirmed the district court's judgment, leaving Everhardt liable for the $3,954,244.04 deficiency. The ruling lands squarely within a well-established but frequently underestimated area of CRE finance risk. Nearly every institutional mortgage loan today is structured as non-recourse to the borrowing entity, with a separate guaranty from a principal that springs into full personal recourse if the borrower does specified things the lender considers bad-faith or value-destroying, commonly an unauthorized transfer of ownership or control, or a voluntary bankruptcy filing. Borrowers and their counsel sometimes treat these carve-outs as boilerplate, or assume that a transfer made under financial duress, or executed by someone other than the guarantor personally, will be viewed more sympathetically by courts. The Eleventh Circuit's opinion confirms the opposite: where a guaranty makes a borrower's voluntary bankruptcy petition a full-recourse event, the guarantor cannot escape liability by arguing that the petition was filed by new owners who lacked authority to file it. For CRE owners, developers, and guarantors, the case is a pointed reminder that eleventh-hour maneuvers around a scheduled foreclosure sale carry serious personal financial risk. Any transfer of membership or ownership interests in a borrowing entity, even one intended to install new management or bring in a rescue capital partner, should be run past the loan documents and, where required, past the lender, before it closes rather than after, and guarantors should assume that a subsequent bankruptcy filing by the transferred entity will be read by courts as part of the same chain of events they set off rather than as an independent act by an unrelated party, since arguing that new management lacked authority to file offered Everhardt no protection once the borrower's petition had been filed. Because so much of this exposure turns on definitions buried in loan agreements, including what counts as a Permitted Transfer, which entities need lender consent, and how control is defined, borrowers facing distress should have counsel review those provisions well before a default notice arrives rather than after a foreclosure sale is already on the calendar, bearing in mind that even an unpublished, non-precedential opinion like this one is likely to be cited persuasively by lenders' counsel in future carve-out disputes within the circuit.
live-048: Held Properties, a family-owned company, has sued WealthStone, a tenant at its 1880 Century Park East office tower in Century City, over unpaid rent, The Real Deal reported. WealthStone is a real estate firm run by brothers Andres and Jean Paul Szita, who also started the development company Laurus Corporation and its fundraising arm, Ethika Investments. The early August complaint says WealthStone "fell behind on payments" and "has failed and refused" to pay rent. This is the landlord's second suit against the tenant. Held Properties was awarded $393,000 in an earlier case and now says it is owed another $708,000 in back rent, other charges and interest. live-049: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court on Aug. 19, 2026 affirmed a Superior Court judgment allowing Boston's rebuild of White Stadium in Franklin Park to continue, WBUR reported. The project is a public-private partnership that splits its $325 million cost between the city and Boston Legacy FC, which is paying $190 million. The suit (SJC-13865) was brought by the Emerald Necklace Conservancy and 20 individual plaintiffs, who argued that the rebuild illegally privatizes public parkland and would require an act of the Legislature. Writing for the court, Justice Gabrielle R. Wolohojian first held that the plaintiffs have no cognizable individual interest in the George Robert White Fund, the public charitable trust that owns the stadium, and so lack standing to challenge alleged violations of its terms. The plaintiffs urged a more relaxed standing test because the Attorney General had decided not to bring an enforcement action. The court declined, holding that membership in an organization whose mission is in harmony with a trust's purpose, or recreational use of trust land as a member of the public, is not enough. On the main issue, the court held that the stadium parcel is not subject to Article 97 of the state constitution, which requires a two-thirds vote of the Legislature to dispose of parkland or convert it to another use. The city took the land by eminent domain for a public park in 1883, but a 1947 statute authorized conveying the parcel to the White Fund and a 1950 statute designated the stadium as a school building and yard. Together, the court held, those statutes removed the parcel from parkland status more than 20 years before Article 97 was ratified in 1972. The court also rejected the plaintiffs' challenges to planned uses of areas of Franklin Park outside the stadium parcel. Mayor Michelle Wu praised the decision and said construction was on track for a planned summer 2027 opening. The Conservancy's president said the group was disappointed and repeated its call for a smaller, fully public project, and Boston Legacy FC called the ruling a "tremendous victory," according to WBUR. The suit was filed in Superior Court on Feb. 20, 2024; after a three-day bench trial, the trial judge entered judgment for the defendants, and the SJC transferred the appeal from the Appeals Court on its own initiative.
live-050: Cushman & Wakefield has replaced SL Green Realty as property manager of Worldwide Plaza, the 49-story Midtown Manhattan office tower at 825 Eighth Ave., according to court filings reported by Bisnow on Aug. 10, 2026. According to the lawsuit as described by CPE, the 2017 loan was split into a $705 million CMBS loan and a $235 million companion loan, and beginning in 2025 the borrowers repeatedly missed or only partly made interest payments, including a payment of more than $2.9 million due Dec. 8, and did not pay $6.5 million of a $21.6 million tax bill in January. live-051: U.S. District Judge Nitza I. live-052: Wilmington Trust National Association, acting as trustee for a Redwood Trust Inc. subsidiary that holds the loans, has sued in the Circuit Court of Cook County to foreclose on 137 condominium units spread across seven Chicago buildings, along with the rents those units produce. live-053: A New York Supreme Court judge has ordered a foreclosure auction of 500 and 512 Seventh Avenue, two Midtown office buildings, to satisfy a $356 million debt, The Real Deal reported on Aug. 24, 2026. It says the Chetrit Group ran up more than $1 million in unpaid rent, and an attorney for the lender told the court the failure was "evidence of self-dealing or, at a minimum, severe negligence and mismanagement," given that the guarantor is an insider of the borrower. live-054: A commercial property owner's bid to strike down one of the steepest municipal reporting penalties in the country has failed, but not without a notable wrinkle. On August 6, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit affirmed a $4.8 million fine levied against The Retail Property Trust, the entity that holds title to Roosevelt Field, one of the largest shopping malls in the United States, for failing to file mandatory financial disclosures with Nassau County's Department of Assessment. The decision is a clean win for local tax authorities, but a separate opinion from one judge on the panel raises a constitutional question that could echo well beyond Long Island. At issue is Nassau County's Annual Statement of Income and Expense Law, known as the ASIE Law, which requires owners of income-producing commercial property to report detailed financial data, including rent rolls and operating expenses, to the county assessor each year. The purpose is straightforward: assessors cannot accurately value large commercial properties, and therefore cannot tax them fairly, without visibility into the income those properties actually generate. Owners who decline to comply do not face a flat penalty; the ASIE Law calculates fines as a percentage of the property's market value, an approach designed to make noncompliance costly in direct proportion to what is at stake. The Retail Property Trust, an entity within the ownership structure controlled by Simon Property Group, did not file the required statements for two consecutive years, and Nassau County assessed a cumulative fine of $4.8 million. Rather than pay and report, the Trust sued, arguing the ASIE Law's penalty scheme violates the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause, the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause, and several New York state-law provisions. The case had been working its way through the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York for years before the district court granted summary judgment in the county's favor, teeing up the appeal. The Second Circuit's core holding tracks a familiar proportionality analysis. Excessive Fines Clause claims turn on whether a penalty is grossly disproportional to the gravity of the underlying offense, a standard that looks at both the harm caused and the defendant's culpability. The panel reasoned that a $4.8 million fine, while large in absolute terms, amounts to a small fraction of one percent of the assessed value of a multi-hundred-million-dollar regional mall. Weighed against two straight years of willful noncompliance with a valid, generally applicable reporting law, rather than a one-time lapse or a good-faith interpretive dispute, the court found nothing grossly disproportional about the county's response, and the due process and state-law claims fared no better. The more consequential thread runs through a separate opinion by one member of the panel, who agreed the fine should stand but declined to join the majority's apparent assumption that the Excessive Fines Clause protects corporate entities in the first place. Whether a constitutional guarantee rooted in protecting individuals from punitive government overreach extends with equal force to corporate landowners has never been squarely resolved by the Supreme Court in this context, and the concurrence's skepticism signals the issue remains live even where, as here, it did not change the outcome. For commercial owners, the immediate lesson is procedural rather than constitutional: disclosure mandates like the ASIE Law are not paperwork to treat as optional, because the penalty structure is built to scale with exactly the kind of high-value assets that draw the least sympathy from reviewing courts, and owners in Nassau County and the growing number of jurisdictions with comparable income-and-expense reporting regimes should treat annual filing deadlines as fixed compliance obligations tied directly to dollar exposure rather than discretionary submissions weighed against the cost of preparing the underlying data. At the same time, the panel's internal disagreement over corporate standing under the Excessive Fines Clause is worth watching closely, since if that reasoning gains traction it could reshape how commercial owners contest not just ASIE-style penalties but a broader universe of value-linked regulatory fines, including code-violation penalties and rent-registration fines, that municipalities increasingly use as revenue and compliance tools against large corporate property owners; portfolio owners with holdings across multiple jurisdictions would be well served to audit their local reporting-compliance calendars now, given how readily other tax authorities appear to be adopting Nassau County's model.

live-060: The Arizona Supreme Court ruled unanimously on June 17, 2026 that a contractor may continue an unjust enrichment lawsuit against landowners who benefited from public infrastructure work, even without any direct contract between the contractor and those landowners. Chief Justice Ann A. Scott Timmer authored the opinion in Markham Contracting Co., Inc. v. Cahava Springs Phase I, Inc., et al., reversing lower courts that had dismissed the contractor's claims for lack of privity. The dispute grew out of a planned community development in Cave Creek, Arizona, where Markham Contracting agreed with a public improvement district to build roads, water lines, and related infrastructure. The landowners behind the project had helped create the district and agreed that special assessments on their parcels would fund its payment obligations to Markham. Partway through construction, a dispute arose and the district stopped paying. Markham took its claims to arbitration and won an award of roughly $6.5 million, but the district's limited assessment revenue left Markham unable to collect the full amount. Markham then sued the landowners directly for unjust enrichment, arguing they had authorized the district's creation, agreed to fund it, and received a tangible, uncompensated benefit in the form of completed infrastructure serving their land. The landowners moved to dismiss on the theory that their only legal relationship ran to the district, a separate entity, and that unjust enrichment could not substitute for a contract claim where no direct agreement existed between them and Markham. A trial court agreed and dismissed the claims, and the court of appeals affirmed in an unpublished decision. The Supreme Court reversed, holding that an owner who requests, authorizes, or accepts improvements performed by a contractor or subcontractor can be liable for unjust enrichment when it fails to compensate the party that actually did the work, regardless of whether a formal contract connects the two. The absence of privity, the court explained, is not fatal to an equitable claim designed precisely for situations where no adequate remedy at law exists between the party that performed the work and the party that benefited from it. The decision lands on a financing structure used well beyond Arizona: developers routinely fund infrastructure through special improvement districts, community facilities districts, or similar vehicles, with landowners agreeing to repay the district through assessments rather than carrying the debt directly. That approach is popular because it keeps infrastructure costs off the landowners' own balance sheets while still letting them control, through their role in creating and funding the district, how the work gets done. Markham confirms that structure will not fully insulate landowners if the district itself cannot pay, giving contractors and subcontractors left holding an uncollectible award added leverage to pursue the landowners who actually benefit from the finished work. Owners and developers using these structures should build reserves, guarantees, or completion bonds sufficient to cover potential assessment shortfalls, and counsel drafting district-formation and assessment documents should revisit indemnification provisions in light of the ruling, since Arizona courts have now made clear they will look past the financing structure to the party that received the benefit.

live-068: The Hawaii Intermediate Court of Appeals, in a published opinion by Judge Sonja M.P. live-080: Commercial property owners who buy surplus lines coverage rarely stop to ask what happens if their policy is split across a dozen different insurers, some domestic and some overseas, and a hurricane forces a coverage fight. On September 3, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit answered that question for Louisiana, holding that an arbitration clause in a surplus lines commercial property policy is unenforceable against the domestic insurers on the policy even though the identical clause remains enforceable against the foreign insurers subscribing to the very same contract. The underlying facts are unremarkable for coastal Louisiana. Transportation Consultants, Inc. owned commercial property insured under a surplus lines policy subscribed by nine domestic insurance companies and two foreign underwriters at Lloyd's of London. The policy contained a broad arbitration clause covering virtually any disagreement over the insurance, along with a contract allocation endorsement treating the policy as a series of separate bilateral contracts between the policyholder and each individual subscribing insurer rather than as one contract among many co-insurers. When Hurricane Ida damaged the insured property, a coverage dispute followed, and Transportation Consultants sued all eleven insurers together in Louisiana state court. The insurers removed the case to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, invoking the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards as the basis for federal jurisdiction given the Lloyd's syndicates' involvement. The district court initially granted the insurers' motion to compel arbitration across the board and stayed the entire case, then reversed course on reconsideration as to the nine domestic insurers, holding that Louisiana Revised Statutes 22:868, which generally voids policy provisions depriving Louisiana courts of jurisdiction over suits against an insurer, barred enforcement of the arbitration clause against insurers domiciled in the United States. The court lifted the litigation stay for those nine defendants while leaving the arbitration order intact for the two Lloyd's underwriters, whose contracts fell within the Convention's separate, preemptive framework for international arbitration agreements. On appeal, the Fifth Circuit affirmed that split result. Following its own recent precedents in Town of Vinton v. Indian Harbor Insurance Co. and Crescent City Surgical Operating Co. v. Interstate Fire & Casualty Co., the panel held that the Convention's preemptive reach over arbitration agreements extends only to the contracts between the policyholder and the foreign insurers, not to the parallel contracts, created by the same policy language and contract allocation endorsement, between the policyholder and the domestic insurers. Because those domestic contracts are governed by ordinary Louisiana law rather than the Convention, Section 22:868's anti-arbitration rule applies to them in full force. The court also rejected the domestic insurers' fallback argument that equitable estoppel should let them ride along with the enforceable arbitration obligations of their foreign co-subscribers simply because all eleven insurers signed the same policy form. The practical significance for commercial real estate owners and their brokers is direct: any surplus lines program covering Louisiana property that mixes domestic and foreign capacity now creates two separate dispute-resolution tracks that diverge the moment a claim is contested, one heading to court against the domestic carriers and one heading to arbitration against the foreign carriers, even though the underlying coverage grant and facts are identical. Sophisticated insureds should press their brokers at the placement stage for clarity on which subscribing markets are domestic versus foreign, since that distinction can otherwise sit unnoticed as boilerplate until a storm turns it into a jurisdictional battleground, and should budget for the real cost of potentially prosecuting the same coverage theory in two forums at once rather than assuming a single track will resolve the whole dispute.

The lender alleges the $25.4 million loan on 1816 North Clark Street, the site of Hotel Lincoln across from Lincoln Park, matured earlier this year without being repaid. It also claims $842,580 in accrued interest and default fees. The loan is on the land, not the hotel building. The suit seeks the fee simple interest and the landlord's rights at 1816 North Clark Street, and leaves intact the operating ground lease and the leasehold held by a separate Nakash-led entity that runs the 184-room hotel. The building has its own $35 million loan from Delaware Life Insurance Company, which The Real Deal said does not appear to have been securitized. The Nakash family bought the land and the building together for $73 million in 2016 from Neil Bluhm's Walton Street Capital. According to Morningstar loan data cited by The Real Deal, the land loan was originated by LStar Capital Finance in 2016 against a $30 million valuation. Ground-lease rent from the hotel entity covered debt service in 2025, but the appraisal was cut by nearly $6.4 million in May. After the maturity default the loan moved to special servicer LNR Partners. The borrower hired workout firm Iron Hound to negotiate an extension, but servicer updates show LNR filed suit while it was still waiting for a written proposal. Wilmington's attorney and representatives of LNR and the Nakash family did not immediately respond to The Real Deal's requests for comment. The publication also reported that Wells Fargo filed a separate foreclosure complaint in New York over the Nakash-owned retail space at 633 Third Avenue days earlier, and that the family has defaulted on a loan on the Ocean Drive Breakwater Hotel in Miami Beach.
live-088: The Alder at Lake Park LLC, an entity linked to Daniel Goldstein of New York-based Bofsa Properties, filed a federal lawsuit against the Town of Lake Park on Aug. 27, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, and amended its complaint the next day. Alder owns a seven-parcel site at Park Avenue and 10th Street in the Palm Beach County town, where it plans The Kelsey at Park Avenue, a mixed-use affordable housing project. The case is assigned to Judge Ed Artau. According to the complaint as reported by The Real Deal, the town persuaded Alder to buy and include a run-down historic building at 918 Park Avenue in exchange for a larger project and faster approvals, then repeatedly rejected the project and fined Alder daily for the building's condition. The complaint says shifting requirements forced Alder to cut the project from 720 to 426 units. It alleges Baird told Alder's team he would "never let Alder build what it wants" and that "all problems would go away" if Alder sold to a developer he had lined up, and that after Alder refused, Baird had a code officer issue 34 violations. Alder seeks an order barring further code fines, an order requiring the town to rule on its applications, and damages. In a statement to The Real Deal on behalf of himself and the town, Baird denied all the allegations against him, said the suit was meant to retaliate against him and town officials for doing their jobs, and said the town enforced its codes against Alder as it would against any owner that lets its properties decay. He said the owner admitted to code violations before the code magistrate, who found violations in six cases. Benjamin Diehl, a representative of Alder, said the team admitted no violations; Goldstein said no one disputes the current violations but called them "targeted" and "insignificant." "This is not about money," Goldstein told the publication. "We just want to get the project approved." The court docket shows a motion to dismiss filed Oct. 9, 2026, an Oct. 27 order referring the case to mediation and setting a schedule, and a response in opposition filed Nov. 13.
live-089: Friends of the Abajos, doing business as Kane Creek Development Watch, and the environmental nonprofit Living Rivers filed suit on February 10, 2026 in Utah's 7th Judicial District Court, The Salt Lake Tribune reported in a story first published by The Times-Independent. The defendants are Lt. Gov. Deidre M. Henderson in her official capacity, developer Kane Creek Preservation and Development LLC, the Echo Canyon preliminary municipality and the governing board's chair. The suit seeks to overturn SB258 and void Echo Canyon's certification, which would return land-use authority over the area to Grand County. SB258, a 2024 law, lets qualifying landowners on unincorporated land petition the lieutenant governor's office to form a transitional entity that can make zoning and certain infrastructure decisions while pursuing incorporation as a town. The entity cannot levy taxes. Its five-member board typically has four landowner-affiliated members and one county appointee, and the status lasts up to six years, or four years after the first certificate of occupancy, whichever comes first. Echo Canyon, a proposed 176-acre project near the Colorado River in the Kane Creek corridor, became the first certified preliminary municipality in June 2025; current plans call for about 478 housing units, 102 overnight accommodations and 67,000 square feet of commercial space. Projects in Summit, Morgan and Kane counties have also applied. The plaintiffs argue SB258 violates Utah constitutional bans on special laws, uniform-operation requirements and limits on delegating government power to unelected commissions, noting it allows a governing entity before any residents exist, applies only in certain lower-population counties and lets board members with a financial stake exercise municipal power. A Kane Creek Development Watch representative said the law appeared to be intended specifically for Echo Canyon. The developer said it is reviewing the suit with counsel, that the project "complies with all applicable requirements of SB 258," and that repeated challenges do not change its property rights or approvals already granted. The lieutenant governor's office said it typically does not comment on pending litigation. The same groups filed a separate case in 2025 seeking a ruling that the project's claimed groundwater and Colorado River water rights are invalid because they were not put to beneficial use for years; the developer disputes that claim.
live-090: Denver-based Four Mile Capital bought River's Edge, a 10-story, 212-unit apartment building at 505 Porter St. in Richmond's Manchester area, in 2021 for $47.5 million, Richmond BizSense reported. Four Mile sued the development team, Reynolds South Tower LLC, which includes principals of CMB Development and Purcell Construction Corp., in Richmond Circuit Court in May 2025. The suit alleges three counts of fraud, breach of contract, negligence and business conspiracy, and seeks more than $40 million and a jury trial. Four Mile says it knew of leaks before the sale and that the sellers agreed to make repairs before and after closing, but that Purcell refused further repairs in 2022. In 2023, a firm Four Mile hired reportedly found the building was 'not built in accordance with its design' and lacked waterproof sheathing Four Mile says it was told was there. Four Mile says the facade must be reclad at a cost of millions, requiring tenants to relocate. At an August 7, 2026 hearing, the defense sought dismissal of the fraud counts. Reynolds South argued Four Mile was not misled, had time for further inspections and accepted the repair work in writing before closing, and Purcell said it fulfilled its contractual responsibilities. In a September 21 opinion, McClenney largely denied the demurrer but sustained it on certain counts against Purcell, finding it was not a party to the sale and not contractually bound to Four Mile, BizSense reported on October 21. Four Mile amended its complaint on October 13 to drop Purcell from the breach of contract claim. Four Mile's attorney called the ruling a win; the defendants have denied wrongdoing, and no trial date has been set.
live-091: X Denver, a 12-story apartment complex that opened in 2021, is the subject of a receivership suit by its lender, BusinessDen reported. Its then-owner, Chicago-based The X Co., took out a $170 million loan on the property from New York's Mack Real Estate Group in January 2022. On Thursday, September 3, 2026, Mack sued in Denver District Court to have a receiver appointed, alleging the note has been in default since it matured in January 2025. BusinessDen said the current owner is unclear; Bisnow describes a 455-unit building at 3000 and 3100 Inca St., near Coors Field. Mack asked the court to appoint Trigild IVL LLC, and Denver District Court Judge Heidi Kutcher did so on Friday, October 9, Bisnow reported, citing the Denver Business Journal. Representatives of X Denver did not appear in court and had not responded to the lender's complaint. Under the order, they had three business days to give Trigild access to the building and to documents including current leases. Trigild will manage the property and may sell it if Mack approves, according to the DBJ. Trigild, which specializes in court-appointed receiverships, is also the receiver of Republic Plaza in Denver. Bisnow reported that The X Co. also defaulted on a loan tied to a Phoenix property, and that debt on the Phoenix and Denver properties was listed for sale in May 2025.
live-092: Rialto Capital, a Miami-based special servicer, has filed suit in Cook County to foreclose on the Calumet Center shopping center in Calumet City, Illinois, seeking $45.6 million, The Real Deal reported. The defendant is WC MRP Calumet Center, LLC, an entity backed by Austin developer Nate Paul. Rialto acts for the financial institutions that bought the pool of securitized loans that includes this one. Representatives of Paul's firm, World Class Holdings, and the lender's attorneys did not immediately respond to The Real Deal's requests for comment. According to Cook County records cited by The Real Deal, the Paul-backed entity bought the retail center, more than 159,000 square feet at 410-500 River Oaks West Road, for $7.7 million in 2014. It was later folded into a $38.3 million loan that German American Capital Corporation made in 2015 against six World Class-owned retail centers in Illinois, Iowa, Missouri and Oklahoma. The loan was then pooled with other commercial mortgages and sold to investors. The suit says an earlier alleged default led the lender to sue in 2022, and that case was dismissed after the borrower came back into compliance through a reinstatement agreement with Rialto signed about a year before this filing. That agreement called for $500,000 quarterly payments beginning in September 2025. According to the complaint, the borrower paid the first installment but not the December payment or the 2026 payments, Rialto sent a notice of default in January 2026, and it accelerated the debt in March. The lawsuit also says the lender has already foreclosed on the portfolio's Kansas City-area property in April 2026 with a $4.6 million credit bid and on its Oklahoma City-area property in July with a $7 million credit bid. Public loan data cited by The Real Deal shows the portfolio's combined appraised value fell from $56.6 million when the loan was made to $46.3 million as of December, and Fitch said in May that the loan makes up nearly 30 percent of the CMBS trust. The suit comes after Paul's federal criminal case. The Real Deal reported that federal authorities raided his offices in 2019, which led to charges that he submitted false financial statements to secure $172 million of loans, and that in April 2025, after he pleaded guilty to making false statements to financial institutions, a federal judge sentenced him to four months of home confinement, five years of supervised release and a $1 million fine.
live-093: Solera Multifamily, LLC and Hickory Investors, LLC allege they invested almost $3 million in Old Hickory Village, a 2022 real estate development in St. Peters, Missouri, and that Jeffrey J. Tegethoff and the development companies he owns used the money for other purposes, Missouri Lawyers Media reported. The plaintiffs say contractors were not paid on time, the project was delayed, and other investors had to make additional capital contributions that diluted their shares, and that a request to review the books was ignored. The suit, filed December 26, 2025 in the Eastern District of Missouri (No. 4:25-CV-1877-JMB), asserted breach of contract, breach of fiduciary duty, fraud in the inducement, state and federal securities fraud, theft and conversion, unjust enrichment and declaratory relief. The defendants moved to dismiss, arguing the fraud allegations lacked particularity.
