The plaintiffs did not respond to the motion and instead sought leave to file an amended complaint that dropped the federal securities claim; the defendants argued the change was meant to avoid federal limits on discovery. In a June 17, 2026 order, Judge Bodenhausen noted that the plaintiffs had 'wholly failed to respond' to the dismissal arguments but granted leave to amend under Rule 15's generous standard, denied the motion to dismiss without prejudice to refiling as to the non-bankrupt defendants, and stayed the case as to Tegethoff Development, LLC and Tegethoff Development Co, LLC, which had filed for Chapter 11. On September 22, 2026, the court stayed the whole case. The order notes that the automatic bankruptcy stay does not apply to non-bankrupt defendants, but finds it efficient to pause the case given the intertwined claims, denies a renewed motion to dismiss and a motion to stay discovery without prejudice, and requires status reports on the bankruptcy starting December 18, 2026. Lawyers for both sides did not respond to Missouri Lawyers Media's requests for comment.
live-094: Three family-owned businesses on Brentwood, Missouri's Manchester Road Corridor, Feather-Craft Fly Fishing, Time for Dinner and Convergence Dance and Body Center, along with the owners of the building Feather-Craft leases, sued the city in December 2023 over its designation of their properties as blighted, according to their attorneys, a public-interest firm. The designation would let the city use eminent domain to turn the land over to a private redeveloper. Reason reported that the designation supports a $436 million redevelopment plan and that the city's 2018 blight study by PGAV Planners relied on the corridor's floodplain location and other factors. In September 2025, after a four-day trial, Judge Kristine Allen Kerr ruled for the city, according to Reason and the plaintiffs' attorneys. She held that 'so long as substantial evidence exists on both sides,' the blight question is 'fairly debatable' and the city's determination stands, and she found the city did not act arbitrarily and capriciously. The court found that an $80 million flood mitigation project completed in 2022 reduced flood risk but did not fully resolve it, according to Reason; the plaintiffs' attorneys describe a $120 million city project to upgrade the streets and mitigate flooding in the corridor. The plaintiffs' attorneys argue the court applied the wrong standard of review and placed the burden on the plaintiffs, and say the ruling lets the city take 75 properties over conditions like peeling paint and cracked pavement on some of them. Brentwood officials did not respond to Reason's request for comment; the plaintiffs' attorneys said in October 2026 that the city has publicly downplayed the threat of eminent domain. The plaintiffs asked the Missouri Supreme Court to take the case, and on April 21, 2026 it denied their application to transfer it from the Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District, according to the court's minutes.
live-095: Wilmington Trust National Association filed suit on February 2, 2024 in Marion Superior Court to foreclose on Regions Tower, the 36-story office tower at 211 N. Pennsylvania St. in downtown Indianapolis, the Indianapolis Business Journal reported. The IBJ described Wilmington as acting as trustee, with Cleveland-based KeyBank as the debt servicer and Morgan Stanley Mortgage Capital Holdings LLC as the loan's owner. The defendants are owner entities NG 211 N. Pennsylvania St LLC and Regions Tower MF LLC; New York-based The Nightingale Group bought the tower in 2014 for $65 million. The suit says the owners missed an October 1, 2023 deadline to pay off the outstanding balance, and WISH-TV reported the owners owe $74,894,311.90. Wilmington asks for immediate repayment with interest and legal fees or, alternatively, foreclosure and a sheriff's sale, and asks the court to appoint a receiver from Riveron RTS LLC. JLL's Indianapolis office asked to keep its role as property manager. Completed in 1970 as Indiana National Bank's headquarters, the roughly 685,000-square-foot tower was Indiana's tallest building until 1982. It was about 75% occupied according to the building's website, and Regions Financial Corp. houses its Indiana operations there as a tenant, the IBJ reported. The paper called it at least the second major downtown office building to face foreclosure in six months, after Circle Tower. Neither outlet reported a response from the owners, and we have not found later reporting on a receivership or sale.
live-096: J.C. Hart Co. and Chase Development proposed The Elements, a $61 million apartment project on the former Willows Event Center property at 6729 Westfield Blvd., north of Broad Ripple. The Metropolitan Development Commission voted 8-0 on December 20, 2023 to approve a rezoning for 192 apartments and 16 town houses, sending it to the City-County Council for final adoption, the Indianapolis Business Journal reported. Oxbow Estates Homeowners Association, Spirit Lake Co-owners Association and two individuals with property abutting the site then sued the MDC, the developers and property owner Evergreen LLC in Marion County Superior Court. They argued the commission did not consider a 2003 set of commitments for property around Spirit Lake that limits density to 1.94 units per acre and can be enforced by owners within two properties or 660 feet of the rezoned land. The project covers 21.4 acres counting Spirit Lake, or about 8 acres without it, according to the IBJ. The neighbors said they would accept up to 144 units. J.C. Hart chairman John Hart called the suit "unfortunate" and said the claims were meritless. The project had already been scaled back once: Hart announced it in late 2021 with 256 apartments and 18 townhouses and withdrew the plan in mid-2022 amid opposition from nearby residents, the IBJ reported. On February 5, 2024, about 20 minutes into the council meeting, the developer and the neighbors reached a deal for 168 apartments with no condos or town houses, fewer ancillary buildings, a two-acre park, and a commitment from Hart not to develop other property it controls around Spirit Lake for at least five years after occupancy begins. The council approved the rezoning 24-0, with one abstention. The IBJ reported the lawsuit was expected to be dismissed with prejudice the next day; we have not confirmed the dismissal. Hart said in a statement that the company is "grateful that we have been able to work effectively with our neighbors."
live-097: Fairlane Town Center, which developer A. Alfred Taubman opened in Dearborn on March 2, 1976, has been in receivership since January 2026, the Detroit Free Press reported on July 9, 2026. Taubman Centers sold the mall to Starwood Retail Partners in 2014, Starwood sold it to Dallas-based Centennial in 2022, and Centennial sold it in April 2023 to New York-based Kohan Retail Investment Group. In January 2025, Crain's Detroit Business reported that the mall had avoided receivership in a lender's suit for the time being. Early in the week of July 9, one of Fairlane's lenders asked a Wayne County judge to declare the mall and its owner in default on a loan with an outstanding balance of more than $35 million, according to the Free Press. The paper reported that the owner has also owed millions in unpaid property taxes. The court-appointed receiver told the Free Press he is working on bidding and sale procedures for a future sale of the mall. A local attorney for Mike Kohan and the mall's main office did not respond to the paper's requests for comment. The mall's anchors include Macy's, JC Penney, H&M and a Powerhouse gym, and many storefronts remain occupied with scattered vacancies, the Free Press reported.
live-098: Waukesha State Bank filed a foreclosure suit on August 3, 2026 in Milwaukee County Circuit Court against 225 East Michigan Street LLC, the owner of the Mackie Building at 225 E. Michigan St. and an affiliate of developer J. Jeffers & Co., according to Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reporting republished by The Daily Reporter. The bank said the LLC defaulted on a five-year, $6.57 million loan due in June 2027 and owed $6.2 million, including $5.9 million in principal plus interest and fees. The bank also sued Jeffers & Co. and its CEO, Joshua Jeffers, in Waukesha County Circuit Court seeking a money judgment. Jeffers told the Journal Sentinel that the building's 25 apartments and smaller commercial tenants were performing well, but that The Grain Exchange, an event venue run by Bartolotta Restaurant Group, had not returned to its pre-pandemic level of business. The venue pays rent based on a percentage of its revenue, and Jeffers said the lower rent made it hard to cover the mortgage. Bartolotta's lease was winding down, with a renewal still under discussion. Jeffers' group bought the building in 2014 and completed a $14 million renovation in 2016 that turned three underused office floors into apartments. Both suits were dismissed by stipulation: the foreclosure through a September 14 order from Milwaukee County Circuit Judge William Pocan, and the money-judgment case through a September 15 order from Waukesha County Circuit Judge Zachary Wittchow, the Journal Sentinel reported. "The matter is resolved," Jeffers said. "The loan has been reinstated." Waukesha State Bank did not immediately respond to the paper's request for comment, and Bartolotta said it was pleased the matter was resolved quickly.
live-099: The Dayton's Project, New York developer 601W's $350 million redevelopment of the former Dayton's department store on Nicollet Mall into 1.2 million square feet of office and retail space, is headed toward foreclosure after a judge's recent ruling approving it, Axios Twin Cities reported on April 27, 2026. 601W owes lender Fortress Investment Group about $220 million in unpaid principal, interest and fees, while the city assesses the building at about $27 million. Axios reported in October 2024 that a Hennepin County judge placed the property in receivership on September 23, 2024, removing 601W from management and operations, according to court documents first reported by Twin Cities Business. Fortress Credit Corp. alleged in its complaint that 601W and its partner, Hightower Initiatives, had missed mortgage payments and owed $177 million in principal, interest and advances, and said it had put up nearly $4 million to avoid the "termination of various utilities and essential services." An attorney for 601W declined to comment at the time. The project launched in 2017 with plans that included an Andrew Zimmern-curated food hall. The building once reached 28% occupancy but is losing its largest tenant, accounting firm EY, and the food hall has been dropped, Axios reported. At a January 2026 hearing, a Fortress attorney said that if it forecloses, the lender will get "the privilege of owning an empty building that is going to require significant operating costs." Court filings indicate building out the remaining office space would cost about $110 per square foot. Fortress declined to comment on its plans, and 601W's attorney did not respond to Axios, so it was not clear whether 601W would appeal. No auction date had been set as of the April report.
live-100: The Foshay Tower, the 32-story Art Deco landmark in downtown Minneapolis that houses the 229-room W Minneapolis hotel, is scheduled for a foreclosure sale on December 18, 2026, Connect CRE reported, citing the Minneapolis/St. Paul Business Journal. The sale follows an August 25, 2026 ruling by a Hennepin County District Court judge that the tower's owner owes more than $42.3 million on a defaulted loan on the property at 821 S. Marquette Ave. Deutsche Bank filed the foreclosure complaint as trustee for bondholders in an affiliated commercial mortgage-backed securities trust, Weekly Real Estate News reported in April 2026, citing the Star Tribune. The suit alleged that the owners failed to pay off a $51 million mortgage that matured in May 2025, and asked the court to appoint a receiver to manage the property and to award roughly $43 million in unpaid principal, interest and fees. The tower was built in 1929 as the headquarters of utilities magnate Wilbur Foshay. It was Minneapolis's tallest building until the IDS Center was built in 1972, was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1978, and was converted from offices into a W hotel in 2008, according to Weekly Real Estate News.
live-101: Dillard's sued the owners of Winrock Town Center in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Mexico on December 1, 2022, naming Winrock Partners LLC and Integrated Property Services Company, according to the court docket. KRQE reported that the current developers bought the former Winrock Center in 2007 and gradually redeveloped it into an open-air, mixed-use town center, and that Dillard's alleges the work breached its 1992 lease, which promised an attractive and accessible shopping area. According to KRQE's account of the complaint, Dillard's says the developers demolished parts of the old mall and changed the parking lot without its written consent, including demolitions in 2016 and again from late 2019 that left several of its entrances closed or unfinished. Construction resumed in June 2022 to build an outdoor space that includes a park. Dillard's alleges that work blocked its entrances and parking, created safety hazards and at one point cut its phone, internet and alarm lines, and that the developers extended it about five months past an October completion date, into the holiday shopping season. Winrock representatives declined to comment to KRQE. The case is still in pretrial proceedings. The docket shows the defendants filed a counterclaim in June 2025, and on June 24, 2026, Magistrate Judge John F. Robbenhaar granted Dillard's motion to compel discovery. In late October and November 2026, the parties briefed a Dillard's motion for a protective order to block the deposition of a company executive.
live-102: Kansas-based Diode Ventures proposed Gemstone Technology Park, a 620-acre data center project in Kuna, Idaho. The Kuna City Council rezoned the farmland from agricultural to industrial on a 3-2 vote after hours of public comment, with Mayor Joe Stear breaking a tie in favor of the project, Idaho News 6 reported. The project is separate from a data center Meta Platforms is building in Kuna, BoiseDev noted. In August 2025, a neighboring farmer and two dairy companies, Toledo Dairy I LLC and Toledo Land Holdings LLC, petitioned for judicial review of the city's approval, according to BoiseDev. They argued that council member Greg McPherson, who voted on the project, should have recused himself because he was employed by the farmer and so had an economic conflict of interest. District Judge James Cawthon denied the petition in May 2026. He wrote that the evidence the farmer presented at the planning and zoning commission and council hearings "did not establish an immediate or direct economic impact," and that his concerns about traffic, possible rezoning of his own land and higher power rates were speculative or would be felt by the whole community. Without a direct conflict on the farmer's part, the judge found, McPherson was not required to recuse. The farmer and the Toledo entities appealed to the Idaho Supreme Court in June 2026.
live-103: William Martens, the owner of a commercial property in Nebraska, leased it to BB's Childcare, LLC and its principal, Tasha McNeil, under a written commercial lease executed in September 2020 for a childcare business. The lease ran an initial five-year term ending October 1, 2025, with options for second and third terms extending as far as June 2035, monthly rent of $3,000, and a default trigger of ninety days' non-payment. Notably, the lease also granted the tenants options to purchase the property in future terms, credited a portion of rent payments toward that purchase price, and restricted Martens's ability to sell the property to a third party without first offering the tenants a chance to exercise their purchase option. In December 2023, Martens filed a forcible entry and detainer action in county court, alleging BB's Childcare had failed to pay rent as required. The tenants countered that the county court lacked subject matter jurisdiction, arguing that resolving the case required deciding a dispute over their equitable interest in the property itself -- something forcible entry and detainer's summary possession procedure isn't built to adjudicate. The Nebraska Supreme Court agreed. In its May 8, 2026 opinion (321 Neb. 335), the Court held that a forcible entry and detainer action is not the proper vehicle to resolve what is, in substance, a contract or title dispute between landlord and tenant, and that where a claimant's right to possession depends on resolving the defendant's separate legal or equitable rights in the property, the court must dismiss for want of jurisdiction. Because the lease's purchase options, rent credits, and right-of-first-refusal provisions gave the tenants an equitable interest bound up with the rent dispute, the Court vacated the judgment below and remanded with instructions to dismiss the case for lack of jurisdiction. The ruling matters well beyond a single Nebraska strip-mall or standalone-building tenancy: any commercial landlord using a lease-to-own or lease-purchase structure -- common in build-to-suit deals for small commercial users like childcare centers, medical offices, or single-tenant retail -- now has clear Nebraska Supreme Court authority that a straightforward eviction filing may not be available once nonpayment intersects with the tenant's contractual path to ownership. Landlords in that position should expect to litigate rent and possession disputes in district court under ordinary civil procedure rather than through the faster forcible entry and detainer track, and should weigh that added litigation friction against the leasing incentive a purchase option provides.
live-104: AltEn ran an ethanol plant near Mead, Nebraska that turned pesticide-coated seed corn into fuel, according to the Nebraska Examiner. The state shut it down in February 2021 and filed its own lawsuit that year, which accuses AltEn of using pesticide-treated seed rather than the ordinary field corn its permit described and of improperly storing and disposing of byproduct. Seed companies that had worked with AltEn, organized as the AltEn Facility Response Group, took over the cleanup, which the Examiner said is privately funded and has removed a roughly 165,000-ton pile that included about 84,000 tons of contaminated byproduct. Pioneer Hi-Bred International and other seed companies sued AltEn and related entities in the U.S. District Court for the District of Nebraska on February 22, 2022 (No. 8:22-cv-00070, consolidated with Nos. 8:22-cv-00071 and 8:22-cv-00082). The court entered a preliminary injunction in each case on February 8, 2023. In 2025 the parties sought several extensions while they obtained subordination agreements required by the state environmental regulator and recorded environmental covenants, according to the docket. On November 26, 2025, Judge Brian C. Buescher accepted their joint stipulation, dismissed all claims with prejudice with each side bearing its own fees and costs, and dissolved the injunction. The Examiner reported that the deal limits the industrial property's future use, including a bar on using the land for homes, schools or child care facilities even after remediation, and keeps the state's access to sample the land and water. The Attorney General's suit in Saunders County District Court remains paused for settlement talks.
live-105: Fundamental Data obtained an air permit in 2025 for the Ridgeline project, which includes a natural-gas-fired power facility intended to support a planned data center complex near Thomas and Davis, according to the West Virginia Record. Tucker United, the West Virginia Highlands Conservancy, the Sierra Club and Friends of Blackwater brought two appeals, and Fundamental Data intervened. In No. 26-ICA-92, Tucker United, the Highlands Conservancy and the Sierra Club challenged a February 5 order of the Air Quality Board upholding the permit. The court held that a statutory exception requires such challenges to be filed in the Supreme Court of Appeals within 30 days unless all parties agree to proceed in Kanawha County Circuit Court. Because the parties did not agree, it dismissed the appeal as improvidently docketed, saying the outcome reflected a jurisdictional dispute rather than any lack of diligence by the petitioners. In No. 25-ICA-391, Tucker United, Friends of Blackwater and the Highlands Conservancy challenged the board's handling of a draft permit and Fundamental Data's claims that some of its materials were confidential business information. The court held that such challenges go to the circuit court of the county where the pollution originates, or to Kanawha County Circuit Court by agreement, and that the appeal was moot because the final permit had already been issued and appealed. It left the trade-secret questions and the merits for the final-permit appeal, and each side bears its own costs. Chief Judge Daniel W. Greear and Judge Charles O. Lorensen sought to recuse themselves after project opponents raised concerns about family and professional ties to Fundamental Data's outside counsel. The Supreme Court of Appeals granted the recusals in June and temporarily assigned circuit judges Shawn D. Nines and Gregory L. Howard Jr. to hear the cases.
live-107: In February 2019, Hembree Insurance Trust leased a 135,847-square-foot industrial building in Scottsboro, Alabama to Maples Industries, Inc. for five years, from January 1, 2020 through December 31, 2024. Maples, already in possession under a lease dating to 2011, was responsible for maintenance and for roof replacement or repair, with Hembree paying 50% of agreed roof replacement or major repair costs. Hembree sued on March 3, 2024, alleging Maples had failed to repair or replace the roof. Maples moved to dismiss, arguing Hembree did not own the property because a 2014 warranty deed showed it had transferred the building to Woods Cove Industrial Property, LLC. Hembree responded that it was Woods Cove's sole member, with authority under the LLC's operating agreement to manage it and act as its agent. On July 17, 2024, the Jackson Circuit Court treated the motion as one for summary judgment and declared the lease "null and void in all respects." The Alabama Supreme Court reversed on April 11, 2025, in an opinion by Chief Justice Stewart, Insurance Business reported. The Court held that a lessor need not own property to lease it if it lawfully possesses or controls it, and that under long-standing Alabama law a tenant in possession generally cannot dispute its landlord's title. Because Hembree placed Maples in possession, Maples paid rent and had the benefit of possession, Maples was estopped from challenging the lease on that basis. The Court did not decide whether fraud, misrepresentation or mistake claims could arise from the ownership issue. After remand, Hembree appealed again from the Jackson Circuit Court in the same case. On October 31, 2025, the Supreme Court affirmed without opinion; the order does not describe the judgment under review.
live-108: Hexagon US Federal, Inc. (HexFed) leased two bays in a building on Dunlop Boulevard in Huntsville from a related company, Intergraph Unimproved Properties, LLC, in 2015. A 2016 amended lease put both bays on a five-year term but stated the maximum rent for one bay only for 12 months. CBS Holdings, LLC bought the building in November 2016 and became the landlord. In July 2019 CBS Holdings first asserted that the bay's term had been 12 months; HexFed disputed that and stayed at the lease rate. In December 2020 HexFed sent notice renewing the lease, and CBS Holdings rejected it, citing among other reasons that the notice misstated the renewal rents. HexFed sued in April 2021 for a declaration that it had renewed and for breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment. CBS Holdings counterclaimed for breach of contract, ejectment and unjust enrichment and sought a landlord's lien. Following a December 18, 2023 bench trial, the Madison Circuit Court ruled for HexFed on all claims and counterclaims. It found CBS Holdings had waived its 12-month argument by accepting rent without objection and by signing a 2020 lease amendment without changing the term, reformed the lease to correct the parties' mutual mistake on the maximum rent, declared that HexFed had properly renewed, and awarded HexFed costs and attorneys' fees in an amount to be set later. The Alabama Supreme Court affirmed on October 18, 2024 (No. SC-2024-0077), holding among other things that the miscalculated rent in the renewal notice did not void a renewal sent with the required 90 days' written notice. It overruled CBS Holdings' application for rehearing on December 20, 2024. On April 16, 2024, after a hearing, the trial court awarded HexFed $174,987.45 in costs and attorneys' fees in a short order. CBS Holdings appealed, arguing that HexFed's invoices, with 449 of 458 charges fully redacted on privilege grounds, did not let the court judge whether the work was reasonable and necessary. On July 11, 2025 (No. SC-2024-0308), the Alabama Supreme Court agreed in an opinion by Justice Cook, holding that a fee application based on time spent must describe the billed work well enough for the court to calculate a fee, and that the order must show how the court calculated the award and considered the Peebles factors. It reversed and remanded with instructions. Justice Sellers, joined by Justices Wise and Bryan, concurred in the result. The lease dispute itself was resolved in HexFed's favor, with the trial court declaring HexFed entitled to occupy the space through at least March 31, 2026. What remained on remand was the amount of costs and fees CBS Holdings must pay.
live-109: Ready Capital Mortgage Financing 2023-FL 12, LLC filed a verified petition to foreclose on Drexel Flats, an apartment complex in southwest Oklahoma City, together with a motion to appoint a receiver, in Oklahoma County District Court on February 18, 2026 (No. CJ-2026-1275). The docket names as defendants the borrower entities Drexel Flats Acquisition LLC and Drexel Flats Acquisition TIC LLC, Marc Kulick, YSA Investments 1, LLC, several contractors and suppliers, and Oklahoma County's commissioners and treasurer. KFOR reported that M Group announced its acquisition of the property in 2021 in partnership with Vesta Capital, and that Kulick is CEO of Vesta Capital and Vesta Realty, which managed the property. According to KFOR, the loan was for $28 million and matured in January 2025, and court documents say more than $30 million is now owed; the station quoted the lender's filing as saying the borrowers 'have not turned over rents and other proceeds from the property.' Tenants told KFOR of overflowing trash, which the service provider attributed to nonpayment, along with security lights going out and repeated water shut-off notices. Vesta Realty did not respond to KFOR; the company previously told the station it takes 'resident health, safety and essential services seriously.' The borrower defendants opposed the receiver motion. After a hearing on May 20, 2026, Judge Amy Palumbo granted it, and an order appointing a receiver from Resolute Commercial Services, LLC was signed May 28. On June 3, the Drexel Flats entities posted a $200,000 cash appeal bond and filed a petition in error (Oklahoma Supreme Court No. 124122). Ready Capital moved for summary judgment on June 17. A suggestion of bankruptcy was filed for YSA Investments 1 on July 30, and the foreclosure claim against YSA was marked disposed on that basis. The summary-judgment hearing, reset several times, was continued on November 3 to December 4, 2026.
live-110: West Center Partners, LLC sued Thompson Thrift Construction, Inc. in Washington County Circuit Court in July 2019, alleging Thompson Thrift was responsible as prime contractor for construction defects in a Fayetteville student housing project West Center owned, according to the Arkansas Court of Appeals' opinion. The parties agree the project was substantially complete on August 14, 2014. On August 14, 2019, Thompson Thrift and its surety filed a third-party complaint against eight third-party defendants, including the project's architect, Modus Studio, PLLC, asserting negligence, contribution, breach of contract, breach of warranty and indemnity to the extent Thompson Thrift was liable to West Center. West Center then nonsuited to pursue arbitration, and on December 2, 2020 the circuit court dismissed Thompson Thrift's third-party complaint without prejudice as moot. In May 2022, after Thompson Thrift had subcontractors joined in the arbitration, the circuit court entered a declaratory judgment that West Center and Thompson Thrift could not arbitrate with four of them. West Center went on to win a $13,529,726 arbitration award against Thompson Thrift alone, which Thompson Thrift paid. Thompson Thrift refiled its claims 364 days after the 2020 dismissal, within the one-year window of Arkansas's savings statute, Ark. Code Ann. § 16-56-126, but more than seven years after substantial completion, outside the five-year statute of repose in § 16-56-112. The circuit court ruled the savings statute does not extend the repose periods. Only Modus was dismissed on that basis, because Thompson Thrift's contractual-indemnity claims against the other defendants are not subject to § 112, and the court certified the Modus ruling for immediate appeal under Rule 54(b) to avoid trying the case twice. In an opinion by Judge Brandon J. Harrison, joined by Judges Tucker and Thyer, the Court of Appeals reversed. The court held that § 112 sets a time to commence an action, that Thompson Thrift commenced its action in time, and that the savings statute therefore let it "commence a new action" within a year of the nonsuit. If the legislature had meant to exclude such claims from the savings statute, the court said, it would have said so more clearly.
live-111: The dispute began with a map the Mississippi Secretary of State published in 1994 to mark the line between private property and State-owned public trust tidelands along the coast. The map put a waterfront parcel south of U.S. 90 and west of Oak Street in Biloxi on the State's side of the line. The family that owns the land challenged the boundary in Harrison County Chancery Court in 1998, and the State countered that the land was artificial fill rather than part of the family's property, WLOX reported. The Supreme Court's opinion and the Sun Herald describe the parcel as about one acre; WLOX described it as 1.5 acres. In 2022 the chancellor ruled for the family. As WLOX summarized the ruling, it rested on a 1784 Spanish land grant at the root of the family's title, on the State's failure to follow the statutory procedures for drawing its map, and on insufficient proof that the fill was not oyster shells and dredge spoils deposited by outside parties. The State and Secretary of State Michael Watson appealed. The Supreme Court affirmed on April 4, 2024, in an opinion by Justice David Ishee. The Sun Herald reported that the court found the family's title traces to the Spanish grant and held that filled land built for "a higher public purpose" belongs to the upland owner. The City of Biloxi and Harrison County sided with the family. The Secretary of State's office told the Sun Herald it was still reviewing the opinion. The family once ran the Fisherman's Wharf restaurant on the site, and the land was leased for the Lady Luck Casino, which opened onshore in 1992 and closed in 1998, according to the Sun Herald. WLOX reported that the property is part of the planned Tullis Gardens Hotel & Casino project, whose developers were waiting on the ruling before applying for site approval, and that a pending bill, Senate Bill 2780, would bar the previously approved gaming site from being used for a casino again. The owner told WLOX the litigation had kept him from selling or leasing the land, and Harrison County's attorney said the decision matters for coastal waterfront owners, especially those whose titles trace to Spanish land grants.
live-112: The dispute concerns public trust tidelands at the foot of Veterans Avenue in Biloxi, where the Biloxi Port Commission had built a pier decades earlier without a tidelands lease from the Secretary of State; Hurricane Katrina destroyed that pier in 2005. On July 2, 2019, the City of Biloxi authorized an option agreement with RW Development, LLC to build and lease a new public municipal pier. Under the agreement, RW could use the pier as part of its adjacent commercial developments, but no gaming was allowed on the pier or on vessels docked there. On July 11, 2019, the State, through then-Secretary of State Delbert Hosemann as trustee of the public tidelands, sued the city and RW, seeking a declaration that a party must obtain a tidelands lease from the Secretary of State before building on tidelands, along with injunctive relief. Harrison County intervened as a defendant, and the case later proceeded in the name of Secretary of State Michael Watson. In April 2021 the county and city approved a joint lease to RW. In October 2021 the Harrison County Chancery Court, with Judge Jennifer T. Schloegel presiding, granted summary judgment to RW, finding the city and county had authority under the state's ports and harbors statutes and the Seawall Act to lease the property for public use. The Mississippi Supreme Court affirmed on March 2, 2023 (No. 2021-CA-01134-SCT). Writing for the en banc court, Justice Coleman held that Mississippi Code Sections 59-15-1 and 59-7-405 gave the city authority to acquire the site by reclamation and to build and lease the pier, and that the general statutes the State relied on must yield to those specific grants. The court noted that the county had rebuilt the sand beach with federal help after a 1947 hurricane and that the port commission had maintained a pier at the site for decades. WLOX reported in December 2023 that the Mississippi Gaming Commission had approved RW's site application for a casino at Veterans Avenue and Highway 90 after four tries in 16 years, along with a plan to rebuild the pier and make it handicapped accessible. RW's lawyer said the lease upheld by the courts helped win approval, while an attorney for opponents argued the lease limits the premises to non-gaming use. Officials said construction of the $3 million pier would begin before work on the casino site.
live-114: Service Credit Union (SCU) filed a 35-page, 10-count civil suit on June 24, 2026 in Grafton Superior Court over a $30 million construction loan it made for an assisted living campus at 1262 St. Johnsbury Road in Littleton, New Hampshire, the Caledonian Record reported in an article shared by NH Business Review. The plans called for more than 100 units, including cottages, apartments, assisted-living and memory care units, and a medical office building. According to the article, SCU is also seeking to move the unfinished campus into a different chapter of federal bankruptcy. The defendants include Granite Senior Services LLC, the company formed in 2018 for the development; Granite Senior Operations LLC; Blue Lodge Spray Foam LLC, a drywall and insulation business owned by one of the project's owners; CTC Commercial LLC, a mortgage broker's firm that had represented Granite Senior Operations since 2019; the project's two owners and related trusts; and the SCU loan officer who oversaw the loan until he was fired in July 2025. The claims are breach of contract, fraud, civil conspiracy, conversion, unjust enrichment and fraudulent transfer, plus gross negligence against the former loan officer, who SCU alleges acted beyond the scope of his job. SCU alleges the former officer falsely told the credit union that Granite Senior Services had put in its required $9.3 million of equity and quieted staff concerns about the shortfall, and that loan funds were used for personal purposes, including payments to Blue Lodge for spray foam when no buildings stood on the site. By March 2025, SCU had advanced more than $27.4 million, nearly the full loan. The suit also alleges that after problems with the loan surfaced, some defendants transferred interests in personal real estate in November and December to avoid repayment. SCU seeks $30 million from the former officer, Granite Senior Services, Blue Lodge and the two owners, and $1.5 million from CTC Commercial and two individuals connected to it. SCU's president and CEO said a former employee had violated the trust the credit union placed in him. The article did not include a response from the defendants.
live-115: A gunman opened fire in the food court of Greenwood Park Mall, south of Indianapolis, on July 17, 2022, killing three people before an armed bystander shot and killed him. A woman who was shot in the leg and her family sued the mall's owner, Simon Property Group, L.P., and its security contractor, Universal Protection Service, LLC (d/b/a Allied Universal Security Services), in Marion Superior Court in 2024. According to the Court of Appeals' June 9, 2025 opinion, the amended complaint alleges the gunman walked through the parking lot and into the mall past security patrols and cameras carrying a long backpack of the kind used for rifles, spent more than an hour in a food-court restroom stall assembling weapons, and that no security personnel were in the food court when the shooting began. Simon and Universal moved to dismiss, arguing a mall shooting is not foreseeable as a matter of law, so no duty arises. Judge Christina R. Klineman denied the motions on May 14, 2024, and the Court of Appeals affirmed on June 9, 2025. The Indiana Capital Chronicle described both courts as rejecting the dismissal bids on procedural grounds. At the January 15, 2026 argument, according to the Capital Chronicle, the family's attorney said the victims should be able to investigate the mall's security as the gunman passed at least a dozen cameras. Simon's attorney argued that seeing someone walk into a mall with a backpack does not put anyone on notice of a mass shooting, and pointed to Indiana law allowing people to carry guns openly. Justice Christopher Goff asked whether the security contractor should take steps to recognize a potential shooter; the attorney warned against 'judicially sanctioned profiling.' Wrongful-death suits by the families of the three people killed are on hold until the court rules.
live-116: The family of a man shot and killed at the mall has sued Houston's Galleria mall, its parent company and the security companies responsible for the property over his death, ABC13 reported on September 3, 2026. According to court documents cited by the station, He was killed on June 3, 2025, in a Galleria parking garage after leaving the mall with his fiancee and young child. The family alleges two men shot him after an altercation that began when the men harassed his fiancee. The Galleria is a Simon Property Group mall. The family's attorney said the case centers on allegations that the suspects had been banned from the mall but were able to come back. Videos posted to social media appear to show the men being removed by security several times, including the day before the shooting, according to the family and its attorney. The suit alleges the Galleria and its security providers were negligent in failing to enforce their own safety policies and keep the men out, and argues they should have had a system to identify barred people and stop them from returning. "This shooting was completely preventable if they had just followed their own procedure of enforcing the ban," the attorney told ABC13. The suit seeks more than $1 million in damages. ABC13 said it asked the public relations firm representing the Galleria and its parent company whether the suspects had been banned before the shooting and had not received a response by publication.
live-117: A shopper slipped on liquid in the soft drink aisle of the Publix on North John Young Parkway in Kissimmee, Florida on June 5, 2023, and sued Publix Super Markets, Inc. for negligence in Osceola County circuit court (Case No. 2024-CA-001128), according to News 6 (WKMG ClickOrlando) and a press release from her law firm. The firm said she later had three spinal surgeries, one on her neck and two on her back. After a six-day trial, the jury in February 2026 found Publix 100% responsible and awarded $3,967,000: $411,000 for past medical expenses, $556,000 for future medical expenses, $750,000 for past pain and suffering and related losses, and $2.25 million for future pain and suffering and related losses, News 6 reported. The firm said evidence showed employees had cleaned liquid in the same area before the fall. Publix denied liability throughout the case, argued she was not injured and tried to attribute her injuries to unrelated earlier complaints; the firm said Publix's last settlement offer before trial was $600,000. In March 2026, Publix moved for a new trial on all damages, arguing the court allowed evidence of inflated medical bills instead of the restricted evidence required by section 768.0427(2) of the Florida Statutes, News 6 reported. Alternatively, Publix asked the court to reduce the past economic damages award to just under $34,000. No ruling on the motion was found in the sources reviewed.
live-118: The longtime operator of the Original Saugus Café, a Santa Clarita restaurant whose history KHTS traces to the late 1800s, sued North Valley Construction Co. LLC and two individuals tied to the landlord family's trust on January 14, 2026 in Los Angeles County Superior Court's Chatsworth Courthouse, KHTS reported. The plaintiffs are the operator, individually and doing business as the café, and The Original Saugus Café LLC. The operator says he bought and began running the restaurant in 1998 and for nearly three decades operated under a month-to-month oral lease with the landlord family. He alleges that after the longtime landlord died in August 2025 he was told he had to sign a formal rental agreement to stay, and signed it under duress to avoid an immediate lockout, and that the lease wrongly stated the landlord supplied equipment and fixtures he says he owned. He also alleges the defendants tried in late August 2025 to file trademark applications for "The Original Saugus Café," "Saugus Café" and similar names without his consent, and that he was never formally told the property had been placed under North Valley Construction Co. LLC. On January 5, 2026, the operator says, he arrived to find the locks changed and a notice on the door saying the café would be "reopening under new management soon," and was kept from retrieving equipment, supplies, alcohol inventory and other property. The 16-count complaint includes breach of contract, improper self-help eviction under California Civil Code § 789.3, improper removal of tenant property, state and federal trademark infringement and unfair competition, conversion, interference and fraud-in-the-inducement claims. It alleges damages exceeding $1 million and seeks compensatory and punitive damages, attorney's fees and injunctive relief. KHTS noted the allegations have not been tested in court and reported no response from the defendants; a case management conference was set for June 23, 2026.
live-119: In 2013, the Texas Department of Transportation offered to buy the owners' property at 19502 Mueschke Road in Tomball for a new road along the Grand Parkway (State Highway 99), Texas Scorecard reported. After the owners pushed back, the State filed an eminent domain suit in 2014. That suit was dismissed when the owners agreed to sell at $1.05 per square foot. Years later, TxDOT said in an email that about 20,000 square feet of the property was surplus because Mueschke Road had been rerouted, but it denied a request to sell that land back. JRJ Pusok Holdings, LLC, standing in for the former owners according to Texas Scorecard, sued the State and the director of TxDOT's Right of Way Division in Harris County Civil Court at Law No. 4 to enforce the repurchase right in Chapter 21 of the Texas Property Code. The State argued the repurchase statutes did not apply because it acquired the land by settlement rather than a final condemnation judgment, that any repurchase would have to cover the whole parcel, and that sovereign immunity barred the suit. The trial court granted the State's plea and dismissed the case. On December 28, 2023, the Fourteenth Court of Appeals in Houston reversed the dismissal, finding a valid waiver of immunity and holding that the State acquired the property through eminent domain because it compelled the transfer by filing a condemnation action. The Supreme Court of Texas affirmed and remanded on June 12, 2026, holding, as quoted by Texas Scorecard, that the State has "no immunity from Chapter 21 claims to repurchase condemned property no longer necessary for public use." The opinion said repurchase claims derive from constitutional limits on the State's eminent domain power and that Chapter 21 permits repurchase of a portion of condemned property. Justice Bland wrote for the Court, joined by Justices Lehrmann, Devine, Busby, Huddle and Young; Justice Young also filed a concurrence, and Justice Hawkins dissented, joined by Justice Sullivan and, except as to Part III(A), Chief Justice Blacklock. The case returns to the trial court for proceedings on the merits. For owners whose land lies along a planned or existing road or utility corridor, the decision means a later reroute or smaller footprint can give the former owner an enforceable right to buy back the surplus land, even where the original acquisition settled before judgment.
live-120: In 2003, the City of San Antonio and Toyota Motor Manufacturing Texas entered into the Project Starbright Agreement to bring Toyota's manufacturing plant to newly annexed land on the city's South Side. A companion City Agreement addressed zoning within a three-mile "Enhanced Zoning Area" around the plant. In January 2004 the city rezoned a 97-acre tract, then owned by Presto Tierra LLC, to an industrial classification that does not permit multifamily housing, and in April 2017 rezoned it again at Presto Tierra's request. The tract was conveyed on June 29, 2017 to FLG Preserve, LLC, later renamed Southside Affordable Development, LLC, according to the appeals court's opinion. In 2022 and 2023, Southside sought to rezone about 34.5 acres of the tract for multifamily housing; in 2023 a council member and the City Attorney's office said the city would not support the project. Southside sued the city and Toyota on Dec. 4, 2023 in Bexar County's 285th Judicial District Court, alleging the agreement amounted to unconstitutional, illegal contract zoning and a taking of private property, and citing the Private Real Property Rights Preservation Act, KSAT reported. Southside said the land's value fell from $15 million to $3 million to $4 million. City Attorney Andy Segovia said the city would defend the suit, and Toyota declined to comment, according to KSAT. The Fourth Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's May 8, 2024 denial of the city's plea to the jurisdiction and rendered judgment dismissing Southside's claims against the city with prejudice. Writing for the panel, Justice H. Todd McCray held that Southside lacked standing because all of the challenged ordinances were adopted before it acquired the property, and it identified no assignment of Presto Tierra's claims, nor did its deed contain assignment language. The court held Southside was not an "owner" under the property-rights statute for the earlier ordinances, and that statements by council members or city staff "are not substitutes for an official act" of the city. A separate appeal by Toyota was dismissed and treated as a mandamus petition, which the court denied as moot after granting the city's appeal. In a footnote, the court said the ruling does not rule out standing for a future claim if the city formally denies a Southside rezoning request. The court of appeals issued its mandate on April 7, 2026, according to its docket.
live-121: ATC Indoor DAS LLC installs and maintains distributed antenna systems that improve wireless coverage inside large buildings. Through a predecessor, it entered a host lease with Collin Creek Mall, L.P., the owner of Collin Creek Mall in Plano, Texas. The lease let ATC license space to AT&T and Verizon, which paid ATC for better in-mall coverage, and ATC paid the landlord 25% of that revenue, according to the Texas Civil Justice League's summary of the case. Both carrier licenses ended automatically if ATC stopped being the tenant. By 2018 the mall was in serious financial trouble. MM CCM 48M, LLC bought it, assumed the lease and agreed to perform its covenants, including quiet enjoyment. A few months later, MM CCM 48M Leasing, LLC sent ATC a letter, as successor to the original landlord, ending the lease, saying the mall had closed and telling ATC to remove its equipment within 30 days. ATC removed the equipment, lost its carrier rent and sent the landlord its final 25% share, which was cashed. ATC sued for breach of contract and attorney's fees. The owner raised impossibility or impracticability, arguing that when the lease was signed it was not foreseeable the mall would lose its customers, and MM CCM 48M Leasing argued it was not a landlord under the lease. The 471st District Court of Collin County ruled for the owners, signing judgment on June 24, 2024. In an opinion by Justice Emily Miskel, the Fifth Court of Appeals reversed. The court's docket shows that a December 18, 2025 opinion was withdrawn and replaced by the January 29, 2026 memorandum opinion. The court held ATC proved as a matter of law that the owner was quasi-estopped from asserting impracticability, because it bought the mall knowing its condition, expressly agreed to perform the lease and performed for months. Separately, it held the defense failed as a matter of law because shifting market conditions, including a mall's loss of customers, do not make performance impracticable under Texas law. The court rendered judgment for ATC on breach of contract, found a fact issue on whether MM CCM 48M Leasing is a proper party, and remanded ATC's fee claim and its claims against MM CCM 48M Leasing. The mandate issued April 15, 2026. For buyers of retail properties, the ruling is a reminder that specialty leases such as antenna, rooftop and signage agreements can survive a mall's closing, and that assuming and performing such a lease makes it hard to argue later that the property's decline excuses performance.
live-122: The case concerns the Holiday Inn Club Vacations Galveston Seaside Resort. According to the court's opinion, the original owner, Silverleaf Resorts, Inc., contracted with CBRE to oversee and manage construction, with T&G as general contractor and with ACI for construction administration and oversight. Construction began in April 2014, Holiday Inn says it took control when it acquired Silverleaf in transactions ending in August 2016, and the City of Galveston issued a certificate of occupancy on October 13, 2016. During construction, a testing firm found water penetration at many tested windows and parts of the curtain wall; after repairs the windows passed retesting in May 2016, though the tester warned that some windows might leak later. Holiday Inn says it noticed water intrusion in fall 2019 and spring 2020, and an April 2020 consultant report attributed leaks to defective work on the pool terrace, parking garage, roof, exterior cladding and stucco, elevated walkways and windows. Holiday Inn sued CBRE in state court on October 8, 2020 and sued T&G and ACI in federal court the next day. The federal court dismissed that case for lack of diversity jurisdiction on May 5, 2023, and Holiday Inn refiled against T&G and ACI in state court on May 9, 2023. The 405th District Court of Galveston County granted summary judgment for all three defendants and signed a take-nothing judgment on December 4, 2023. In a memorandum opinion by Justice Kevin Jewell, the appeals court reversed. On limitations, it held that the discovery rule can apply to construction-defect claims, that Holiday Inn's pleading was not a judicial admission that it knew of the defects it sued over, and that CBRE had not shown that the leaks found during construction, or leaks reported in 2017 and 2018, were related to the damage in the 2020 report. T&G and ACI, which relied on CBRE's arguments, likewise failed to negate the discovery rule, and Holiday Inn raised fact issues on tolling for the period its claims were in federal court. The court also found fact issues on Holiday Inn's standing and capacity to sue CBRE as Silverleaf's assignee, and on the economic loss rule, citing expert evidence of moisture damage to structural components and mold that went beyond the subject of the CBRE contract. The court denied rehearing on March 20, 2025. The Supreme Court of Texas denied review on October 24, 2025, and the mandate issued on December 5, 2025, returning the case to the trial court for further proceedings.
live-124: According to DTSC, Halford's Cleaners operated a dry-cleaning business at 941 McHenry Avenue in Modesto from about 1948 to 2025 and allegedly discharged significant volumes of hazardous substances, mainly tetrachloroethylene (PCE), into the soil, contaminating groundwater and nearby sewer lines. The site, now called the Modesto Groundwater Contamination site, was placed on the U.S. EPA's National Priorities List in March 1989 after a city water supply well was contaminated with PCE from the site. DTSC said it took over operating the groundwater extraction and treatment system in 2012 and the monitoring well network in 2024. On February 26, 2026, DTSC and the Toxic Substances Control Account sued the property's owners in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, seeking recovery of response costs under CERCLA section 107(a) and declaratory relief. The complaint alleges the owners bought the property in 1974 and leased it to dry-cleaning operators from 1974 to 2025. It also states that the EPA sued the owners and a former operator in 2007, and that the owners resolved the EPA's claims in a 2011 consent decree to which DTSC was not a party. Under the consent decree, signed by Judge Mendez on July 7, 2026, the owners will pay a total of $2 million in installments. The decree states that the settling defendants do not admit liability. The court's order made the decree its final judgment and closed the case. DTSC announced the settlement on July 15, 2026.
live-125: The Mission LLC has proposed a 270-unit, eight-story housing development behind the Santa Barbara Mission, with 54 below-market units and three stories of underground parking, using California's "builder's remedy" provision to bypass zoning, the Santa Barbara Independent reported. The paper noted concerns about the site including flood zones, wetlands, a historic graveyard, known archaeological resources, an underground creek, landslide potential and traffic on a narrow exit road from a very high fire-risk area. In October 2025, state legislators passed SB 158, a budget trailer bill that removes builder's-remedy projects from an environmental-review exemption when they meet a set of criteria: a city of 85,000 to 95,000 people in a county of 440,000 to 455,000, a property of four acres or more, FEMA-identified floodways, state-identified wetlands and adjacency to a state historic landmark. The Independent reported that The Mission LLC's project appears to be the only one the law affects. The company sued the state and the city in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California on October 24, 2025, alleging the law illegally singles out its project and that the city lacks a compliant housing element. After a March 5, 2026 hearing on the motions to dismiss, Judge Vera ruled on June 2, 2026 that the case was not ripe because the project application remains under review, calling the complaint "woefully short" on specifics, and that the company had not met the requirements for an exception to the state's sovereign immunity, according to the Independent. He expressed no view on the merits but said SB 158 raises "serious constitutional questions," called the ripeness defects "eminently curable," and gave the company until June 22 to amend. The company did not respond to the Independent's request for comment. The CourtListener docket shows an amended complaint filed July 10, 2026, a renewed motion to dismiss filed July 24, 2026, and further entries on that motion in October and on November 2, 2026.
live-127: The Anchorage Community Development Authority filed a complaint on July 21, 2026 in state Superior Court against Hughes Family LLC and Anchorage Innovation District LLC, seeking a court-ordered sale of the former Nordstrom building at Sixth Avenue and D Street, the Anchorage Daily News reported on August 12. The three-story building has been vacant since 2019, when Nordstrom closed after 44 years there. ACDA owns 80% of the building, four of its five lots, according to the Daily News. The fifth lot belongs to Hughes Family LLC, which is owned by four individuals, and which has an agreement with Anchorage Innovation District LLC to develop its share. Anchorage Innovation District is owned and managed by entities tied to developer Mark Pfeffer. The complaint says ACDA is at "an impasse" with the two companies over how to redevelop the property and argues that the building cannot be divided with a party wall or partition. It asks the court to order all five lots sold and the proceeds split proportionally. In February 2026, Mayor Suzanne LaFrance's administration announced plans to convert the building into an "iconic development that would anchor downtown." At a July 17 Assembly committee presentation, ACDA director Mike Robbins said the project was more than a year from starting and that construction could begin next fall. Neither ACDA nor its attorney responded to the Daily News, and Hughes and Pfeffer Development did not respond to requests for comment. As of the article's publication, no further court action was scheduled. The Daily News later updated the article to clarify aspects of the Nordstrom and JCPenney garage projects.
live-129: LDG proposed Prospect Cove, a four-story, 198-unit affordable apartment complex for seniors in Prospect, a Louisville suburb, in 2016. According to LDG's counsel, Louisville Metro Council denied the project in 2017 after strong opposition from the City of Prospect and local residents. LDG sued Prospect and Metro that year, arguing, as Louisville Public Media summarized it, that the city opposed the project because of its association with low-income, senior, disabled and racial-minority residents. Louisville Metro settled with LDG, in a settlement LDG's counsel announced in December 2025, agreeing to pay $6 million and to make changes that include a smaller Metro Council role in zoning changes the Planning Commission approves unanimously, longer approval windows for affordable housing projects, and Fair Housing Act training for council members and staff. The claims against Prospect went to trial on August 10, 2026. After a two-week trial, the jury found for LDG on five of eight counts, including violations of the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Protection Clause, and awarded $36.3 million. Law360 reported that the jury found the suburb's officials conspired to block the project. Prospect Mayor Doug Farnsley said the city "disagrees with the jury's decision" and is evaluating its next steps. LDG has said it plans to break ground at the end of 2026 or early 2027. Louisville Public Media reported that the Kentucky Housing Corporation awarded LDG $26 million in tax-exempt bonds in August 2026, and an LDG spokesperson said construction costs have doubled since the suit began.
live-130: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court has ruled that the Town of Nahant may proceed with an eminent domain taking of roughly 12.5 acres of Northeastern University land on the town's East Point peninsula, reversing two lower court decisions that had sided with the university and reviving an eight-year dispute over whether a municipality can use its condemnation power to stop a private landowner's development plans. The decision, issued September 3, 2026 in Town of Nahant v. Northeastern University, is authored by Justice Elizabeth Dewar and turns on a question that reaches well beyond one small coastal town: how much scrutiny courts should give a municipality's stated public purpose when the same taking also happens to block a project the town opposed for other reasons. East Point is a roughly 28.7-acre peninsula that the federal government originally acquired by eminent domain in 1941 for a military installation before the land eventually passed into private and institutional hands, with Northeastern acquiring the bulk of the parcel and operating its Marine Science Center there, while the town retained a smaller parcel at the tip that it has long maintained as a public park. Tensions escalated in 2018, when Northeastern announced plans to expand the Marine Science Center with new construction on its undeveloped acreage, drawing organized opposition from residents concerned about losing one of the town's last significant stretches of open coastal land. Nahant voters in 2021 authorized the town's Board of Selectmen to acquire conservation and access easements over the disputed acreage through eminent domain, formally taking the position that the land should remain open space rather than campus infrastructure. Northeastern challenged the taking, and for several years the university had the better of the litigation. In April 2024, a judge of the Essex Superior Court invalidated Nahant's eminent domain order, concluding that the town had acted in bad faith because its dominant purpose was blocking the university's expansion rather than genuinely preserving the land for conservation, a distinction that matters because eminent domain doctrine requires that a taking serve an actual public purpose rather than functioning as pretext for a less legitimate objective. The Massachusetts Appeals Court affirmed that reasoning later that year, finding the town had no reasonable expectation of following through on dedicating the land to public conservation use. The Supreme Judicial Court reversed both rulings following oral argument on February 2, 2026. Justice Dewar's 43-page opinion did not dispute that blocking the university's expansion was one of the town's motivations, but held that a mixed motive does not defeat an otherwise genuine public purpose, pointing to Nahant's long-documented position, predating the current dispute, that it wanted the East Point acreage kept undeveloped. The court emphasized that a municipality's exercise of eminent domain authority is a legislative act entitled to a presumption of validity, and that courts should not substitute their own judgment for a town's on whether and when to take land for open space, recreation, or conservation purposes. With liability now resolved in the town's favor, the case moves to the compensation phase, where the dollar stakes will be determined. Nahant's own selectmen have estimated the taken interest is worth approximately $2.2 million, a figure Northeastern has signaled it will contest as too low, while the university had separately suggested the town could face damages of up to $9 million tied to construction delays if it abandoned the taking once compensation costs became clear, a scenario now considerably less likely given the SJC's ruling on the merits. A commission process under the supervision of a Superior Court judge is the typical mechanism for resolving contested just-compensation disputes of this kind in Massachusetts and is expected to take the better part of a year to resolve. The practical upshot for institutional and commercial landowners is that resisting a municipal taking by pointing to mixed motives is now a harder path in Massachusetts: a town's independently documented conservation or open-space rationale can coexist with, and survive scrutiny alongside, an intent to stop a disfavored project, so a challenge needs to show the stated public purpose itself is not credible or documented rather than simply that the town also wanted to block the development. Landowners should also expect that liability and compensation are fought as separate battles, with valuation disputes like the one now looming between Nahant and Northeastern often taking months to resolve even after the taking itself is upheld, and municipalities eyeing eminent domain as a tool against unwanted institutional expansion would be well served to build a contemporaneous public record, through votes, open-space plans, and public statements, of an independent, legitimate purpose well before a specific development dispute arises.
live-131: Jovia Financial Federal Credit Union, based in Westbury, New York, has sued to foreclose on a 10-story office building in Chicago's South Loop, The Real Deal reported. The September 4, 2026 complaint, filed in Cook County Circuit Court, names S Indiana Avenue LLC, an entity controlled by Lakewood, New Jersey investor Reuven Y. Rivlin, and seeks $17.1 million. Jovia alleges the borrower defaulted on a $17.5 million mortgage on the 129,200-square-foot building, built in 1996 at 1911-1921 South Indiana Avenue, after a three-month forbearance agreement expired in June. Neither Rivlin nor Jovia's attorneys responded to The Real Deal's requests for comment. The complaint also seeks to hold Rivlin personally liable under an unlimited guaranty he signed in 2022 as part of the loan, which would let the credit union pursue him for the full $17.1 million balance whatever the foreclosure produces. Rivlin's entity bought the building on December 31, 2021 for $14 million and took the $17.5 million loan from Jovia on January 5, 2022. The Real Deal noted that court filings do not say how the loan proceeds above the purchase price were used. The default traces to the Illinois Department of Central Management Services, which leased 129,126 square feet on behalf of the Department of Children and Family Services. According to the lender's court filings, the state stopped paying rent after December 2025. A CMS spokesperson told The Real Deal that 'this lease was terminated for cause per the terms of the lease.' City records show more than three dozen open code violations at the building since 2024 and several failed inspections, and the City of Chicago sued the landlord in August 2024 seeking more than $39,000 in fines and penalties, a case still pending in the circuit court's municipal division. After the lease ended, the borrower filed a claim against CMS in the Illinois Court of Claims seeking unpaid 2026 rent and property tax escalation payments for 2024 and 2025. In January, the property tax appeal firm Schmidt Salzman & Moran filed a lien of nearly $52,000 against the property over unpaid legal fees, according to county records. The Real Deal also reported that three days before the foreclosure was filed, Rivlin's company ABS Management announced a nationwide office and retail acquisition strategy.
live-132: Portland Music Holdings LLC, the company behind a proposed 3,300-seat concert venue at the corner of Cumberland Avenue and Myrtle Street next to Merrill Auditorium, sued the City of Portland in federal court on June 9, 2026, the Portland Press Herald reported. The company had told the city in May that it planned to sue, less than a month after the City Council's April vote to create a buffer between large music venues. The court docket lists the case as a civil-rights claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983. The complaint alleges that the "actual reason" councilors voted for a 180-day moratorium before passing the buffer was that some members had a "personal animosity" toward the company and Live Nation and were trying to shield other venues from competition, the Press Herald reported. It calls the retroactive zoning changes "fundamentally unfair and an abuse of power" and notes the Planning Board had unanimously opposed the buffer. The project had drawn opposition from local musicians, independent venues and residents concerned about traffic and pedestrian safety near City Hall. Live Nation, which said in May it no longer had an interest in the venue or the company, is not part of the suit. A city spokesperson said officials do not comment on pending litigation. Councilor Wes Pelletier, who sponsored the buffer, said he was confident in the city's legal standing, and Councilor Ben Grant had argued at the April vote that the council had authority to adopt the retroactive moratorium and zoning changes. The city moved to dismiss the complaint on July 21, 2026; the parties consented to have Magistrate Judge John C. Nivison decide the case, and he heard oral argument on the motion on September 30, 2026, according to the docket.
live-133: In June 2024, KKR Real Estate Finance Trust lent Lubert-Adler Real Estate Funds and Keystone Development + Investment $83.7 million to buy Philadelphia's 131-year-old Bourse building and convert part of it into a hotel, and to buy 400 Market St., which was converted into apartments as planned, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported. The loan required the hotel project to be near completion by the end of May 2026. KKR says 400 Market is not part of its lawsuit. On July 28, 2026, KREF Capital LLC sued LAK Bourse Owner, LLC and LAK Bourse Master HTC Landlord, LLC in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. According to the Inquirer, the complaint says the development team "abandoned its plans" for the hotel and stopped conversion work earlier in 2026, defaulting the mortgage with more than $24 million in principal outstanding, and that the owners missed mortgage payments starting in June. It sought a $24.2 million judgment plus interest and fees and a public auction of the building. At least five contractors had filed more than $2 million in liens for unpaid work, the paper reported. The suit followed a breakup between real estate investor Dean Adler and Keystone. Adler decided to scrap the hotel and event-space plan and, according to the Philadelphia Business Journal, planned to work with PMC Property Group on a multifamily conversion. Keystone sued Adler in Delaware Chancery Court for breach of contract, alleging he failed to provide promised funding, and Adler countersued, accusing Keystone of unauthorized spending and "gross negligence." In a March ruling reported by Law360, a judge rejected Adler's attempt to oust Keystone and kept Keystone in control of the project, the Inquirer said. Keystone declined to comment on the lawsuit but said it remained "confident" it would prevail against Adler in Delaware. Adler told the Inquirer he believed the Keystone case was near resolution, that KKR's potential foreclosure would follow, and that the Bourse would be revitalized as 400 Market was. On October 12, 2026, KREF Capital filed a notice voluntarily dismissing the federal case under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(a)(1)(A)(i); the notice gives no reason.
live-134: Unit owners at the Palm Beach Marriott Singer Island, a 239-unit hotel-condominium at 3800 North Ocean Drive in Riviera Beach, Florida, have spent more than a decade in court with the hotel's owner, Urgo Hotels, over fees they call unfair and duplicative, The Real Deal reported. The condo association sued Urgo in 2015, claiming owners were billed for maintaining shared hotel facilities with no assurance the charges were fair. In August 2026, association attorneys Stevan Pardo and Greg Weiss asked the court for punitive damages and a temporary stay of the fees while the case awaits trial early next year. Maryland-based Urgo, led by CEO Donald Urgo, bought the building in 2009 for $7.1 million from developer WCI Communities and rebranded it under the Marriott flag. The association first sued Urgo in 2010 over shared-facility maintenance charges, and that case settled in 2013, according to court documents. Owners later said the overcharging continued and asked Urgo for its accounting records; after Urgo produced an audit, they accused it of using an arbitrary formula, not its actual expenses, to set shared-facility costs. One disputed charge is an administrative fee of about $45 for each day a unit is occupied, which court records say covers the cost of 'integrating' hotel guests into the building. Owners also pay a quarterly assessment for shared facilities, and the suit claims both charges are excessive and make owners pay twice for the same upkeep. Pardo told The Real Deal the fees collected since 2013 could total more than $45 million. Urgo's lawyers have argued in court filings that the 2010 case, which was settled, barred this lawsuit from going forward. The company also says some owners no longer back the suit and that the association's board put off elections to keep opponents from gaining control. Ronald Gache, a lawyer for Urgo and its entity UH-SI LLC, declined to comment to The Real Deal. Association president Marina Shtutman told the publication the board would prefer to avoid long, costly litigation but sees the courts as the only way to hold Urgo accountable.
live-135: Soros Fund Management took back 224 West 57th Street at a foreclosure auction on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, Crain's New York Business reported. The Billionaires Row office building, linked to George Soros, was one of two Midtown towers sold back to their lenders that day; the other was a former headquarters of the Chetrit family. Crain's reported that the foreclosure judgment against owner Eretz Group was $158.7 million. Eretz bought the building in 2015 for $213.8 million and in 2018 borrowed $145 million from Aareal Capital to refinance it, The Real Deal reported in 2024, citing Crain's. Soros Fund, which bought the note from Aareal in the fall of 2023, filed its foreclosure suit in April 2024, alleging Eretz failed to repay the principal by June 2023, the loan's deadline after two extensions. The Open Society Foundations, the grant-making group Soros founded, occupies the office space under a lease running through 2042. Eretz has alleged that Soros Fund's purchase of the mortgage and its foreclosure were part of a scheme to let Open Society leave its lease early, arguing that taking the property through foreclosure would cost less than the penalties for ending the lease before 2042. Counsel for Eretz told Crain's that the company's "efforts to repay the mortgage and redeem the property apparently were stymied by forces beyond control." On September 16, 2026, Commercial Observer reported that Soros Fund Management had put the building up for sale at roughly $100 million and, citing The Real Deal, that Open Society plans to move out once a deal closes.
live-136: Former owners of a 474-unit apartment complex in College Park, Georgia have sued Arbor Realty Trust, alleging the lender kept them on a high-interest bridge loan by promising a later refinancing and then foreclosed, The Real Deal reported. Brothers Yisroel and Hanoch Cimerring filed the suit in late March 2026 in New York state court and seek $175 million in damages. 'Arbor firmly denies all allegations,' a spokesperson told The Real Deal, adding that the owners mismanaged the property, that Arbor foreclosed after monetary defaults, and that it will seek a deficiency judgment for the balance owed. According to the complaint, the brothers bought the complex, Chelsea Gardens Apartments at 2135 Godby Road, in 2022 for nearly $45 million with a $37.1 million bridge loan from an Arbor affiliate, paying more than $350,000 for a rate cap that held the rate at 5.75 percent for two years. They say they spent more than $4 million on renovations, raised occupancy from 50 to 90 percent and reached a $55 million appraisal. When they sought permanent financing in late 2023, they allege, Arbor ordered repeated inspections, demanded hundreds of thousands of dollars in immediate repairs, never approached Fannie Mae and delayed sending the loan to its loan committee. They also allege Velocity Consulting downgraded the property's rating below Fannie Mae's refinancing standard as part of the scheme. After the rate cap expired in March 2024 the interest rate nearly doubled, the brothers defaulted, and an Arbor affiliate bought the property at a foreclosure auction for $40 million, the suit says. Arbor gives a different account in its June motion to dismiss. It argues the brothers sued to avoid a deficiency judgment in Georgia state court, where Arbor has asked the court to confirm the foreclosure sale. Arbor says it did contact Fannie Mae and obtained a pre-approval that depended on resolving the scope, budget and schedule of improvements, but it could not proceed because the owners refused to make repairs, including to fire-damaged units its engineer found on follow-up inspections in 2024. Arbor says it then modified the loan and released renovation funds to help the owners keep paying, but they defaulted anyway and its affiliate was the only bidder at the public auction. Velocity's lawyer, Neal Klausner of Davis + Gilbert, told The Real Deal the single claim against the firm 'is completely without merit' and that Velocity has moved to dismiss.
live-137: Joshua Schuster, a former New York real estate developer, was sentenced on August 11, 2026 to four years in federal prison and three years of supervised release, The Real Deal reported. U.S. District Judge Valerie E. Caproni of the Southern District of New York imposed the sentence after Schuster pleaded guilty to one count of securities fraud, which carries a maximum of 20 years. The Real Deal described the scheme as a $13 million Ponzi scheme. The court's judgment orders Schuster to forfeit $13,830,665 under a consent preliminary order of forfeiture and money judgment signed the same day. The court docket shows a two-count indictment filed on May 6, 2025 and unsealed the next day, when Schuster was arrested in the Southern District of Florida. He first pleaded not guilty, then on February 27, 2026 pleaded guilty to Count Two; the remaining count was dismissed at sentencing on the government's motion. A later defense filing describes the offense conduct as tied to his former work in real estate. At the sentencing hearing, Schuster told the judge that drugs and alcohol had sent his life out of control, that he had been sober for four years and that he was no longer the man who lied to and stole from his investors, according to The Real Deal. Judge Caproni questioned whether the change was real, noting that after moving to Boca Raton, Florida, he rented an expensive house and bought a Ford Bronco while his wife drives a Mercedes-Benz. 'I don't think you've given up the desire to look like you're successful,' she said. She denied his request for home confinement, saying the sentence should deter white-collar crime; the federal guidelines range was 4.25 to 5.25 years. The judgment deferred the restitution decision, and the court entered an order of restitution on October 7, 2026, followed by an amended judgment on October 13.
