Schuster had been due to surrender to the Bureau of Prisons on October 20, 2026; on October 5 the court moved the date to November 17, 2026 and said it would not be extended again.
live-138: The Wyoming Supreme Court on February 2, 2026 revived a $14 million lawsuit by Gunwerks, LLC, a maker of custom guns and optics, over the manufacturing facility built for it in Cody, Cowboy State Daily reported. In a unanimous opinion by Justice Bridget Hill, Gunwerks, LLC v. Forward Cody Wyoming, Inc., 2026 WY 16, the court reversed the Park County District Court's dismissal of Gunwerks' claims against architect Plan One Architects and contractor Sletten Construction of Wyoming, Inc., and also reversed its grant of summary judgment to Forward Cody Wyoming, Inc. Because only a community could receive money from the Wyoming Business Council's Business Ready Communities program, Gunwerks worked with the City of Cody and Forward Cody, a nonprofit economic development group, to obtain a $3 million grant and a $3 million loan for the building, according to the opinion and Cowboy State Daily. Gunwerks provided the land and was to lease the facility from Forward Cody with an option to buy it. Forward Cody hired Plan One to design the facility and Sletten to build it; Gunwerks signed neither contract. Gunwerks alleges the finished building had poor climate control, pervasive water leaks, a failing shooting tunnel and crumbling concrete, and the opinion notes a 157-page punch list of construction issues. Gunwerks sued Forward Cody in 2021 and added the architect and contractor in 2022, Cowboy State Daily reported. Forward Cody disputes the $14 million figure, which its brief says includes $7.44 million in what it calls speculative lost profits from a six-month shutdown, and argues Gunwerks tried to take control of the project. Plan One argued it owed Gunwerks no contractual duty. Justice Hill wrote that the city and Forward Cody "did not, one day, randomly decide to build a generic building," and that Gunwerks had negotiated with them to build it a custom manufacturing facility. The court held that Gunwerks had pleaded enough to proceed as an intended third-party beneficiary of the Plan One and Sletten contracts, and that Forward Cody had more duties than managing the $6 million. The case returns to the Park County District Court.
live-140: The foreclosure case over Jeff Sutton's retail property at 29 West 34th Street in Herald Square has been settled, The Real Deal reported. Helaba, the German bank formally named Landesbank Hessen-Thüringen Girozentrale, originated the $50 million mortgage in 2018. Sutton, whose net worth Forbes estimates at $2.7 billion, bought the property in a joint venture with SL Green in 2006 and bought out SL Green's stake a few years later. Sutton and the lawyers involved did not respond to The Real Deal's requests for comment.
live-143: An Orange County, Florida jury has returned a verdict of $644,751,855.08 against Soho WP and BE-1 Concept Holdings, the companies that owned and operated Park Social, a bar on the second story of a Winter Park building built in 1926, WKMG ClickOrlando reported on March 12, 2026. The station's report was based on a release from the plaintiff's law firm and did not give the date of the verdict. According to the release, the plaintiff, then 57, fell down a flight of about 20 stairs while leaving the bar in November 2017. The firm said the fall caused fractures in his neck and skull and left him partially quadriplegic, with no feeling from the chest down, and that he lost his senses of taste and smell. live-144: The Ruins, LLC filed for Chapter 11 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of North Dakota on January 6, 2025, and the case was converted to Chapter 7 on December 31, 2025, according to the court docket. Its main asset is a downtown Watertown, South Dakota redevelopment site at 315 E. Kemp Avenue known as The Ruins. Build, LLC, a company owned by the project's original developer, won the trustee's auction with an $11.265 million bid, and the court entered a sale order on June 4, 2026, Northeast Radio SD reported. On July 7, the trustee moved to amend that order to list 16 separate mortgages, mechanic's liens and court claims so the sale would meet South Dakota title insurance requirements. Build objected and sued the trustee in an adversary case, and Red River State Bank, the primary secured lender, argued Build was trying to stall the closing. In late July, the trustee and Build agreed to a court-approved stipulation giving Build until August 14 to pay the price; if it did not, its deposit would go to the estate, its suit would be dismissed and the property would pass to the backup buyer. On August 17, Judge Hastings authorized the sale to Archer Land Co. free and clear of liens for $6,100,000, ordered Build's $1,126,500 earnest money turned over to the trustee, and dismissed Build's adversary case with prejudice. According to the station, after taxes, assessments, closing costs and commissions, the remaining proceeds go to Red River State Bank toward its $10.49 million mortgage cap, so second mortgage holder Watertown Development Company and more than a dozen contractors holding mechanic's liens are unlikely to be paid from the sale. In a separate case, Red River State Bank sued Generations on 1st, LLC, Craig Holdings, LLC, Watertown Development Company, Codington County and others in South Dakota's Third Judicial Circuit Court in Codington County, alleging defaults on promissory notes totaling more than $22 million secured by Watertown real estate, Hub City Radio reported in July 2024.
live-145: Proven Business Skills, Inc. filed a complaint on September 15, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas (No. 3:26-cv-03130) against Phoenix American Hospitality, LLC (PAH), American Hospitality Properties REIT, Inc., American Hospitality Properties REIT II, Inc. and PAH's president, according to the court docket. Plaintiff's counsel announced the filing in a Business Wire release on September 16. Fitzwater and was reassigned the same day to Senior Judge Jane J. Boyle. No response from the defendants on the merits has been reported.
live-146: Blue Sky Towers IV LLC, suing on its own behalf and for the benefit of Cellco Partnership d/b/a Verizon Wireless, filed suit on September 11, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine against the Town of Waldoboro, its Board of Appeals and its Planning Board, Wireless Estimator reported on September 15. The company wants to build a 194-foot self-support tower at 2734 Friendship Road in South Waldoboro, with Verizon antennas at 190 feet, to fill what it says are coverage gaps along Route 220, Finntown Road, Back Cove Road and nearby areas. The case (No. 2:26-cv-00440) is assigned to Judge Stacey D. Neumann. Waldoboro's Rural Zoning District allows wireless facilities with Planning Board site-plan approval, but a separate provision limits them to within 300 yards of Route 1; the site is about five miles away. Blue Sky sought a dimensional variance. Town attorney Amy K. Tchao advised that the provision is a location requirement rather than a setback, that Maine law left the Board of Appeals without jurisdiction to vary it, and that the federal effective-prohibition question belonged to the courts. The board unanimously denied the variance on August 20, 2026. The complaint also alleges that the Planning Board chairman spoke against the tower at a July 9 hearing and later recused himself at Blue Sky's request. The complaint claims the denial effectively prohibits personal wireless services under Section 332(c)(7) of the Telecommunications Act and was not supported by substantial evidence, and adds a state-law claim that the board erred by not considering the effective-prohibition issue. Blue Sky seeks expedited review, a declaration that the 300-yard rule is invalid as applied, an order requiring site-plan approval within 30 days after it resumes its application, and costs and attorneys' fees. A separate federal docket shows that Blue Sky Towers III LLC sued the Town of Nobleboro's Appeals Board in February 2026; that case closed in May 2026.
live-147: Commercial property owners and the convenience-store and retail operators that occupy their sites received a reminder in May that the 'open and obvious' defense to a premises-liability claim is narrower than many defendants assume, particularly where an employee actively creates the hazardous condition. In Lewis v. Circle K Stores Inc., the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed a grant of summary judgment for the store operator, holding that a jury should decide whether a wet, freshly cleaned parking-lot surface was truly open and obvious and whether the plaintiff needed expert testimony to prove what caused his fall. The case arose after Jonathan Lewis was injured leaving a Circle K convenience store in South Carolina. A store employee had just cleaned a painted line in the parking lot using water and a powdered concrete cleaner, and according to the complaint no warning signs, cones, or hazard markers were placed around the area despite the store's own internal policies calling for such warnings. Lewis slipped on the wet surface exiting the store and severely injured his right leg. The case was removed to the U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina, where the district court granted Circle K summary judgment on three grounds: that the wet, visibly cleaned surface was an open and obvious hazard eliminating any duty to warn, that the specific risk was not foreseeable, and that Lewis lacked expert testimony establishing causation. On appeal, a Fourth Circuit panel led by Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III, joined by Judges Julius N. Richardson and Toby Heytens, rejected all three grounds and reversed. The panel held that genuine disputes of material fact remained as to whether the hazard was truly open and obvious given that a store employee had just created the condition and no warning was posted despite an internal policy requiring one, and that a jury could conclude the danger was less apparent to a departing customer than the district court assumed. The panel also held expert testimony is not categorically required to establish causation on facts of this kind, where a jury could rely on ordinary experience and timing to connect the wet surface to the fall. The ruling matters beyond one convenience store because open-and-obvious is among the most heavily litigated defenses in commercial premises-liability practice, and is frequently resolved at summary judgment before trial exposure materializes. The opinion signals that visibility of a wet or altered surface alone does not automatically satisfy the defense, particularly where a defendant's own employee created the condition and its own internal protocols called for an unheeded warning — and that combination of a self-created hazard plus a documented, unfollowed policy gave the panel enough to find a reasonable jury could see the case differently than the trial judge did on a cold summary-judgment record. Commercial landlords, retail and convenience-store operators, and insurers should treat the case as a prompt to audit actual compliance with cleaning and maintenance warning protocols, not just their existence on paper, and to confirm lease indemnification and insurance coverage account for liability arising from a tenant-operator's own maintenance activities. The case now returns to the District of South Carolina for further proceedings, most likely trial, since the Fourth Circuit's ruling only restores Lewis's right to have a jury hear the case rather than resolving liability itself.
live-148: Clark County District Judge Maria Gall on July 28, 2026 approved a motion by court-appointed receiver Logic Commercial Real Estate to sell the Hughes Center, at Flamingo and Paradise roads a mile east of the Las Vegas Strip, to Borden Industries, the Las Vegas Review-Journal reported. The order approved the purchase agreement and authorized Logic to close; Logic's motion said the sale was expected to close around September 2026. The price was redacted from the purchase agreement filed in court, and Logic moved to seal the deal's terms, arguing they were confidential and still being negotiated and that the public had little interest in them, the Review-Journal reported. In Clark County, a sale price is routinely public once a deed is recorded after closing. Blackstone bought the office park in 2013 for $347 million. The complex later lost tenants to newer buildings in the southwest Las Vegas Valley and Summerlin, and by 2023 the landlord had reportedly stopped making payments on its $325 million loan. In 2024, District Judge Susan Johnson appointed Logic as receiver. A Logic filing put office vacancy at about 61 percent, while about 85 percent of the property's roughly 98,000 square feet of retail space was occupied. CBRE was hired to find a buyer, and Borden Industries' website describes plans to redevelop the property.
live-149: An affiliate of Miami developer OKO Group, led by billionaire Vlad Doronin, has sued four insurers for $22.4 million it says they still owe on a builder's-risk claim for the Missoni Baia condo tower in Edgewater, The Real Deal reported. The complaint, filed April 3, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida by 700 Edgewater Development, LLC, names Zurich American Insurance Company, Allianz Global Risks US Insurance Company, ACE American Insurance Company and National Fire & Marine Insurance Company. Attorneys for the OKO affiliate and spokespeople for the insurers did not respond to The Real Deal's requests for comment. The suit alleges the 60-story tower's foundation was damaged by uneven settling during construction in 2021. According to the complaint, fixing it set back the tower's temporary certificate of occupancy at least 16 months, delaying sale closings and causing losses it lists as business interruption, lost rental value, soft costs and financing expenses. The affiliate began submitting claims in 2023; it says the total reached $55.7 million, the insurers paid $33.9 million, and they have refused to pay the remaining $22.4 million despite more than a year's notice. OKO and Cain International completed the 249-unit tower at 777 Northeast 26th Terrace, the first residential project branded by Missoni, in 2024. The coverage suit follows a January 2026 suit by the tower's condominium association in Miami-Dade Circuit Court against OKO's affiliate and nearly two dozen contractors and design firms. live-150: The Idaho Supreme Court has affirmed the dismissal of business-damages claims arising from the State of Idaho, Idaho Transportation Board's condemnation of part of Triple Crown Development, LLC's land in Canyon County for a highway interchange. The opinion, by Justice Colleen D. Zahn in Docket No. 52872-2025, was filed September 2, 2026; Mealey's reported on it September 14. The State and Triple Crown had stipulated to the value of the condemned land, and they also stipulated to let four companies intervene: Thueson Construction, Inc.; Americrete Ready Mix Concrete, Inc., which does business as G&B Redi-Mix; Americrete Land Holding LLC; and River Rock Sand & Gravel LLC. According to the opinion, Triple Crown and the intervenors are all controlled by the same person. The claims rested on a plan to mine gravel from the condemned parcel. Americrete Land Holding owns land next to Triple Crown's property, and G&B runs a concrete plant there. According to the opinion, the plan was for River Rock to mine gravel on the condemned land and for Thueson Construction to haul it to the G&B plant, but no permits were obtained and mining never began. Canyon County District Judge Gene A. Petty granted the State summary judgment, finding no evidence that Triple Crown owned a business operating on the condemned property and that the intervenors did not do business on land Triple Crown owned. On appeal, the companies argued that a joint venture among them, or their common owner, held a beneficial interest in both parcels and the businesses. The Court rejected that argument. Reading section 7-711(2) together with the rest of Idaho's eminent domain chapter, it held that "owned" means fee title ownership: a qualifying business must be owned by the fee owner of the condemned land, or must operate on adjoining land that fee owner also owns. Triple Crown did not own the intervenors' businesses, those businesses were not on the condemned property, and Americrete, not Triple Crown, holds title to the adjoining land. The Court found the ownership issue dispositive and did not reach the State's other arguments, and it distinguished an earlier decision involving a closely held corporation owned by the condemnee. The State asked for attorney fees on appeal under Idaho Code section 12-117. The Court declined, finding that the companies' arguments were supported by legal authority and that the appeal was not frivolous, unreasonable or without foundation. Chief Justice Bevan and Justices Brody, Moeller and Meyer concurred.
live-151: Florida's Second District Court of Appeal affirmed a final judgment entered on a jury verdict against Wal-Mart Stores East, LP on June 24, 2026 (No. 2D2025-0567), the Tampa Free Press reported. Judge Sleet wrote for a unanimous panel that included Chief Judge Lucas and Judge Rothstein-Youakim. According to the opinion, the plaintiff, a service technician for D.H. Pace Door Company, went to a Walmart store in July 2020 to replace a manual door with an automatic one in the order pick-up area. The new door had to be connected to an existing metal junction box in a restricted room that a store manager opened with a key card. The technician could not find the right breaker because about 200 breakers in the breaker room were unlabeled, so he decided to check the wires with a voltmeter. When he touched the loosened metal cover of the box, he was shocked, fell from his ladder to the concrete floor and injured his head. He then found the wires uncapped and the grounding wire unsecured. Experts for both sides agreed the box did not comply with the National Electrical Code, which Florida has adopted as part of its building code. Walmart argued that a property owner owes no duty to an independent contractor's employee injured while doing the work he was hired to do, and that neither exception to that rule applied. The court disagreed. It held that the evidence supported constructive knowledge: Walmart built the store and installed its junction boxes, the box sat in a locked area only Walmart personnel could enter, and the condition had existed for an extended period. Because the hidden danger was not inherent in installing a door, the court held, the trial court properly denied Walmart's motions for summary judgment and directed verdict.

live-163: Commercial developers who have spent the past several years trying to plan multifamily projects in Greater Boston's transit-served suburbs got a significant dose of legal certainty this month. On September 18, 2026, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court unanimously rejected a challenge brought by the Town of Marshfield and its select board to the MBTA Communities Act, the 2021 state law that requires the 177 cities and towns served by the MBTA to adopt zoning that allows multifamily housing as of right near transit. The decision in Town of Marshfield and another v. Commonwealth and another, SJC-13840, is the second time in less than two years that the state's highest court has upheld the law against a coordinated municipal revolt, and it closes off several of the strongest remaining legal theories towns had floated for resisting it. Marshfield and its select board argued that the Act, codified at General Laws Chapter 40A, Section 3A, amounted to an unfunded state mandate imposed on municipalities without corresponding funding, that it violated the Home Rule Amendment to the Massachusetts Constitution by intruding on matters of purely local concern, and that it conflicted with the state's existing Zoning Act framework. They also argued that the Act infringed the constitutional voting rights of Marshfield's town meeting voters, who had twice rejected proposed compliant zoning amendments. Writing for a unanimous court, Justice Serge Georges, Jr. rejected each theory. On the unfunded-mandate claim, the court held that Marshfield's complaint did not plausibly allege that the Act or its implementing regulations impose costs beyond the incidental local administration expenses that the state's mandate law expressly excludes from protection, and found it unnecessary to resolve the broader question of whether zoning-compliance costs are categorically excluded from unfunded-mandate protection at all. The court found the town's allegation of future direct costs too conclusory and speculative to state a claim, and held that Marshfield and its select board lack standing to assert a constitutional voting-rights claim on behalf of Marshfield's town meeting voters. On the Home Rule Amendment theory, the court reaffirmed that while the amendment protects municipal authority over genuinely local matters, it does not prevent the Legislature from imposing substantive statewide requirements that municipalities must implement through their existing local procedures, so long as the underlying statute is a valid general law addressing a matter of statewide concern, as the SJC had already found housing production to be. The ruling builds directly on the SJC's January 2025 decision in Attorney General v. Town of Milton, SJC-13580, which first upheld the Act's core enforceability and confirmed the Attorney General's authority to sue noncompliant municipalities, while separately invalidating the state housing agency's initial implementing guidelines for having skipped required rulemaking procedures under the Administrative Procedure Act. Those guidelines have since been re-promulgated in compliance with the APA, and Marshfield's case represents the first major test of the law's durability once that procedural defect was cured. Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell, whose office defended the Act, said the ruling leaves the multifamily zoning mandate fully intact across every covered community. For commercial real estate developers, the practical effect is to remove a meaningful category of entitlement risk from projects sited in MBTA Communities Act zoning districts. A developer who has spent months or years assembling a multifamily deal near a commuter rail stop or subway station no longer has to price in the possibility that a late-breaking municipal lawsuit could unwind the underlying zoning district itself, at least on the legal theories Marshfield advanced. Compliance and enforcement remain live issues distinct from this ruling, however: some of the 177 covered communities still have not adopted conforming zoning, and the Attorney General's office has separately pursued enforcement actions, including a pending suit against nine noncompliant communities, using the same tools validated in Milton. Developers evaluating sites in MBTA Communities Act districts can now treat the underlying statutory mandate as settled law rather than a pending legal question, though they should still confirm that the specific municipality's zoning has been found compliant by the state's housing agency before relying on as-of-right multifamily capacity. Municipalities considering further resistance to the Act should recognize that both the unfunded-mandate and Home Rule theories have now been squarely rejected, narrowing the realistic paths left to challenge compliance obligations to procedural or as-applied claims rather than facial attacks on the law itself, and counsel advising REITs or institutional developers on transit-oriented zoning disputes elsewhere should watch how other states treat similarly structured mandates, since Massachusetts's two-round validation of this law is likely to be cited as persuasive authority as more states adopt comparable transit-zoning statutes.

live-171: The Supreme Court of Ohio ruled on Tuesday, September 15, 2026, that Sheetz may pursue a second lawsuit seeking damages from the City of Centerville over its rejected plans for a store at 6318 Far Hills Avenue near Interstate 675, the Dayton Daily News reported. Centerville, 2026-Ohio-3531, answered a question of state law certified by the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio, where Sheetz's damages suit is pending. Chapter 2506 administrative appeal to avoid a res judicata bar, because those claims cannot be brought in such an appeal. live-172: The California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, Division Two, on Aug. 26, 2026 granted a writ petition by warehouse owner Schurman Family Company TIC and directed the Alameda County Superior Court to enter summary judgment in its favor, Business Insurance reported. The trial court had allowed a worker's negligence and premises liability claims against the landlord to proceed. Schurman owned an Oakland warehouse and leased portions of it to Verizon for communications equipment. Verizon hired L.D. Strobel as an independent contractor to work on the site. In June 2021, a Strobel employee sent to check equipment in an enclosure on the roof left a steel walkway, stepped onto a sloped section of roof and fell through a skylight, suffering serious injuries, according to the report. He sued Verizon and Schurman. The trial court granted summary judgment to Verizon under the Privette doctrine, which generally shields those who hire independent contractors from liability for the contractors' workplace injuries, but refused to extend it to Schurman because the landlord had not hired Strobel. In an opinion by Justice Desautels, the appeals court held that the doctrine reaches non-hiring parties within the "chain of delegation." It found that Schurman's lease expressly allowed Verizon to install, operate and maintain equipment at the property, that Verizon hired Strobel to do that work, and that Strobel knew about the skylights before the accident. The court said it would be "anomalous and inequitable" to potentially impose greater liability on Schurman, which did not control the worker's activities, than on Verizon or Strobel. It held that when a lease contemplates work by an independent contractor and the tenant hires one to do it, the landlord is protected unless a recognized exception applies.

live-175: U.S. District Judge George H. Wu has dismissed a proposed securities class action against Alexandria Real Estate Equities, the largest owner of U.S. lab buildings, and three of its executives, Bisnow reported on September 14, 2026. The court issued a tentative ruling on September 8 and, after oral argument on September 10, adopted it as final, granting the motion to dismiss with leave to amend, according to the CourtListener docket for the case, No. 2:25-cv-11319 (C.D. Cal.). Defendants named included Executive Chairman Joel Marcus, CEO Peter Moglia and CFO Marc Binda. Wu wrote that Alexandria's argument "is the more cogent-and-compelling explanation related to the events described" in the complaint, according to Bisnow. The docket shows the lead plaintiffs, Menora Mivtachim insurance and pension entities, filed an amended complaint on October 15, 2026, and the court later extended the defendants' deadline to answer.
live-176: Citibank, acting as trustee for holders of commercial mortgage-backed securities, and special servicer LNR Partners have sued in Cook County to foreclose on 625 North Michigan Avenue, a 28-story office building on Chicago's Magnificent Mile. The lenders allege that Golub & Company and BlueFive Capital defaulted on a $50.6 million loan that Cantor Commercial Real Estate made in 2019 at 4.63 percent interest. Neither Shefman nor Golub responded to The Real Deal's requests for comment.
live-177: A downtown Seattle retail property owned by an entity linked to Unico Properties has been placed in receivership after a default on a $14.5 million loan that matured two years earlier, the Puget Sound Business Journal reported, according to Connect CRE's September 24, 2026 lender roundup. live-178: Developer Charles Cohen satisfied a $187 million judgment owed to Fortress Investment Group in June 2026, but the two sides are still fighting. In a letter to the court on Thursday, June 25, Cohen's attorney wrote that Cohen "is committed to pursuing his defenses and counterclaims against Fortress for substantial damages," Bisnow reported. Crain's New York Business first reported the letter, which followed a June 18 letter in which Fortress told the court it planned to continue two other suits against Cohen. According to The Real Deal, Cohen's letter refers to a lawsuit he filed about a year earlier seeking about $204 million in damages over the foreclosure auction of four of his former properties. The dispute dates to 2022, when borrowers connected to Cohen took out a $534 million loan that he guaranteed. Fortress sued in 2024 and took the properties later that year in what The Real Deal called one of the largest UCC foreclosures on record. Fortress's two remaining suits concern Cohen's property loan guarantees and transfers of personal assets that Fortress calls "fraudulent"; Cohen plans to move to dismiss and to pursue his counterclaims, according to Bisnow.
live-179: In April 2018, Marketplace Home Mortgage, LLC, a mortgage-loan company, signed a three-year lease for space in the Pinnacle North Office Center, owned by Pinnacle North, LLC. It defaulted on rent that summer. MHM sold its assets to New American Funding in a deal that closed December 31, 2018; the buyer assumed some liabilities but not the lease, and MHM was insolvent by then. In January 2019 MHM told the landlord it was no longer operating and had no revenue or employees. In December 2019 its sole member and president had MHM write him a $50,000 check. Pinnacle North later obtained a default judgment against MHM for $52,548.24 plus interest, costs and attorney fees. Unable to collect, Pinnacle North sued the principal in Oakland Circuit Court to pierce MHM's veil and to avoid the $50,000 payment under Michigan's voidable-transfer statute, MCL 566.31 et seq. After a two-day bench trial, the court ruled for the landlord in 2023, holding him liable for the full default judgment plus costs, fees and interest, and later awarded about $92,000 in attorney fees covering both lawsuits. A panel of Judges Patel, Swartzle and Mariani affirmed. It rejected the principal's late request to apply Minnesota law, where MHM was organized. On veil-piercing, the court pointed to evidence that he personally borrowed money to capitalize MHM, which MHM then repaid through a $193,000 payment in 2018; that MHM kept paying a $270,000 American Express debt ahead of other creditors because of his potential personal liability; and that he wrote himself the $50,000 check while MHM was insolvent. On the voidable-transfer claim, the court held MHM received no reasonably equivalent value for the payment, which the trial court found was a return of a prior capital contribution rather than a loan repayment. The court also upheld the fee award under the lease clause covering suits to collect rent.
live-184: 100 Summer St., a 32-story, 1.1-million-square-foot office tower at Summer and Devonshire streets near South Station, went to a foreclosure auction after its lender, Wells Fargo, foreclosed in September 2026, the Boston Globe and Bisnow reported. Owner Rockpoint, a Boston-based real estate private equity firm, bought the tower in October 2019 for $806 million with a $470 million Wells Fargo mortgage, according to Suffolk County deed records cited by the Globe.
