The auction, first scheduled for Oct. 20, was rescheduled and held outside the building's entrance on the afternoon of Tuesday, Oct. 27, Bisnow reported. The auctioneer set the opening bid at $260 million, and Rockpoint was the sole bidder. Rockpoint did not respond to requests for comment at the auction.
live-186: The $49.7 million commercial mortgage-backed securities loan on the Embassy Suites by Hilton Portland Airport, a 251-key hotel next to Portland International Airport, moved to special servicing after missing its August 2026 maturity date, Connect CRE reported in its September 24, 2026 lender roundup. The loan is held in two 2016 securitizations, GSMS 2016-GS3 and GSMS 2016-GS4. According to Connect CRE, the loan remained current for its entire term despite years of debt service coverage below 1.00x. The Registry, in a September 22, 2026 report, said the sponsor had propped the hotel up for years and that the maturity default hands Rialto Capital Advisors a workout on a loan that barely clears breakeven. KBRA, in an October 9, 2026 surveillance release on GSMS 2016-GS4, said that deal's $23.8 million portion transferred to special servicing on September 11, 2026. No foreclosure complaint or receivership request had been reported, and the sources reviewed did not name the borrower or sponsor.
live-187: The Granary District office campus formerly known as Industry SLC has been renamed Foundry43, Building Salt Lake reported on September 24, 2026. Lincoln Property Company and lender ACORE Capital announced the relaunch, and JLL is leading leasing. The parking structure and retail space are complete, and work continues on more than 64,000 square feet of creative office space and a 34,000-square-foot fitness center. The announcement describes a 230,000-square-foot campus and 12,000 square feet of retail to be added at the 1,000-stall garage. Industry SLC, which opened in 2020 in a converted 1943 foundry, was widely seen as a catalyst for the Granary District. After developer Makers Line collapsed in 2023, Catalyst Opportunity Funds took over the office building and the unfinished garage. In fall 2025, ACORE Capital Mortgage sued Catalyst in Utah's Business and Chancery Court, alleging it had defaulted on a $97.3 million loan that September. The property went into receivership, garage construction stalled, and a foreclosure sale was scheduled for early March 2026. According to Building Salt Lake, ACORE conveyed the parcels at 513 and 517 W. 600 South to Marwood Investment Trust, a Delaware statutory trust, by a deed signed March 9 and recorded June 1, 2026.
live-188: A nonprofit group, Joliet Residents For Responsible Growth, and three members who live near the project sued the City of Joliet in Will County Circuit Court on May 18, 2026, seeking to void the City Council's 8-1 vote on March 19 approving an annexation agreement for the $20 billion, 795-acre Joliet Technology Center, The Herald-News (Shaw Local) reported. The other defendants are Powerhouse Hillwood Holding, HW Technology Park Development and American Real Estate Partners. The approvals annexed the site and rezoned it from agricultural to light industrial for a 24-building, 1.8-gigawatt data center campus. The complaint alleged that a Feb. 18 Plan Commission notice did not disclose that the proposal involved a data center, that residents were denied a right to cross-examine the developers' witnesses at a March 16 council meeting, that the March 19 meeting violated the Open Meetings Act, and that the rezoning bore no substantial relation to public health, safety or welfare. The city and developers responded that the notice was legally sufficient, that annexation is a legislative decision carrying no cross-examination right, that no one at the March 16 meeting tried to cross-examine witnesses, and that the Open Meetings Act does not allow voiding action taken at an open meeting. The city also argued the group lacked standing. On October 19, 2026, Judge Victoria Breslan ruled for the defendants on every count, according to a law-firm analysis of the order. She dismissed the notice count with prejudice, granted summary judgment to the defendants on the open-meetings and due process counts, and dismissed the zoning count without prejudice, finding that the alleged harms to regional water supply, the power grid, infrastructure and traffic were public harms rather than injuries to specific parcels. She also found the group lacked associational standing but allowed it to file an amended pleading.
live-189: Two Edgerton residents and their nonprofit, Public Trust Collective Inc., circulated a petition for an ordinance to stop data centers from being built in the city and gathered 208 signatures, the Johnson County Post reported. The Post said the county election office verified the signatures. At its July 23 meeting the city council declined to adopt the ordinance, saying it contained inaccurate statements, and instead voted to approve a lawsuit. The article references a data center proposed by Dubai-based DAMAC Digital at the Logistics Park Kansas City warehouse in Edgerton. The city sued on August 4, calling the petition 'legally and factually deficient' and arguing that the proposed ordinance would work as a zoning restriction, making it administrative rather than legislative and so outside the citizen petition process. On September 3, Judge Stephanie Goodenow granted the defendants' motion to strike, finding the suit violated their rights under the Kansas Public Speech Protection Act, which bars lawsuits meant to silence public participation. Their attorney called the ruling 'a major victory.' The city said it respects the court's decision but has serious concerns that the ordinance exceeds its authority and misstates facts about water and power, and that it is evaluating options. A separate suit against the city clerk argues the petition belongs on the ballot; when the Post's article ran, it had not been decided whether the measure would appear on the November ballot.
live-192: A&F Williams Street LLC, which bought the five-story office building at 165 Main Street in White Plains in 2014, sued the New York Power Authority on September 15, 2026 in Westchester County Supreme Court, alleging negligence and trespass, according to Westfair Communications. The building sits across from the former Galleria mall and next to NYPA's headquarters at 123 Main Street, separated from it by William Street, a short lane. According to the complaint as reported by Westfair, A&F agreed last year to give NYPA access to its property for seven months to conduct a survey and install monitoring devices for a demolition and construction project at NYPA's parking garage, and NYPA agreed to fix any damage the project caused. A&F alleges the work produced excessive vibration that cracked its rooftop parapet and pulled a roofing membrane away from the masonry beneath it. It says it put up scaffolding to protect the public at a cost of $12,000 a month and that rebuilding the roof will cost more than $3 million. NYPA allegedly denied responsibility. The complaint further alleges that on August 5, months after the access agreement expired, NYPA resumed construction within 30 feet of the building, and that tenants have complained about noise and dust, with some seeking rent reductions or lease terminations. It says NYPA "should have known" that demolition right next to an occupied commercial building risked structural damage. A&F seeks more than $3 million, an order holding NYPA responsible for repairs, and an order stopping demolition and construction until NYPA agrees to a reasonable access arrangement. Asked for comment, a NYPA spokeswoman told Westfair that the authority does not comment on pending litigation. The allegations have not been tested in court.
live-193: Seven Baltimore residents have sued to block MCB Real Estate's $900 million plan to demolish and replace the Harborplace pavilions at Pratt and Light streets, Baltimore Fishbowl reported. The suit was filed Monday, September 21, 2026, in the Circuit Court for Baltimore City against the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, the City Council, the Board of Estimates and MCB HP Baltimore LLC, the MCB affiliate. Six of the plaintiffs live in the city, and most belong to a group called the Inner Harbor Coalition. MCB unveiled the project in October 2023: two apartment towers with 900 or more residences, plus offices, shops, restaurants and public space. MCB owns the pavilions, and the city owns the land beneath them. The complaint alleges city officials pursued a rushed, behind-the-scenes plan to hand public land and parkland to a favored developer, and says the three bills that advanced the project were drafted by MCB's attorney and introduced at MCB's request. It also cites a three-year rent abatement in the March 2023 lease and a property tax reduction approved by the Baltimore Development Corporation. The complaint claims that Bills 23-0444, 23-0446 and 23-0448 are "special laws" passed for MCB's benefit in violation of the Maryland Constitution, and that the city granted MCB a franchise and rights in Harborplace and Inner Harbor Park "by implication," without the ordinance, Board of Estimates review and time limits the City Charter requires. It says a Charter amendment ratified by voters authorized the project on 1.3 acres previously dedicated in perpetuity as public land, and it alleges City Code and Zoning Code violations. The plaintiffs seek declarations that the bills and the lease are void, a writ of mandamus, and injunctions against demolition, construction and permits until the city complies. The Mayor's Office declined to comment; a representative said the city would "reserve comment for the appropriate judicial forum." MCB had not responded to a request for comment. According to the complaint, MCB has applied for permits for a first phase that includes demolishing the pavilions, with a proposed start date of October 15, 2026. Tenants told Baltimore Fishbowl they had been notified the pavilions would stay open until the beginning of 2027.
live-194: The builder of a planned 315-unit multifamily project in Riviera Beach sued the city's water utility district on Sept. 18, 2026, in Palm Beach County Circuit Court, the Palm Beach Post reported in an article republished by The Boca Raton Tribune. The plaintiff, 7920 Riviera Beach Holdings LLC, alleges the Riviera Beach Utility Special District is charging it new, much higher water and wastewater impact fees instead of the fees in effect when it submitted its plans. The district's board approved the new fees on Feb. 19, 2025, raising the combined water and wastewater impact fee 157%, from $3,940 to $10,126 per unit, effective June 1, 2025. The lawsuit says the developer had submitted all permits for its project at 7880 N. Military Trail by April 24, 2025, and that the new fees would cost it $2.6 million and raise the project's cost by $1.6 million. It quotes a city official telling the developer that utility impact fees are set by the date of payment, not the date a permit number was issued. The developer says that position conflicts with the Florida Impact Fee Act, which provides that new or increased impact fees may not apply to permit applications submitted before the fee's effective date. According to the suit, the district later issued revised invoices relabeling the fees as water and wastewater "capital charges," and its counsel asserted they are connection fees excluded from the Act; the district said it had "mistakenly used the word 'impact fee'" in its resolution. The Post reported that district documents, and the district's chief financial officer at the February 2025 meeting, described the charges as impact fees. The CFO said the increase was needed to help pay for a proposed water treatment plant estimated at $400 million, and the board imposed it immediately rather than phasing it in, citing extraordinary circumstances. Riviera Beach did not respond to the Post's request for comment.
live-196: According to WCSC Live 5, the attack happened just before 10 a.m. on March 4, 2026, when a stranger allegedly stabbed the woman with an eight-inch kitchen knife in the mall's food court. She was treated at a hospital for stab wounds and lacerations to her torso. The suspect was charged with attempted murder and possession of a weapon during a violent crime, the station reported. The suit alleges the mall failed to maintain reasonable security measures for shoppers and employees, that security did not detect or stop the attacker, and that no security was stationed in or patrolling the food court. Citing the complaint, WCSC reported that North Charleston police received more than 1,400 reports at the mall from January 2021 until the attack, including several assaults. The plaintiff told the station she wants accountability and more security at the mall. WCSC's 2026 reports do not name the corporate entity that owns the mall, and they do not identify the court or the damages sought. In 2023, the station reported on suits by victims of a February 14, 2021 shooting in the mall's parking lot, which alleged inadequate security and patrols, and it identified CBL as the mall's parent owner at that time.
live-197: SDCL Tennessee Propco LLC, a Delaware company with its principal place of business in New York, sued Bradley County in Chancery Court on Sept. 17, 2026, WTVC NewsChannel 9 reported after obtaining the complaint. The Chattanooga Times Free Press described the developer, SDCL, as a London-based firm with U.S. headquarters in New York City and reported that Bradley County Mayor Gary Davis shared the suit on Monday, Sept. 21. The project, Project MidSpan, is a planned data center campus on about 306 acres behind Walker Valley High School, in the Hiwassee River Industrial Park near Exit 33. According to WTVC's account of the complaint, SDCL took an option on the land in July 2024 and bought it on April 28, 2025 for $19,904,950. At the time, all but about 2.5 acres were zoned I-1 General Industrial, which the company says permitted a large-scale data center; the suit includes a September 2022 letter from the county's planning director saying the district was appropriate for one. On April 20, 2026, commissioners voted 14-0 to allow data centers only in the I-2 Special Impact Industrial District and to bar them within 3,000 feet of an existing home, school or church. Davis said the project's nearest proposed building would be about 1,700 feet from the high school. SDCL argues that the version commissioners approved was materially different from the one the county's regional planning commission considered and should have gone back to that commission, that the county did not give proper public notice of the final version, and that taking up the substitute without listing it on the April 20 agenda violated Tennessee's Open Meetings Act. It also claims the rules are arbitrary and discriminatory, violate equal protection and due process, and effectively exclude data centers from all of unincorporated Bradley County. It seeks a declaration that the rules are invalid, an order barring their enforcement against its property, and legal costs and attorneys' fees. Bradley County had not yet filed a response when WTVC reported. Davis said the county will defend the regulations: "Bradley County will defend its position and the regulations adopted by your county commission."
live-199: The dispute concerns Paterson Plank RD J-C, LLC, which owns The Cliffs Lofts, a 120-unit residential building in Jersey City that was converted from a warehouse and has been leased as rentals since it was completed during the 2008 financial crisis, according to a November 21, 2025 opinion of Delaware's Court of Chancery. Under a June 29, 2021 LLC agreement, Brass Works, an affiliate of the family that developed the building, was the manager and held the Class A interest, and ASVRF, an affiliate of American Realty Advisors, contributed $18 million for the Class B preferred interest. After Brass Works defaulted on its payment obligations, ASVRF exercised a contractual right to remove it as manager. After an expedited trial, Vice Chancellor Lori W. Will held that the removal was valid and that Brass Works breached the agreement by refusing to hand over management, rejecting its defense that ASVRF had gone along with a plan to convert the building to condominiums. Brass Works filed its Chapter 11 petition in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of New Jersey on May 22, 2026 (Case No. 26-15809). On June 4, ASVRF and the property-owning company moved to dismiss the case under Section 1112(b) of the Bankruptcy Code or, alternatively, for relief from the automatic stay. In a June 30 objection, Brass Works argued that the LLC agreement remained in force and that it could cure its default under a reorganization plan, be reinstated as manager and redeem ASVRF's interest, noting that the building was about 95% leased as of March 2026. It also accused ASVRF of breaching fiduciary duties and said a planned foreclosure sale of its membership interests rested on a defective notice. Brass Works filed proposed plans and disclosure statements in June and August. After hearings in September, the court entered an order dismissing the case on September 25, 2026. Law360's September 28 report on the ruling said the judge cited the harm that continuing the case would cause the creditor that sought dismissal.
live-200: St. Louis Public Radio reported on Sept. 17, 2026 that the developer behind a planned $3.1 billion data center in Midtown St. Louis had sued the city that week. TerraWatt plans a 120-megawatt data center in the old Famous-Barr warehouse on Market Street, near the Armory, as part of a planned technology district. The petition, filed by TerraWatt partner David Lambiaso against the city's Board of Adjustment, challenges two conditions the board attached to the project's conditional use permit. The first condition requires the data center to use 2.4 megawatts of renewable energy, which the complaint calls "practically impossible on the 11-acre site." The second requires the Board of Aldermen to approve a community benefits agreement. The suit alleges both requirements "exceed the scope of authority" of the board and asks that they be struck from the permit. According to the station, the city's Land Clearance for Redevelopment Authority approved the community benefits agreement the same week. Mayor Cara Spencer did not immediately respond to the station's request for comment. The board had voted unanimously on July 29, 2026 to let the permit proceed with amendments after more than 11 hours of public comment, St. Louis Public Radio reported; its changes included barring backup generator testing on bad air quality days and requiring a small amount of on-site renewable energy generation. On Aug. 28, a group of opponents that includes the Missouri Coalition for the Environment sued the city, arguing the board "erred in deciding to deny the appeals and grant" the permit and acted "contrary to law." That suit also names Lambiaso. The opponents asked the court for a stay while the case proceeds and for reversal of the board's decision; a spokeswoman for the mayor said the city does not comment on pending legal matters. Consultants working for TerraWatt estimate the project would generate about $445 million in tax revenue over 10 years for the city, St. Louis Public Schools and other local taxing authorities, according to the station.
live-201: The lenders on Eastview Mall, the Rochester region's largest retail center, have filed for foreclosure and are opposing a Town of Victor plan to take much of the mall by eminent domain, the Rochester Business Journal reported on September 28, 2026. U.S. Bank National Association and Wells Fargo Bank hold the $210 million mortgage. After three extensions negotiated between September 2022 and September 2025, the loan's most recent maturity date of September 6, 2026 passed, and the lenders filed for foreclosure in state Supreme Court in New York County on September 8. According to the RBJ, Wilmorite and Town Supervisor Jack Marren worked between July and September 6 on a plan under which the town would acquire the mortgaged portions of the mall by eminent domain, likely paying assessed value, and then sell the property to Victor 2040 LLC, an entity owned by Wilmorite, which would also pay the legal fees. Marren says about 20 percent of the town's operating budget and close to 4,000 jobs are tied to the mall. He and Wilmorite say Rialto Capital Advisors, the loans' special servicer, has hindered upkeep by refusing to release funds, and Marren said Wilmorite told him it had paid Rialto $10 million in fees it cannot use. In a letter sent Friday, September 25, to Marren and the town, counsel for the lenders and Rialto called the plan a 'debt evasion scheme' and disputed Wilmorite's account. The letter says Rialto has disbursed about $9.4 million to Wilmorite since January for operating expenses, tenant improvements and leasing commissions, and that reserve funds on the defaulted loan paid about $6 million in property taxes and PILOT payments. The lenders asked that the letter be read at the Town Board's September 28 public hearing on the proposal.
live-202: 2100 Ross Avenue, a 33-story office tower in downtown Dallas's Arts District, was flagged for an October 6, 2026 foreclosure auction, according to The Real Deal, which cited Roddy's Foreclosure Listing Service. The building has about 840,000 square feet. It was built in 1982 and last renovated in 2014. The tower is owned by Dundon Capital Partners, the firm of Dallas billionaire Thomas Dundon, which allegedly defaulted on a $98 million loan that Wells Fargo made in 2016. Pacific Elm Properties manages the building. The Real Deal noted that the owner could still work out an agreement with the lender before the auction. The previous owner, Atlanta-based Cousins Properties, bought the tower out of foreclosure in 2012 for $59 million. It renovated the building, leased it to 90 percent occupancy, and sold it to Dundon Capital in 2015 for $131 million, The Real Deal reported, citing The Dallas Morning News.
live-203: Slate Property Group and The Carlyle Group filed a foreclosure suit on September 22, 2026 against MG Developer, a Coral Gables-based developer, over Metro Parc South, a 10-story, 347-unit apartment project in Hialeah. The lenders allege MG defaulted on $31.1 million of a $105 million construction financing that closed in April 2025. They seek the $31.1 million plus accrued interest, attorneys' fees and court costs, The Real Deal reported, citing court documents and a Vizzda report. According to the complaint, MG let construction liens be recorded against the property, did not make reserve-account deposits the loan required, and did not pay its 2025 property taxes. The lenders say they sent default notices in January, May and June 2026 and then entered a forbearance agreement with MG, which has since expired. Metro Parc South is one phase of MG's three-phase development on nearly 2 acres along East 24th and East 25th streets near Ninth Avenue, which MG bought in three deals in 2024 for $16.3 million. MG built the first phase, Metro Parc, with Baron Property Group, and Baron later bought out the second phase, Metro Parc North. The suit does not name Baron or the other two projects. The Real Deal also reported that MG principal Alirio Torrealba and his affiliates face eight other suits in Miami-Dade Circuit Court, filed since summer 2026, mostly by entities tied to individual investors who made loans of $750,000 to $6 million. Those suits allege breaches of promissory notes, do not seek foreclosure, and together seek $21.4 million. A spokesperson for MG told The Real Deal the company remains "actively engaged in good-faith negotiations, including securing an additional investor, to bring this matter to a prompt resolution." MG has also said it is in "good-faith discussions" with most of its lenders and has reached verbal agreements with some.
live-205: American Heavy Plate Solutions, LLC (AHP) has sued the Monroe County Port Authority and three Bitdeer entities, Erie Creek LLC, Whitetail Creek LLC and Bitdeer, Inc., in the Court of Common Pleas of Monroe County, Ohio. According to a Feb. 5, 2026 SEC filing by parent Bitdeer Technologies Group, Erie Creek received notice of the complaint on Feb. 2, 2026, and AHP seeks declaratory and injunctive relief concerning certain leasehold rights at an industrial property in the county where the port authority is landlord. Bitdeer said it "intends to vigorously defend against the claims." JDJournal described the suit as AHP's claim that Bitdeer and others are violating rights tied to AHP's lease in connection with Bitdeer's data center project. Bitdeer leases land at the Hannibal Industrial Park in Clarington, Ohio from the port authority under a 30-year agreement announced in June 2024, Cointelegraph reported at the time. In its third-quarter 2026 results, Bitdeer said the timing of power availability and construction at its 570-megawatt Clarington site may be affected by the legal proceedings filed by AHP, a neighboring company, that design and other preparation work continues, and that the site is currently being developed for Bitcoin mining. In April, Bitdeer moved to disqualify AHP's law firm, which also represents Bitdeer in a separate federal case in New York, arguing the dual role created a conflict and could give the firm access to Bitdeer's private information, JDJournal reported. Judge Julie Selmon denied the motion on Sept. 8, 2026. According to JDJournal, she found it important that Bitdeer had signed an advance waiver allowing the firm to take on certain future matters against it, considered that the firm had kept its Bitdeer lawyers separate from the AHP team, found no evidence that Bitdeer's information had been misused, and weighed the time and added cost AHP would face with new counsel. Bitdeer's Ohio counsel did not immediately comment, and AHP's firm welcomed the ruling. The underlying lease claims remain pending.
live-207: New Jersey's attorney general and Division of Consumer Affairs sued RealPage and a group of landlords in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey on April 23, 2025 (No. 2:25-cv-03057). The state alleges that landlords using RealPage's revenue-management products share confidential rent, occupancy and other data, and that the software's rent recommendations, which RealPage enforces through monitoring, are used to raise rents in violation of federal and state antitrust law and the New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act. Besides AvalonBay, the landlord defendants include Morgan Properties Management Company, The Kamson Corporation, LeFrak Estate, Greystar Management Services, AION Management, Cammeby's Management Co. of N.J., Veris Residential, Bozzuto Management Company and two Russo entities. The caption now names Attorney General Jennifer Davenport, who was substituted as a plaintiff. On March 31, 2026, Judge Arleo ruled on five motions to dismiss. She found the conspiracy adequately pleaded against RealPage and the other landlords, but dismissed without prejudice the federal and New Jersey antitrust claims, and some consumer-fraud claims, against AvalonBay. AvalonBay uses RealPage's Lease Rent Options product under a contract that bars RealPage from sharing AvalonBay's data with other landlords or using their data in its recommendations to AvalonBay. She let an unconscionable-commercial-practices claim proceed against all of the landlords, including AvalonBay. The amended complaint alleges that AvalonBay employees obtained competitors' confidential information, including by phone, and entered it into the software's user-specific database, which AvalonBay's contract does not restrict, and that AvalonBay shared its own data with other landlords. AvalonBay opposed amendment, relying on its contract and internal documents to argue it used the software on its own and relied on public information. Judge Arleo declined to resolve that dispute before discovery, granted leave to amend, and denied as moot AvalonBay's motion to reconsider the consumer-fraud ruling. The state filed the amended complaint on October 2, 2026, and defendants filed answers to it in October.
live-208: Seventeen investors in an entity controlled by landlord Mike Kohan, most of them from Great Neck, N.Y., sued The Davis Companies on September 29, 2026 in New York State Supreme Court to try to stop the mezzanine lender's UCC foreclosure auction of 345 Seventh Avenue, a Garment District office building. They alleged the sale process was defective and could result in the building selling for less than its value. Their request for a temporary restraining order was denied. Davis then used a credit bid to acquire an equity stake in the property, which Davis's attorney said puts the firm on a path to control the building, The Real Deal reported. The complaint also makes broader fraud allegations against Kohan. The investors allege he persuaded them to give him more than $80 million in exchange for promised membership interests in entities that owned real estate, including 345 Seventh Avenue. Instead, the complaint says, Kohan drew up fraudulent operating agreements and used them to obtain financing, and the investors never received the stakes they had been promised. The complaint alleges Kohan "concealed or omitted investor equity, thereby deceiving both investors and lenders," and that he refused to give the investors documents to assess their rights after they learned of the UCC sale. Kohan and the investors' attorney did not immediately respond to The Real Deal's requests for comment. One of the loans at issue is the building's mezzanine loan, which Davis acquired in July 2026. Davis moved to foreclose in August 2026, accusing Kohan of defaulting on a $73 million loan, falling behind on bills and not resolving building violations, The Real Deal reported. A buyer group that included Kohan and Katan Realty Group bought the 25-story, 190,000-square-foot building in 2025 for $85 million, when it was 39 percent vacant. A representative for Kohan Retail Investment Group told The Real Deal that 345 Seventh Avenue is controlled by an affiliate of Kohan individually. Separately, The Real Deal reported that Kohan was recently removed as chief executive, president and a director of Kohan Properties Ltd., his British Virgin Islands-based company that raised about $112 million on the Israeli bond market. The removal followed the discovery of an allegedly unauthorized $4.5 million loan on five Manhattan office properties and $7.4 million in personal withdrawals in July 2026.
live-210: Rialto Capital, acting as special servicer, has taken over 580 Market Street, a 35,000-square-foot office building more than a century old beside the Montgomery BART station in San Francisco's Financial District. The San Francisco Business Times first reported the foreclosure, according to The Real Deal. The owner, Paragon Company, had a $15.7 million loan on the building that matured in June 2025. A notice of default served on Paragon in October 2025 said the loan had not been repaid. A trustee's deed recorded in July 2026 put the unpaid debt at $17.5 million, and Rialto paid $5 million to take the property. Appraisers valued the building at $9.9 million in March 2026, up from $8.9 million in 2025 but nearly 60 percent below the $24.2 million, or $690 a square foot, that Paragon paid in 2015 in its first Bay Area purchase. The building was 53 percent occupied in December 2024, and four major tenants with about half the leasable space had leases ending between January 2025 and January 2026. Current occupancy is not known, The Real Deal reported. Bondholder notes cited by the Business Times say Rialto is weighing whether to lease up the building or sell it as-is, with a sale now expected in the first quarter of 2028. The notes favor leasing, citing the floor plates and demand from tech companies, startups and tenants looking to expand. Colliers handles leasing, Transwestern manages the property, and work on spec suites was scheduled to begin in September 2026, according to the report.
live-211: An affiliate of Criterion Real Estate Capital, the noteholder, filed a foreclosure notice on Monday, September 28, 2026 for 450 Fifth St. NW, a large Brutalist office building near Judiciary Square in Washington, D.C., the Washington Business Journal reported, according to Connect CRE. The notice says the owner, Judiciary Plaza LLC, owes $166.6 million on a $177.5 million note from 2007. The 539,478-square-foot building was scheduled for an October 28, 2026 foreclosure auction at the D.C. office of Alex Cooper Auctioneers. The report described the building as slated for conversion into 500 residential units.
live-212: Four trade associations whose members own or manage large buildings in Colorado (the Colorado Apartment Association, the Apartment Association of Metro Denver, the Colorado Hotel and Lodging Association, and NAIOP Colorado) sued state and Denver officials in April 2024. They challenge Colorado's Regulation 28 and Denver's Energize Denver ordinance and rules, which require large buildings to cut energy use or greenhouse gas emissions on a set schedule. The groups allege the standards are strict enough that owners can comply only by replacing furnaces, water heaters and other EPCA-covered appliances with units that exceed federal efficiency standards, which they say amounts to state and local regulation of those products' energy use that EPCA bars. The court dismissed the original complaint without prejudice for lack of standing on March 28, 2025. The groups filed an amended complaint on August 29, 2025, and the state defendants, the Denver defendants and four intervenors defending the programs (the Coalition for Community Solar Access, the Colorado Solar and Storage Association, the Natural Resources Defense Council and the Sierra Club) moved to dismiss it. On August 21, 2026, Magistrate Judge Kathryn A. Starnella recommended letting the case proceed in part, and every side objected. The United States filed a statement of interest on September 15, 2026. Judge Rodriguez overruled all of the objections. She held that the groups plausibly alleged that regulations imposing building-wide energy-use reductions could be preempted by EPCA, while noting that the merits may prove the defendants right. She agreed that claims concerning consumer appliances are subject to Colorado's two-year limitations period and dismissed them with prejudice, leaving the claims based on EPCA's industrial-equipment provisions. She also rejected the groups' arguments that the standards regulate covered products directly and that Regulation 28's greenhouse-gas intensity cap is preempted. The state defendants, the Denver defendants and the intervenors answered the amended complaint on October 14, 2026. The magistrate judge set a status conference for November 17, 2026 to discuss the plan for the case and what discovery is needed.
live-213: A Penobscot County judge has ruled that Namdar Realty Group, the New York-based owner of the Bangor Mall, must pay just over $1.1 million to Tri-State Insurance Company of Minnesota, the Bangor Daily News reported on October 2, 2026. Judge Bruce Mallonee signed the decision on September 24, after Namdar failed to respond to multiple letters and did not appear at a September 23 hearing. Namdar did not respond to the newspaper's request for comment. Tri-State sued in Penobscot County Superior Court on June 30, 2026, the Bangor Daily News reported in July. According to the complaint, the furniture store Furniture, Mattresses & More alerted mall ownership in February 2023 to a ceiling leak in the vacant former Sears, where it stored inventory; it took the mall two hours to shut off the water, and a sprinkler pipe in the ceiling later burst. The store's insurer reimbursed it just over $1.3 million and sued the mall's owners, Namdar Realty Group LLC, Bangor Mall Realty LLC, Bangor CH LLC and Bangor Nassim LLC, alleging negligence and that the owners "falsely represented" that sprinkler and code violations had been corrected. The suit also names Maine Fire Protection Systems, which it accuses of failing to properly maintain and monitor the sprinkler and alarm systems. That company has appeared in court and responded to filings, so it is not covered by the judgment, and the insurer's claims against it are expected to continue. The newspaper reported that this is the second million-dollar ruling against Namdar this year over the mall: Namdar was ordered to pay the city of Bangor a $1.1 million fine and make repairs over code violations, including a leaky roof and a sewer line break, and had not paid by a July 31 deadline.
live-214: A commercial developer's lawsuit against the City of Fresno over downtown parking was set for a jury trial beginning October 12, 2026 before Fresno County Superior Court Judge D. Tyler Tharpe, GV Wire reported on October 2. The developer owns the Grand 1401 building, whose anchor tenant is the construction firm Tutor Perini. He says the city, under then-Mayor Ashley Swearengin, promised him 100 free parking spaces in perpetuity to help bring Tutor Perini downtown. The city disputes that such an agreement existed, though it honored the arrangement for six years, according to GV Wire. In 2018 the city told him he would have to pay about $6,400 a month for the spaces. Construction of a new parking garage, which Mayor Jerry Dyer calls key to downtown revitalization, has cut off access to the spaces at least for now, and his request to halt the garage work during the case was unsuccessful. The developer says Tutor Perini will leave if the lot closes and that losing the tenant could cost him more than $7 million; in a January filing he said a full closure would cut his net operating income by more than $543,000 a year. The suit also named Councilmember Miguel Arias, alleging he obstructed the project and sought a campaign donation. Arias denies soliciting a donation, and in May 2022 Judge Tharpe granted Arias's anti-SLAPP motion and dismissed him from the case for lack of evidence, GV Wire reported. Neither city officials nor the developer's lawyers responded to GV Wire's requests for comment.
live-215: The Oklahoma Department of Securities has sued Vesta Realty, LLC, alleging the Tulsa-based multifamily company did not provide internal documents the department subpoenaed, Oklahoma Watch reported on October 1, 2026. The suit, filed August 24, 2026, says the subpoena sought records including the identities of, and communications with, investors in a portion of the limited liability companies under the Vesta umbrella. Shaun Mullins, a trial attorney with the department, told Oklahoma Watch the department did not receive the documents and has asked the district court for an order requiring their production. The case is civil, but Mullins said the department's statute allows it to make criminal referrals and share investigative information with agencies that handle criminal enforcement; he said he could not comment on whether either had happened. Kulick told Oklahoma Watch he was aware of the suit. 'We are in the process of engaging an attorney and look forward to getting this matter resolved,' he said in a text. Oklahoma Watch counted at least 28 lawsuits filed in 2026 against Kulick, his company or a property he controlled, including a suit by a business partner alleging Kulick used the business as a personal piggy bank.
live-219: N17 Development sued the City of Menlo Park on October 2, 2026, filing a complaint and petition for writ of mandate over the city's review of Willow Park, a proposed redevelopment of the former Sunset Magazine campus at 80 Willow Road, according to the city's project page. KQED reported the case is in San Mateo County Superior Court. The 6.7-acre project would include about 665 homes, about 100 of them below market rate according to KQED, plus about 332,000 square feet of office space, about 17,000 square feet of retail and a 130-room hotel, in towers ranging from 301 to 458 feet. N17 filed a preliminary application in December 2023 under the Builder's Remedy. The city's timeline shows it found the application incomplete twice in 2024, deemed it complete in November 2024, and then repeatedly found it inconsistent with development standards and ineligible for streamlined processing under AB 2011. The lawsuit says the project is 'by right' and that 'the city is not permitted to say no to the project,' KQED reported. N17 also seeks a refund of roughly $300,000 in legal fees the city had it pay for the review. On July 29, 2026, the Attorney General's office sent the city a notice under AB 712 stating that it had violated AB 2011 and the Housing Accountability Act, and the suit invokes the penalties described in that notice. After a September 29 closed session, the city council said it disagreed with the Attorney General's analysis, and on October 1 the city told the Attorney General it had processed the application under state law. Mayor Betsy Nash told KQED, 'We are not rejecting the project. We are continuing our review in the standard way.' The city's position is that the hotel space keeps the project from qualifying as a housing project under the recent laws, KQED reported. The Registry, which described the city as refusing to approve the project, reported that up to $33 million in state penalties are in play; KQED reported that a loss would require fines of at least $6.65 million under AB 712. According to the city, briefing runs through December 8, a hearing on the writ petition is set for December 14, 2026, and a decision is expected in mid-to-late January 2027.
live-221: Republic Bank of Chicago filed suit on September 1, 2026 to foreclose on Addison Ice Arena, a 73,000-square-foot complex at 475 South Grace Street in suburban Addison with one Olympic-size and one NHL-size rink. The bank alleges that Addison Ice, LLC and its owner defaulted on a $9.5 million loan made in late 2021, and that the full $9.5 million remains unpaid, with costs still accruing. According to the complaint, the bank accelerated the loan after the borrower missed its July and August 2026 principal and interest payments and stopped making tax reserve deposits in April. The bank's filings allege that from August 2025 through July 2026 the owner moved more than $1 million from the arena's operating accounts to family members who do not work at the rink, and spent more than $116,000 of facility money on personal life insurance premiums. The suit also alleges that a broken compressor shut down one rink, forcing anchor tenant Team Illinois AAA Hockey Club to buy ice time elsewhere, and that a leaking roof nearly 50 years old caused mold. The owner and his wife personally guaranteed the loan and are also defendants. On September 30, 2026, Judge Robert G. Gibson placed the arena under the control of receiver Matthew Brash of Newpoint Advisors Corporation, who is authorized to run operations, pay for urgent repairs and explore selling the property as a going concern. The defendants' attorney, David Madden, told The Real Deal that the bank "has misrepresented the funding of the facility in its motion for a receiver." He added that the defendants "fully supported the appointment of the receiver," proposed accelerating it by consent, and will cooperate with the receiver. The defendants' formal response was due October 28, 2026. The Real Deal reported that the arena stayed open after the order, with skaters on the ice during a reporter's visit. The bank's attorney did not return requests for comment, and Brash declined to comment.
live-222: American Hospitality Properties REIT, Inc. and 15 affiliates, including American Hospitality Properties REIT II, Inc., filed voluntary Chapter 11 petitions on October 4, 2026 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Northern District of Texas, WhatNow reported, citing PACER records. The affiliates include a master-lease entity and hotel-owning entities in locations including Cape Canaveral, Bentonville, Baton Rouge, Fayetteville, Fort Myers, Jonesboro, Metairie and Charlotte. The REITs own hotels operated under Marriott and Hilton brands; WhatNow noted the petition does not indicate that either hotel company owns the REIT. The case, No. 26-80071, is assigned to Judge Stacey G.C. Jernigan. According to WhatNow, the board approved the filing after reviewing the company's financial condition, liquidity and obligations. The chief restructuring officer signed the petition, and Vinson & Elkins LLP and FTI Consulting were retained as counsel and financial advisor. The petition lists estimated liabilities of $1,000,001 to $10 million and estimated assets of $0 to $50,000. Its largest unsecured creditors include Marriott International, Inc. (about $1.94 million in franchise fees), Hilton Hotels Corporation (about $191,364 in franchise fees), PAH Management (management fees), Spirit Realty LP (ground rent) and Deutsche Bank AG (a bank loan). Phoenix American Hospitality, LLC (PAH) was the external manager of both REITs until the REITs ended their management agreements effective May 20, 2026, according to SEC filings cited by WhatNow. On June 4, 2026, the SEC filed a settled action against PAH and its president in federal court in Dallas; the court entered judgments the next day, the docket shows. The SEC alleged the two raised about $86 million from more than 2,000 retail investors between March 2022 and July 2024 through two hotel funds, that neither fund was profitable despite claimed distributions of up to 12%, and that investors were told REIT I had acquired about 11 hotels when it held one until January 2024. Without admitting or denying the claims, PAH agreed to pay $591,127 and Nelson $118,225, and Nelson agreed to a five-year officer-and-director bar. On September 15, 2026, Proven Business Skills Inc filed suit against PAH in the same federal court (No. 3:26-cv-03130). A notice from the firm Federman & Sherwood, published on Business Wire, described it as a securities class action against PAH, both REITs and Nelson on behalf of investors who bought between March 2022 and July 2024. As of mid-November, the bankruptcy docket showed a November 24, 2026 hearing set on the debtors' cash collateral, cash management and automatic-stay motions.
live-223: The Greater DC Diaper Bank, a nonprofit, sued its warehouse landlord, WWDC Industrial Park, LLC, and the property manager, Donohoe Real Estate Services, Inc., alleging that a leaking roof at its warehouse on Monard Drive in Silver Spring went unrepaired for years, WJLA/7News reported on September 4, 2026. According to the complaint as described by 7News, the leaks worsened from 2024, staff covered products with tarps and moved inventory during rain and snow, and the nonprofit notified the defendants more than a dozen times, but repairs were delayed or were temporary fixes that failed. A Montgomery County health inspector reportedly found the warehouse unsuitable for receiving and storing items such as baby food and formula, and the Diaper Bank stopped operating there in February 2025. The nonprofit says conditions forced it to close its Baby Pantry program, whose distributed value fell from about $930,000 in 2024 to $313,000 in 2025. It also alleges that at a January 15 meeting the parties agreed to terms that included more than $47,000 in rent abatement and termination of the lease if it vacated, and that after it left the defendants backed away and demanded more rent. The complaint asserts breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of quiet enjoyment, constructive eviction and promissory estoppel and seeks more than $775,000 plus pre-judgment interest. 7News said it had not heard back from WWDC or Donohoe. Court records show the case was filed in D.C. Superior Court (No. 2026-CAB-004696) and removed by WWDC to the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia on August 17, 2026. On August 24, WWDC filed a counterclaim against the Diaper Bank and a motion to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction or to transfer, and Donohoe moved to dismiss. On September 14, Judge Timothy J. Kelly granted a joint motion to transfer the case to the District of Maryland, where it was docketed on September 28 (No. 8:26-cv-03821) and assigned to Judge Deborah K. Chasanow.
live-224: The City of Cleveland has asked to join Fannie Mae's federal foreclosure case over Reserve Square, News 5 Cleveland reported. The motion to intervene was filed September 28, 2026 in Fannie Mae v. Reserve Apartments, Ltd., No. 1:25-cv-01510 in the Northern District of Ohio, before Judge Bridget Meehan Brennan, according to the docket. The city says the property is a public nuisance and that the receiver is not doing enough about 19 open violation notices covering dozens of issues, including elevator outages, water damage and parking-garage deterioration. "We were patient for a long time," Law Director Mark Griffin told News 5, adding that the city "felt that we had to step in." It wants every violation fixed, the current owner held accountable and future owners kept from neglecting the building. A city spokesman said demolition is not being considered at this time. Reserve Square covers a downtown block off East 12th Street between Chester and Superior avenues, with 975 apartments in two 1970s towers, a garage of nearly 1,000 spaces and about 220,000 square feet of commercial space, News 5 reported. It is about 80% vacant. Fannie Mae began the foreclosure in July 2025 over more than $78 million in unpaid principal, interest and fees, and the owner, an affiliate of Willoughby-based K&D Group, cooperated; K&D's CEO blamed a vacancy surge tied to federal immigration policy changes and the loss of international students for making refinancing impossible. The Michigan-based Hayman Company took over as receiver in August 2025. The docket shows the court entered an in rem judgment and judgment in mortgage foreclosure on consent on April 14, 2026, and later confirmed that the receivership remains in place. After a February 2026 letter of concern from the city, the court ordered the receiver to file weekly status reports. The receiver's reports describe removing squatters, treating bedbugs, new cleaning and security crews, and contractors working on water damage and elevators, according to News 5. The property is listed for sale with Institutional Property Advisors, part of Marcus & Millichap, with no asking price. The receiver did not respond to News 5's requests for comment.
live-226: Oak Land and Development LLC, Veritas Development LLC and six other entities that own and operate OAK, a retail and mixed-use development in Oklahoma City, sued Simon Property Group, Inc., Simon Property Group, L.P. and the Penn Square Mall entity on December 2, 2025 in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma (No. 5:25-cv-01444), according to the docket. News 9 reported the suit the next day. The two properties sit across the street from each other at North Pennsylvania Avenue and Northwest Expressway. The case is assigned to U.S. District Judge Patrick R. Wyrick, and the plaintiffs have demanded a jury. The plaintiffs allege Simon worked "to destroy" OAK by using threats or inducements involving leases at Simon properties in other cities to coerce tenants into locating at Penn Square or forgoing OAK. They describe the conduct as "a classic 'tying' arrangement" and bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act, the Oklahoma Antitrust Reform Act and for tortious interference. According to Simon's motion summarizing the complaint, the tenants at issue include the restaurant chain North Italia, which opened at Penn Square instead, and the retailers Alo and Aritzia. The plaintiffs amended their complaint twice, and in April 2026 they voluntarily dismissed Simon's former chief executive, David Simon, as a defendant. A Simon spokesperson told News 9 that the suit is "meritless and fictional" and that Simon plans to keep bringing new tenants to Penn Square. In its June 2, 2026 motion to dismiss the second amended complaint, Simon argues the plaintiffs fail to define the tying markets or show market power, that the alleged threats lack basic detail, that a few tenants choosing Penn Square is not substantial foreclosure, and that OAK, as a competitor, lacks antitrust standing. The motion notes that OAK has won national tenants, including some that left Penn Square. The plaintiffs filed their opposition in July and Simon replied in August 2026; the court has not ruled.
live-228: BusinessDen reported on June 4, 2026 that the owners of 76 Commerce Center, an industrial park in Brighton, Colorado, have sued their tenant, BroadRange Logistics LLC, for $32 million. The plaintiffs, 76 Commerce Center LLC and 76 Commerce Center 3 LLC, are tied to Hyde Development and Mortenson Properties. BroadRange, a Georgia-based third-party logistics company, leased more than 1.1 million square feet at the park in 2024, a deal BusinessDen described as the largest speculative lease in state history. According to the landlords, BroadRange's tenancy of two buildings at 22250 and 22500 E. I-76 Frontage Road began in September 2024 with six months of free rent. They allege the company began missing its roughly $590,000 monthly rent by August 2025, owed $3.6 million by October 2025, signed an amended lease in November 2025 and kept defaulting until its leases were terminated on March 13, 2026. They seek about $8.9 million in back rent, $17.4 million to recover a discretionary tenant-improvement allowance and $3 million in rent abatement they say became repayable on default, plus interest and late fees. The Real Deal reported in July that BroadRange faces other landlord suits, including one filed in New York state court by KSG, the owner of a Pennsylvania warehouse, over an $11 million tenant-improvement allowance. The Real Deal said BroadRange has denied the allegations in court filings.
live-229: KSG, the owner of a 600,000-square-foot warehouse in Mount Pocono, Pennsylvania, has sued Georgia-based BroadRange Logistics in New York state court to recover an $11 million tenant-improvement allowance plus other costs. The suit, filed in May 2026, alleges that BroadRange signed a 20-year triple-net lease and collected the allowance but never intended to make the improvements, and that it stopped paying rent. KSG paid the allowance partly with proceeds of a $32 million commercial mortgage-backed loan it took from Ocean First Bank in connection with the lease. According to the complaint, NFI Industries leased the building until it moved out in 2024. A New Jersey investor then agreed to buy the property for $37 million but backed out in July 2025, citing financing. He instead offered to introduce KSG to BroadRange if KSG would pay the tenant an allowance up front. KSG alleges that BroadRange misstated its finances, missed rent within a month of signing, later claimed the lease included six months of free rent, and in January 2026 stopped paying while citing problems getting a certificate of occupancy. KSG declared the lease void in February 2026 and demanded the allowance back; it says the money was never returned. KSG claims none of the allowance was spent on the property. It says that nine days after receiving the money, BroadRange wired nearly $2 million to the investor's company, Winthrop Equities, as a commission, even though the investor had assured KSG in writing he would receive no more than $100,000. KSG is suing BroadRange and the investor for fraudulent inducement, suing BroadRange for unjust enrichment and breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and seeking to void the commission payment as a fraudulent transfer under Georgia law. BroadRange has denied the allegations in court filings and argues the lease allowed it to use the allowance for "any other business purpose." KSG also sued the attorney it hired to negotiate the lease, alleging he left out any provision letting KSG recover the allowance if BroadRange broke its promises. His lawyer told The Real Deal the claims have "absolutely no merit" and that he plans to move to dismiss. The Real Deal also reported that warehouse owners in Colorado and Texas have sued BroadRange. The Colorado suit concerns two leases near Denver and a $17.4 million allowance. The Texas suit concerns a 648,000-square-foot Houston warehouse whose owner says it is owed more than $44.8 million. BroadRange has denied those allegations as well.
live-230: Eagan Capital, a data center owner, has sued the City of Eagan over the one-year moratorium the city adopted in February 2026 on development projects that would use more than 20 megawatts of electricity within 500 feet of homes, MPR News reported on July 7, 2026. The complaint, filed June 15, argues the city has no authority to regulate electricity and quotes the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission's "exclusive authority to regulate electricity demand in Minnesota." The company seeks $50,000 in damages. According to MPR News, Eagan was the first Minnesota city to impose a hard pause on data centers, and the moratorium does not appear to affect the city's two existing data centers. The city told MPR News that it denied Eagan Capital an interim use permit after staff found temporary trailer-mounted chiller units had been installed and operated without required permits, and that the City Council denied the permit in May because the proposed use was not lawful under the property's current zoning. The city said it is "confident in its position" and will vigorously defend the moratorium.
live-231: DCB Nashville, LLC, a subsidiary of DC BLOX Parent LLC, sued Metro Nashville in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee on August 11, 2026, seeking to strike down the city's moratorium on data centers, Axios Nashville reported. According to the court's later opinion, the company closed on the purchase of about 23.49 acres at 648 and 650 Grassmere Park Drive, next to the Nashville Zoo, for about $23 million on July 16, 2026. The complaint says Asurion previously ran office and data center functions on the property under Metro permits. Axios reported that after the zoo raised concerns about the project's effect on its animals and more than 500,000 people signed a petition opposing it, the Metro Council imposed a moratorium until December 1 and created new rules for data centers. The lawsuit calls the moratorium "a targeted attack against DC Blox," alleges that Metro kept processing another pending data center application while putting the company's demolition, grading and building permits on hold, and argues the project is vested because a data center was allowed there when it applied. Axios reported that Metro officials have signaled they disagree that the property is vested. The company had offered to subdivide the property so the zoo could acquire the remainder. On October 6, Judge Eli J. Richardson granted Metro's motion to dismiss the class-of-one equal protection count, finding no similarly situated comparator plausibly alleged. He also dismissed the substantive due process, procedural due process and takings counts, which depend on a protected property interest, without prejudice to refiling within 21 days. He declined jurisdiction over five state-law declaratory judgment counts, dismissing them without prejudice, and denied the preliminary injunction motion as moot. The docket shows DCB Nashville filed an amended complaint and a motion for reconsideration on October 27, and the court ruled on that motion on October 29.
live-232: Fox Investments LLC filed a complaint on July 23, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin against the City of Kaukauna and insurers Sentry, The Travelers Indemnity Company and Employers Insurance Company of Wausau, plus a placeholder "ABC Insurance Company" for any carrier not yet identified, Insurance Business reported. The property, at 400 Fox Shores Drive, is the Fox Shore Apartments complex, which Fox and affiliated parties owned in whole or in part from about February 1998 to January 2020. Fox alleges the city owned and operated the site from 1967 to 1974, when it was part of a former railyard with a roundhouse, after buying it to clear for redevelopment. It alleges, on information and belief, that the city spread contamination across the property and adjoining land when it burned the structures in November 1974. In 2018, a lender's Phase II Environmental Site Assessment found heavy metals, including arsenic, cadmium, lead, selenium and mercury, in the soil and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in the groundwater at levels the filing says exceeded state standards. Fox reported the contamination to the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources under the state's Spill Law. On January 17, 2019, the DNR named Fox a responsible party and directed it to investigate and clean up the site, which it did through Stantec Consulting; the DNR closed the site on May 10, 2022. Fox seeks $235,683.63 in investigation and remediation costs. Fox claims the city is strictly liable under CERCLA as a past owner or operator at the time of disposal, and also brings negligence and unjust-enrichment claims, alleging the city later hired Stantec and benefited from work Fox paid for. Under Wisconsin's direct-action statute, Wis. Stat. § 632.24, it sues insurers it alleges, on information and belief, covered the city during its ownership; the filing does not identify policy periods or numbers. Insurance Business reported no response from the defendants.
live-235: The Connecticut Appellate Court on March 17, 2026 upheld a $16.8 million jury verdict against the City of Danbury in a dispute over a commercial building addition at the Party Depot store on South Street, according to the published decision, 238 Conn. App. 1 (2026), and a press release from the plaintiffs' counsel. The panel of Judges Seeley, Wilson and Keller rejected the arguments of the city and its building official except for a $280,000 remittitur for money the plaintiffs received from a settling party long before trial. The plaintiffs, the store's owners and their companies, including Party Depot, Inc. and 43 South Street LLC, built a roughly 30,000-square-foot addition intended for wholesale storage and sales displays, Patch reported. They later found it did not meet building code requirements and could not be used for its intended purpose. After a five-week trial in Waterbury Superior Court before Judge W. Glenn Pierson, a jury on October 6, 2023 returned a $16,843,750 verdict, finding the city and one of its building officials acted with reckless disregard for the health and safety of the public during permitting and construction. Judge Pierson entered judgment on March 27, 2024. The Appellate Court remanded the case to the Complex Litigation Docket in Waterbury to apply the remittitur and add statutory interest at 10% a year. The plaintiffs' counsel said that would bring the city's debt to more than $20 million; Danbury's mayor's office cited an approximately $16 million judgment plus about $1.6 million a year in interest. Danbury officials told Patch the city will ask the Connecticut Supreme Court to review and overturn the ruling, arguing the court should have read the statutes narrowly when deciding whether a municipality can be made to pay damages, and warning of a "dangerous precedent" for towns and cities statewide.
live-236: Wixom Industrial One, LLC filed suit against the City of Wixom on August 7, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, alleging the city violated the state's zoning act, WHMI reported, citing Crain's Detroit. The complaint seeks declaratory judgment, injunctive relief and damages, according to the court docket (No. 2:26-cv-12754, assigned to Judge Robert J. White). The property is 54 acres on South Wixom Road north of Interstate 96, assembled for an industrial park by the company's developer according to WHMI. After Missouri real estate firm Sansone Group approached the developer, the site was pitched for a data center. Exhibits to the complaint identify the site as 30625 S. Wixom Road and include a city email stating that the parcel is zoned M-1, Light Industrial. The city adopted a six-month moratorium on data center development after public sentiment shifted, and in July the City Council rejected a proposed waiver from it. The developer alleges the city used its rough site plan for a three-building, 519,400-square-foot campus to write ordinances that would effectively bar data center development on property zoned for it, and it describes itself as the victim of a council more concerned with public opinion than with the law, according to WHMI. live-237: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit has denied a petition for rehearing en banc filed by Whitestone Uptown Tower, LLC, closing out -- absent a petition for certiorari -- one of the last open fronts in a years-long partnership and bankruptcy dispute between Pillarstone Capital REIT and Whitestone REIT. The denial, entered October 5, 2026, follows the panel's September 4, 2026 affirmance of a district court ruling that had itself affirmed a bankruptcy-court decision adverse to Whitestone Uptown Tower's position. Pillarstone disclosed the sequence of events in its Form 10-Q filed with the SEC on October 7, 2026. The litigation traces back to a shareholder rights plan Pillarstone Capital REIT adopted on December 27, 2021, with American Stock Transfer & Trust Company serving as rights agent. Whitestone REIT Operating Partnership, L.P., which holds the sole limited-partner interest in Pillarstone's operating partnership, took the position that the rights plan breached the partnership's Amended and Restated Agreement of Limited Partnership and the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing. Whitestone OP sued in the Delaware Court of Chancery, and on January 25, 2024 the court ruled in Whitestone's favor, finding the rights plan breached the implied covenant and clearing the way for Whitestone to exercise a contractual redemption right. Pillarstone, in turn, sued in Texas: on September 16, 2022, Pillarstone Capital REIT and its operating partnership filed Cause No. 2022-59478 in the 189th Judicial District Court of Harris County, alleging the Whitestone entities breached the limited partnership agreement, related management agreements, and their fiduciary duties. The dispute then migrated into bankruptcy court -- Chapter 11 cases were filed for Pillarstone Capital REIT and its operating partnership on March 4, 2024 -- where Whitestone Uptown Tower, LLC pressed a claim the bankruptcy court ruled against. A federal district court affirmed that ruling, Whitestone Uptown Tower appealed to the Fifth Circuit on August 13, 2025, the panel affirmed on September 4, 2026, and the full court denied rehearing en banc on October 5, 2026. Pillarstone's filing states Whitestone Uptown Tower 'is considering its available options.' This appellate fight proceeded on a separate track from the broader monetary settlement the two REIT families reached in December 2025 under Bankruptcy Rule 9019, in which Pillarstone's operating partnership paid Whitestone approximately $33.4 million tied to a guaranty obligation connected to the Uptown Tower property, with Pillarstone Capital REIT itself recovering roughly $4.05 million. That settlement resolved the bulk of the parties' monetary claims; the appeal decided this month addressed a bankruptcy-court ruling that fell outside its scope. For REIT boards and general counsel, the case is a reminder that a shareholder rights plan adopted against a counterparty that also holds a governance or partnership stake can trigger years of derivative litigation spanning state chancery court, state trial court, and the federal bankruptcy and appellate systems at once -- and that a global settlement rarely closes every open issue when the same parties are tied together through multiple, overlapping legal instruments. Boards should track the full appellate chain independently of any settlement reached elsewhere in a dispute, since release language negotiated in one forum may not reach a claim already pending on appeal in another, and a denial of rehearing en banc does not itself end a case so long as a certiorari petition remains available.
live-239: Preferred stockholders of Cedar Realty Trust, Inc. have reached a proposed $8.5 million cash settlement of a stockholder class action pending in the Circuit Court for Montgomery County, Maryland (Case No. C-15-cv-25-000731), according to a summary notice issued under a court order and distributed on PR Newswire on August 3, 2026. live-250: White Sulphur Springs Holdings LLC (WSSH), a company set up by Texas-based TRT Holdings, parent of Omni Hotels & Resorts, filed suit on April 9, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia against Greenbrier Hotel Corporation, other Greenbrier entities and members of the Justice family, the federal docket shows. live-251: Deutsche Bank has sued to foreclose on Pembroke Lakes Mall, a 748,800-square-foot regional mall at 11701 Pines Boulevard in Pembroke Pines, Florida. live-256: A customer slipped and fell on a puddle of clear liquid in the toy aisle of an H-E-B grocery store and sued. Because she could not show H-E-B actually knew about the puddle, she relied on constructive notice, pointing to roof leaks in other parts of the store during a remodeling project (none documented above the toy aisle), water she said she saw dripping from a ceiling rafter, a companion's initial account of dripping that was later recanted, the puddle's size, earlier rain, and her claim that no employee had inspected the aisle for about two hours. She admitted she had no idea how long the puddle had been there, according to a law-firm summary published on JD Supra. The trial court granted summary judgment for H-E-B, finding no fact issue on constructive notice, and excluded parts of her expert's testimony. The Thirteenth Court of Appeals reversed. The Supreme Court of Texas granted H-E-B's petition for review in No. 24-0310, heard argument on Dec. 3, 2025, and on April 10, 2026 reversed the court of appeals and reinstated the trial court's judgment in an opinion by Justice Bland, according to the court's docket. The court held that constructive notice requires evidence of how long the specific condition existed before the fall. Leaks elsewhere in the store, speculation about where the liquid came from, the size of the puddle and the store's inspection practices did not establish that duration. For retailers and other commercial property owners in Texas, the decision supports summary judgment when a plaintiff's notice evidence goes to the property's general condition rather than to how long the specific hazard existed. Inspection records and video of the area bear directly on that question.
live-257: Hexa Builders, a Princeton-based developer, wants to build a 1-million-square-foot data center and warehouse in Monroe Township, Gloucester County, the New Jersey Monitor reported. live-258: A man who said he slipped and fell on black ice in a Delaware shopping-center parking lot sued the center's owner, Cedar Christina Crossing, LLC, and Eastern LLC, the contractor it hired for snow removal, in Superior Court, alleging they negligently treated snow and ice in the lot. In his deposition he testified that he saw unplowed snow in the lot on the day he fell and saw a person plowing snow. The defendants offered maintenance records showing the lot had been treated earlier, weather data showing no precipitation after that treatment, and surveillance video showing the lot clear and dry with no snow removal under way when he fell, according to a law-firm summary published on JD Supra. The Superior Court granted summary judgment for the defendants, and on March 23, 2026 a three-justice panel of the Delaware Supreme Court affirmed in an order written by Justice Griffiths. Applying Ridgeway v. Acme Markets, Inc., the court said that once the defendants showed reasonable care in addressing snow and ice, the burden shifted to the plaintiff, who offered only self-contradictory testimony that the video refuted and so raised no genuine issue of material fact. For commercial landlords and their snow-removal vendors, the decision shows the weight Delaware courts give to objective records, such as video, treatment logs and weather data, when a plaintiff's account of conditions conflicts with them.
live-259: Shareholders of Franklin BSP Realty Trust, Inc., a publicly traded commercial mortgage REIT trading as NYSE: FBRT, filed a putative securities class action in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York on February 26, 2026. live-260: The Port of Tacoma filed suit on February 20, 2026 against PQ LLC, a Pennsylvania chemical company, in federal court in Tacoma, according to the complaint on CourtListener. live-262: Quantum Maryland LLC, which is managed by Catellus Maryland, filed suit on Thursday, October 8, 2026, in Frederick County Circuit Court against Frederick County, County Executive Jessica Fitzwater and the Frederick County Planning Commission, the Frederick News-Post reported. live-263: Three affiliates of Denver-based Broe Cos., GWIP Land Company LLC, Windsor Renewal I, LLC and GWIP, LLC, filed a 24-page complaint in Weld District Court on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, docketed as Case No. 2026CV31187, BizWest reported. live-264: Microsoft filed suit against JLL on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, in New York County Supreme Court, Bisnow reported on Oct. 12. live-265: Southbridge Associates LLC filed a voluntary Chapter 11 petition in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Massachusetts on October 6, 2026 (Case No. 26-41208). live-266: Travis Property Owner LLC filed a voluntary Chapter 11 petition on October 6, 2026 (Case No. 26-90220), and the case is assigned to U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Mark X. Mullin in Fort Worth. ACORE, acting as administrative agent for the lenders, says the June 10, 2022 loan was for up to $73,407,750, that the debtor owed $74,734,511.36 on the petition date, and that the loan has been in payment default since April 2026.
