live-267: The loan dates to July 2014, when Stradtman Park, LLC borrowed $3.6 million from KeyBank National Association against a commercial property that the court described as worth about $7 million. The loan documents allowed KeyBank to assign and securitize the loan, and in October 2014 it was assigned to Wilmington Trust, National Association, as trustee for the holders of JPMBB Commercial Mortgage Securities Trust 2014-C24, and pooled into a commercial mortgage-backed security under a pooling and servicing agreement. The borrower never signed that agreement. LNR Partners, LLC was designated special servicer for the loan if it became distressed or defaulted. According to the opinion, the borrower paid as agreed from 2014 into early 2020: $18,779.30 a month in principal and interest plus $20,300.39 a month into reserve accounts for taxes, insurance, maintenance and repairs, for a total monthly payment of $39,079.69. In 2019 the borrower sought approvals and reserve draws for lease renewals, expansions and contractor payments. Although the loan was performing, LNR became the point of contact, and the borrower contends LNR stalled its requests and forced it to cover costs out of pocket despite ample reserves. Starting in May 2020 the borrower paid only principal and interest and told the servicer to apply the payments that way. The lender side instead spread the payments across principal, interest and reserves, which produced a default. In November 2020 the borrower stopped turning over rents, and the trustee sued to foreclose. The trial court, Erie County Supreme Court Justice Emilio Colaiacovo, granted partial summary judgment to the trustee on foreclosure and on its right to the rents, a ruling the borrower did not appeal. Skeptical of the fees claimed, the court then held a damages hearing. It awarded the full $583,938.25 in default-rate interest the trustee asked for but refused another $120,882.59 in note-rate interest, reasoning that the default rate was set five percentage points above the note rate and that the trustee had not documented how its default-interest figure was calculated, so awarding both would double count. On attorneys' fees, the borrower's expert testified that a customary rate for experienced commercial foreclosure counsel in Western New York ran $350 to $450 an hour, while the trustee's witness testified that LNR was paying $650 to $800 an hour for partners and $350 to $575 for associates. The invoices did not break out rates by entry. The court cut the roughly $588,000 request to $250,000 and remarked that the trustee had come "perilously close" to losing the whole judgment over its fee demand. On appeal, the trustee argued the trial court misread the loan documents. The Fourth Department acknowledged that unambiguous contracts are enforced as written, but stressed that a foreclosure invokes the court's equitable powers, which reach as far as fairness requires. It held that the plaintiff bears the burden of proving damages at an inquest, that the duplicative-interest ruling rested on a fair view of the evidence, and that contractual fee-shifting is enforceable only for reasonable fees for services actually rendered, measured against hours, rates and what comparable local lawyers charge. The court found no abuse of discretion in the $250,000 award and rejected the trustee's remaining challenges. For lenders and servicers, the practical lesson is documentation. A default-interest claim should show its own arithmetic, and a fee petition should identify the rate for each timekeeper and entry, especially where the servicer uses big-city counsel in a smaller market. Courts will compare those rates to local norms, and an aggressive request can damage credibility on the rest of the judgment. For borrowers, the case shows the value of contesting fee and interest components at the damages stage even after losing on liability: here, a borrower that conceded foreclosure still held the securitized lender to well under half of its claimed fees.
live-268: Long Street Associates, LLP owns the building at 31-55 West Long Street in Columbus, which the lease acknowledged is listed on the national register of historic buildings. On December 9, 2019, it leased the unfinished space to the Young Men's Christian Association of Central Ohio. The lease set out a process for building out the premises: the landlord would furnish preliminary plans, the parties would work in good faith toward final plans, and the landlord would then prepare a construction budget. The landlord was to contribute a tenant-improvement allowance of $30 per square foot, about $323,100, and the YMCA agreed to fund up to $200,000 more, amortized over the initial term at five percent interest, and to pay any excess beyond that. The key provision, Section 10.10, gave the tenant a one-time right to terminate if the construction budget showed improvement costs above a fixed threshold of roughly $523,100, exercisable by written notice within seven days of receiving the budget. On July 30, 2020, the YMCA received a budget showing costs of $1,036,697.38, nearly double the threshold. On August 6, 2020, it gave written notice that it was terminating under Section 10.10. The landlord asked it to withdraw the notice and proposed in writing to share the overrun costs, but no written modification was ever signed. The landlord sued in November 2020 in the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas for declaratory judgment, breach of contract and anticipatory breach, and argued on appeal that the tenant had used the clause to escape the lease because of pandemic-era financial strain. The trial court granted the YMCA summary judgment in May 2024, finding that final plans had been reached and that a budget exceeding the threshold had been delivered, which triggered the termination right. After a remand to resolve the YMCA's claim for attorneys' fees under the lease, the parties entered an agreed fee judgment in January 2026, and the landlord appealed again. Writing for the panel, the court rejected each of the landlord's arguments. The landlord said the spreadsheet sent on July 30 was not the lease's construction budget and that final plans had not been agreed, but its own complaint alleged that it sent the budget in accordance with Section 10.10 after the final plans were finalized. The court treated those allegations as judicial admissions and noted the lease draws no line between an initial and a final budget. The landlord next said it had orally offered on August 6 to cover costs above the threshold, so the budget never really exceeded it. The court held that such an offer would be a material change to price terms, and the lease's no-oral-modification clause required any change to be in a signed writing. Finally, the court found that approvals from the Ohio Historic Preservation Office and the National Park Service, which bore on historic tax credits, were not a condition precedent to the final plans. The takeaways for owners are concrete. If a lease gives the tenant an exit when build-out costs exceed a cap, the landlord should control when and how the budget is delivered, label preliminary numbers clearly, and recognize that any budget sent after plans are settled may start the clock. Fixes to a cost overrun need to be papered and signed before the option window closes, not negotiated by phone afterward. Pleadings matter too: describing a document in a complaint as the one the lease requires can foreclose arguing otherwise later. For tenants, the decision confirms that a cleanly drafted cost-overrun termination right, exercised on time and in writing, will hold up.
live-269: H. Roske & Associates LLP was a commercial tenant of ESRT Empire State Building LLC. It sued its landlord in New York County Supreme Court (Index No. 655283/24), asserting a claim for constructive eviction and a claim that the landlord had breached the lease. Justice Lyle E. Frank granted the landlord's motion to dismiss the complaint, and judgment was entered on June 6, 2025. The tenant appealed. In a short unanimous decision dated October 6, 2026, a four-justice panel of the First Department affirmed on several independent grounds. First, the court found that the tenant had expressly waived its constructive eviction rights in the lease, which by itself barred the claim. The panel relied on recent and older First Department precedent holding that a commercial tenant who gives up constructive eviction remedies in its lease cannot later sue on that theory. Second, the court held that even if there had been no waiver, the claim was inadequately pleaded. Under the long-standing Court of Appeals standard, constructive eviction requires that the landlord's conduct have substantially and materially deprived the tenant of the beneficial use and enjoyment of the premises. The panel found that neither the complaint nor the tenant's affidavits explained how that threshold was met. Third, the court held that the separate breach-of-lease claim was properly dismissed because the tenant did not point to any specific lease provision the landlord had violated. Having resolved the appeal on those grounds, the court did not reach the parties' other arguments. Constructive eviction matters in commercial leasing because it is one of the main theories a tenant can invoke when building conditions interfere with its business, and landlords commonly try to contract around it. This decision confirms that the First Department will enforce an express waiver of the remedy as written and will do so at the motion-to-dismiss stage, before any factual record is developed. The court's alternative holding adds a second hurdle: even an unwaived claim must be pleaded with specifics showing a substantial and material loss of use, not general dissatisfaction with the premises. For owners and asset managers, the practical point is that a clear waiver of constructive eviction can dispose of a tenant's suit on a motion to dismiss, saving the cost of discovery over building conditions. For tenants and their counsel, the decision underscores two lessons: negotiate the waiver, or at least carve out serious interruptions of service or access, before signing; and when suing, tie each breach claim to an identified lease covenant and plead concrete facts showing how much of the premises became unusable and for how long. Generalized complaints about building conditions, without that detail, are unlikely to survive in the First Department.
live-270: The underlying case, filed in New York County Supreme Court under Index No. 657290/19, concerns an HVAC system that Henick-Lane, Inc. installed at property owned by 5 Beekman Property Owner, LLC. The owner and Broadway Construction Group, LLC allege the system leaked, damaging the owner's property and forcing them to spend money containing the damage, and they sued for breach of contract. Henick-Lane counterclaimed for nonpayment and to foreclose a mechanic's lien. Those claims remain pending. While the parties were negotiating, one of Henick-Lane's insurers, apparently believing a deal had been reached, sent $850,000 to Broadway Construction Group even though no final settlement agreement existed. The check described itself as a settlement payment on behalf of Henick-Lane. Justice Andrew Borrok ordered the plaintiffs to give the money back with interest, later held them in civil contempt for not doing so, and entered judgment against them on December 11, 2025 for $850,000 plus prejudgment interest. The plaintiffs appealed the judgment and the contempt order. The First Department affirmed across the board. On procedure, it held that the judgment brought up the earlier disgorgement order for review under the doctrine of implied severance, because the fight over the mistaken payment was separate from the HVAC defect, nonpayment and lien claims still in the case. On standing, which the plaintiffs raised for the first time on appeal, the court held Henick-Lane had a real stake in the money because its insurer paid on its behalf out of a policy Henick-Lane paid for, and it was injured when the plaintiffs kept funds without a settlement. On the merits, the court rejected the plaintiffs' reliance on the voluntary payment doctrine, which bars recovering money paid voluntarily with full knowledge of the facts. The panel reasoned that the insurer had effectively reserved its rights by labeling the check a settlement payment, and because no settlement existed, the payment rested on a mistake rather than a knowing choice. The court also upheld the contempt finding. Although New York's Judiciary Law does not allow contempt to enforce a money judgment, no judgment existed when the contempt order issued, and the court rejected Broadway Construction Group's argument that it could not be held in contempt because the disgorgement order did not name it, noting the plaintiffs' own representative said both plaintiffs received and deposited the check. For owners, developers and general contractors, the decision draws a firm line: a payment from the other side's carrier during settlement talks is not money in hand until the settlement is actually signed, and keeping it once the court orders its return can lead to contempt sanctions on top of a judgment with interest. For contractors and insurers, the case shows the value of describing every payment's purpose on its face, which preserves the ability to recover it if the deal falls apart. The underlying defect and lien claims will continue in the trial court, so the merits of the HVAC dispute remain open.
live-271: Computershare Trust Company, National Association, as trustee for the holders of the BMO 2024-5C5 Mortgage Trust certificates, filed a breach-of-contract suit against Starwood Mortgage Capital LLC in the Supreme Court of New York, New York County, on September 4, 2026, Mortgage Professional America reported. live-272: Milwaukee County Circuit Judge William Pocan entered an order on October 6, 2026 approving the sale of Southridge Mall in Greendale, a Milwaukee suburb, according to Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reporting republished by The Daily Reporter. live-273: The premises are Suite A at 33501 Lake Road in Avon Lake, Ohio, a roughly 15,000-square-foot space in a shopping center. Beach Park Railway, LLC used the space to operate a museum it established with state grant money, and in 2019 it signed a non-disturbance and estoppel agreement with the Ohio Facilities Commission and the then-owner protecting the Commission's interest. The tenant originally occupied as a subtenant of TBP Avon Lake, LLC, paying $583 a month. After TBP sold the property and leased it back, Stop 65, LLC acquired the shopping center, evicted TBP in a separate Lorain County case decided in March 2024, and became the museum operator's direct landlord. Inspecting the space after that case ended, the landlord's representative concluded the museum occupied only about a quarter of it. Deposition testimony and photographs showed an individual running a private motorcycle-repair business out of the warehouse area, storing large quantities of parts, and apparently living on site, with the tenant's board member acknowledging the arrangement and payments toward utilities of at least $1,100. On March 22, 2024 the landlord served a contractual 30-day notice of default for unauthorized subleasing and storing items outside the leased area. The tenant responded that it had ended subleases with two entities and cured, but the landlord served a statutory three-day notice to vacate on April 29 and filed a forcible entry and detainer action on May 3, 2024. The tenant counterclaimed on six counts, including retaliatory eviction, failure to repair with rent abatement, tortious interference, breach of quiet enjoyment and breach of the lease's maintenance duties. The municipal court dismissed the counterclaim in July 2024, granted the landlord summary judgment on the unauthorized-sublease breach in April 2025, and issued a writ of restitution, which was stayed on bond pending appeal. A panel of Seventh District judges sitting by assignment affirmed on every assignment of error. On the central question, the court held that the arrangement was a sublease as a matter of law: the occupant had exclusive possession of dedicated space, used it for a business unrelated to the museum and as a residence, and kept it month after month, so the parties' own labels did not matter. The court rejected the tenant's waiver and estoppel arguments. It held that Ohio's statutory 30-day notice to terminate a tenancy does not govern commercial leases, and that the lease's 30-day language attached to the landlord's optional self-help remedy, not to a court eviction. On the counterclaims, it upheld dismissal of the repair and quiet-enjoyment counts, largely because the arguments the tenant pressed on appeal, including those about the non-disturbance agreement's written notice-of-default requirement, had not been preserved in its response to the dismissal motion. Finally, the municipal court did not have to transfer the case to common pleas court merely because the counterclaim demanded more than its $15,000 limit, once the counts offered to justify that demand were dismissed. The opinion is long and fact-specific, but its holdings travel well. Anti-subletting clauses in shopping-center and industrial leases often collide with informal uses by a tenant's affiliates, volunteers or friends, and the court's focus on exclusive, dedicated and ongoing occupancy gives both sides a workable line between a license and a sublease. Landlords enforcing use or subletting covenants should document actual occupancy with inspections and photographs, follow the lease's cure procedure first, and then use the statutory eviction notice. Where public grant money or a lender sits behind the tenancy, landlords and tenants alike should read any non-disturbance agreement for notice and cure conditions, because here the agreement's notice requirement was central to the fight over the tenant's repair claim. Tenants defending an eviction should also expect a court to look past a large counterclaim demand when deciding whether a small-claims-level court keeps the case.
live-274: The owners of a 98,000-square-foot industrial building at 2000 Folsom Street in San Francisco's Mission District sued tenant Physical Intelligence in San Francisco Superior Court, The San Francisco Standard reported on October 6, 2026, describing the suit as filed the previous week. live-275: The property is the Oakmont 410 industrial warehouse at 542 SE Loop 410 Access Road on San Antonio's East Side. live-276: Silver Fox 606 LLC, the developer of a data center project in Indiantown, Florida, has filed a complaint and verified petition for a writ of prohibition against the Village of Indiantown, its village council and its planning, zoning and appeals board, CBS12 reported on October 12, 2026. live-278: Merchants Bank of Indiana has sued in Cook County Circuit Court to foreclose on three South Side Chicago apartment buildings owned by GRV Jackson Park LLC, The Real Deal reported on October 10, 2026. live-279: Pacific Collective, LLC, a real estate developer, learned in 2018 that ExxonMobil Oil Corporation was selling a parcel at 3800 Sepulveda Boulevard in Culver City that sat inside the city's zone for retail cannabis dispensaries. Pacific signed an option with ExxonMobil in September 2018 and, on September 26, 2018, signed a lease with TGS CC Ventures, LLC, a subsidiary of national cannabis operator Jushi, Inc. Jushi signed a guaranty of the tenant's obligations the next day. Pacific was to buy the land, build a 5,000 square foot building at a cost of no more than $1.75 million, and rent it to TGS for 15 years at a starting rent of $20 per square foot, while TGS pursued a city cannabis license. The lease was made contingent on Pacific acquiring fee title under a purchase agreement with ExxonMobil that had not yet been drafted, and it gave no deadline for closing. Pacific let the option lapse and obtained extensions, signed a $4.2 million purchase agreement only in November 2019, missed the deadline for its $70,000 earnest money deposit, and by early 2020 still had no financing in place. TGS, which had been selected by the city to move forward in the licensing process, would not file its next city submission naming Pacific as owner while Pacific did not own the property. After a failed renegotiation, TGS rescinded the lease on February 28, 2020, and in December 2020 bought the property from ExxonMobil itself. Pacific sued TGS for breach of the lease and Jushi for breach of the guaranty in October 2022, alleging damages above $20 million. A retired judge sitting as a referee under the lease's dispute resolution clause tried the case over five days in January 2024 and found that Pacific never had the funds or loan commitments to close, had been stalling, and was in material breach of a lease that made time of the essence. The trial court entered judgment for the defendants on May 28, 2024. On appeal, the Second District accepted that the lease's reference to acquiring title under the purchase agreement could be read to tie Pacific's deadline to the ExxonMobil contract, but refused to let that reading give Pacific unlimited control over its own performance. Applying Civil Code section 1657 and the implied covenant of good faith, the panel held that Pacific had to close within a reasonable time. It found ample support for the referee's conclusion that Pacific's delay was unreasonable, pointing to the option terms that contemplated a 2019 closing and to testimony that the delay was a deliberate cost-saving choice. The court also rejected Pacific's argument that its duty to buy the land was excused until TGS obtained its cannabis license. Nothing in the lease made the purchase conditional on licensing, while a separate clause expressly deferred construction until permits issued, which the panel read as showing the parties knew how to write such a condition when they wanted one. The court called the risk of buying land before licensing the deal Pacific struck. The judgment for TGS and Jushi was affirmed and they were awarded appellate costs. The opinion is unpublished; an order filed October 13 corrected only the trial court case number. For developers, the practical point is to put a firm acquisition deadline, financing contingency or licensing condition in writing in any lease signed before closing on the land, rather than relying on a pending purchase contract. Tenants and guarantors, for their part, can use the reasonable-time rule to exit a deal when a landlord's delay goes to the heart of the bargain, provided they document repeated requests to perform, as TGS did here.
live-280: Ordinary Faces LLC leased space from Bohemian Brethren Presbyterian Church to operate a preschool in a New York City building. To run the school, the tenant needed a letter of no objection from the city Department of Buildings. The Department initially refused because the building lacked a working fire alarm system, and the Fire Department did not sign off on an alarm until July 26, 2016, nearly two years after the lease was signed. Open Department of Buildings violations tied to a defunct dumbwaiter shaft, in a part of the building outside the leased premises, also stood in the way of a permanent letter. The tenant and its founder sued the church in New York County Supreme Court in 2017. After a jury trial before Justice Joel M. Cohen, judgment was entered on August 20, 2025 awarding the plaintiffs $1,216,177.36. The church appealed the judgment and several pretrial and post-trial rulings, including the denial of its motion to set aside the verdict and its motion to strike the jury demand. The First Department found the evidence sufficient. It held that the church breached section 18(a) of the lease, which required it to cooperate in obtaining approvals for the school, by never having its elevator company file the paperwork needed to clear the violations, and breached a lease rider requiring both sides to move expeditiously and diligently on the fire alarm. Because the violations were issued against areas the tenant did not lease, the court said curing them was the landlord's job. A church officer's own testimony that the requested filing was never made helped seal the point. The panel rejected the church's argument that a 50 percent rent abatement from January through August 2015 was the tenant's sole remedy, noting that the rider did not say so. It also upheld the lost-profits portion of the award, $734,353, or roughly two and a half years of projected profits. The tenant had built its figures from operating data for a preschool that had occupied the same space for nearly 40 years, data the church itself supplied, and its first-year results matched its projections; the church offered no contrary evidence. Two lease defenses also failed. Section 19 limited the tenant to the landlord's estate and interest in the building and its rents, but the court held that language allows recovery from the proceeds of the church's 2019 sale of the building, and the church offered no proof the award exceeded its sale profits. The church's reliance on the lease's jury waivers came four months after the note of issue and after its counsel had told the court there was no dispute about a jury, so the trial court properly found the waiver itself had been waived. The court also declined to order a new trial over brief, unsolicited testimony about the founder's personal history, which the church had not objected to at trial. For landlords, the decision is a reminder that cooperation and diligence clauses in leases to schools, medical users and other permit-dependent tenants carry real damages exposure, especially for violations in common or non-demised areas only the owner can cure. Owners who want abatement to be an exclusive remedy, or who want to keep a jury waiver, need to say so expressly and enforce it early. Tenants should document the owner's specific failures to file or cure, as this tenant did.
live-281: Recycled Properties, LLC operates a construction and demolition debris landfill and borrow pit in Chesapeake, Virginia, operations the court described as legally nonconforming. In May 2024 it submitted a site plan to the city's Department of Development and Permits for a warehouse and an office building on the property. In August 2024 the city disapproved the plan on three grounds: the buildings would expand the nonconforming use, contrary to a provision of the Chesapeake zoning ordinance; approval would wait until the owner provided more information about how the buildings would be used; and a conditional use permit for the nonconforming operations was required first. The city had also cited notices of past zoning violations, a ground it later withdrew. The owner appealed to the Chesapeake Circuit Court under the Virginia statutes that let an applicant challenge a site plan disapproval as not based on the applicable ordinance or as arbitrary or capricious, and attached the city's denial letter to its complaint. It argued that the ordinance did not require it to prove the buildings were not an expansion, to provide "adequate information," or to obtain a conditional use permit, and it sought damages under a state statute on unconstitutional conditions. The city demurred. Circuit Judge David J. Whitted sustained the demurrer, holding the owner had not adequately pleaded its appeal on the requirement to submit more information, and noted the owner "may file a new site plan application." In an unpublished memorandum opinion by Judge Kevin M. Duffan, for a panel that also included Judges Beales and White, the Court of Appeals affirmed. It relied on the denial letter the owner had attached, which cited an ordinance provision barring additional buildings or structures that support a lawfully nonconforming use and the city's authority to review site plans for conformity with the zoning ordinance, and it noted Virginia Supreme Court precedent allowing localities to preclude the expansion of nonconforming uses. Because nothing in the complaint factually disputed that the buildings would alter or expand the nonconforming use, or that more information was needed, the court treated the owner's contrary assertions as legal conclusions that need not be accepted on demurrer. The court also rejected the owner's argument that the circuit court had decided the case on a summary judgment standard rather than the demurrer standard, finding the circuit court had ruled on the adequacy of the pleading. It did not reach the owner's argument that the denial was unconstitutional, because that argument was not included in an assignment of error or argued in the opening brief.
live-282: In December 2023 the City of Bradford, Pennsylvania filed a declaration of taking to condemn 374 square feet of an alley running through the rear of a property owned by DewBoi Properties, LLC, as part of a project to build a new bus station. DewBoi filed preliminary objections, and the parties' lawyers negotiated a settlement over several months in 2024. In October 2024 DewBoi's counsel accepted the city's offer of $30,000 plus the removal and relocation of two telephone poles at the city's expense. The city's draft agreement of sale said the poles would be moved out of the alley to DewBoi's property. DewBoi's counsel revised a related joint stipulation to drop the express reference to DewBoi's property but left the agreement of sale language unchanged, and the city accepted the revisions. The city signed in December 2024, the parties told the court they had settled, and DewBoi's counsel received the city's $30,000 check on January 6, 2025. The deal unraveled when the city sent over the local electric utility's easement, which showed one pole moving to another spot on DewBoi's lot. DewBoi objected that the proposed locations would further cut into parking for its tenants and their customers. After the city began building the bus station and put up a temporary fence across the condemned strip, affecting access to DewBoi's parking lot, DewBoi sought a preliminary injunction in May 2025, arguing the city did not own the land. The city responded with a petition to enforce the settlement. After two days of hearings, the McKean County Court of Common Pleas granted the city's petition and denied the injunction on August 25, 2025. On appeal, DewBoi argued there was no meeting of the minds on where the poles would go and, at most, a mutual mistake. In a non-precedential memorandum opinion by Judge Lori A. Dumas, the Commonwealth Court disagreed. It held that the settlement documents, read together, clearly provided for relocating both poles from the alley to other places on DewBoi's property. It also deferred to the trial court's findings, based on months of correspondence, the city attorney's testimony, the joint report of settlement and DewBoi's request for the $30,000 check, that the owner had approved the deal and later had second thoughts about vehicle access. Without clear, precise and convincing proof of a shared mistaken assumption, the mutual mistake defense failed. The case is small in dollars but common in practice. Commercial owners facing partial takings for transit, road or utility projects should treat site-plan details such as pole, sign, curb cut and parking locations as material terms, attach drawings to the settlement, and confirm the utility's easement before signing. Once a settlement is signed, reported to the court and funded, Pennsylvania courts are likely to enforce it as written.
live-283: ApplianceSmart, Inc. operated a store in the big-box space of a Columbus, Ohio shopping center owned by Trustees Main/270, LLC from 2008 to 2022. The lease began with a predecessor entity, Appliance Recycling Centers of America, which became the guarantor in 2017 when ApplianceSmart took over as tenant and the term was extended to June 30, 2025. That guarantor was later reincorporated as JanOne, Inc. and stayed on the guaranty after JanOne sold ApplianceSmart to Live Ventures, Inc. in 2019. According to the opinion, the tenant defaulted three times. A 2019 rent default ended in a settlement of a state-court suit. A second default during ApplianceSmart's 2021 bankruptcy was resolved with an amendment under which Live Ventures agreed to pay more than $185,000 in back rent, and the landlord gained a new one-sided right to terminate on 30 days' notice. After a third payment default in February 2022, the landlord used a lease clause that let it retake possession and change the locks without ending the lease, leaving the tenant responsible for rent and reletting costs. It then sued ApplianceSmart and JanOne for breach of the lease and the guaranty. The defendants did not dispute that they had breached. Their defense was mitigation. The guarantor proposed an affiliated recycling business that would assume the existing lease and keep trading under the ApplianceSmart name, and Live Ventures offered one of its own portfolio companies, a flooring retailer. The landlord asked the first candidate to prepay all arrears and post a nonrefundable six-month deposit, which JanOne refused. It sent the second candidate a standard questionnaire, which went unanswered. The landlord's broker kept marketing the space, and AutoZone signed a lease in September 2024. Because of zoning and permitting contingencies, AutoZone did not begin paying rent until after the ApplianceSmart term would have ended. The district court awarded the undisputed back rent on summary judgment and held a bench trial on mitigation, finding the landlord's efforts reasonable. In an opinion that is not recommended for publication, the Sixth Circuit affirmed. Applying the Ohio Supreme Court's decision in Frenchtown Square Partnership v. Lemstone and the Restatement (Second) of Contracts section 350, the panel said a commercial lessor must make reasonable efforts to relet but need not accept just any available tenant, and need not take on undue risk. Both proposed replacements shared ownership or key decision-makers with the parties behind the three defaults, so rejecting them, or demanding protective terms, was reasonable. The panel also rejected an analogy to employment-law cases about unconditional job offers, and found the argument about a rejected purchase offer likely forfeited, noting that Ohio landlords are not required to sell the building to mitigate. Before reaching the merits, the panel raised on its own that the complaint had not properly alleged the citizenship of the parties, including the landlord LLC's members. It accepted supplemental letter briefs that traced the landlord's membership through partnerships and trusts to Ohio and Florida citizens, and treated them as amendments under 28 U.S.C. section 1653 to confirm diversity jurisdiction. For landlords, the practical lesson is to document the re-leasing process: broker outreach, why each candidate was accepted or declined, and the credit concerns behind any conditions. A tenant's or guarantor's affiliate is not owed an easy path back into the space. Tenants and guarantors who want to cap their exposure through a substitute tenant should offer real credit support and full financial disclosure. Counsel filing diversity suits for LLC or trust-owned landlords should plead each member's citizenship in full from the start.
live-284: The dispute concerns a 117-bed assisted-living facility built on land in Conroe, Texas. The property-owning company, Conroe WM LLC, financed construction with a loan from Greystone Funding Company LLC, insured by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development under its Section 232 program for residential care facilities. HUD required Greystone to collect three escrows: working capital, minor movable equipment and an initial operating deficit. HREF Senior Worthington LLC, which once operated under a MidHudson name, came into the deal in May 2019 to fund them. HREF put $4.5 million into WM Conroe Property Holdings LLC, the holding company that manages the property owner. About $3.24 million covered the HUD escrows. The other $1.27 million funded the first 25 months of HREF's monthly return. HREF took special membership interests rather than common equity or management rights. In exchange, it bargained for the right to become the holding company's sole manager immediately if it was not paid. The redemption date was later extended to August 2024, and the monthly payment was raised to $40,000. According to the Chancery opinion, payments stopped after February 2024. HREF declared its step-in right in November 2024 and sued in the Court of Chancery that month. One count sought a summary declaration under 6 Del. C. Section 18-110 that HREF was now the holding company's sole manager. That count was tried on a paper record in August 2025. The defendants were the property owner and WM Property Holdings LLC, the sponsor-side manager. They argued that the HUD documents and the property owner's operating agreement barred any change in management without HUD's prior written approval. They also argued that HREF's step-in addendum was illegal and that HUD had to be part of the case. In a January 12, 2026 memorandum opinion, Vice Chancellor Morgan T. Zurn rejected each argument. The court held that the HUD approval provisions bound the property-owning borrower, not the holding company above it. It also held that the HREF addendum was not illegal and that the parties before the court were enough to resolve the control dispute. The court ruled that HREF was entitled to become the holding company's sole manager immediately. It held HREF's fee request in abeyance while the remaining claims proceed. The defendants appealed. After briefing and oral argument, the Delaware Supreme Court affirmed by order on October 8, 2026, on the basis of and for the reasons in the Court of Chancery's opinion. The panel was Chief Justice Seitz and Justices Traynor and Griffiths. When the Court of Chancery ruled in January, five other claims remained pending there. For investors in HUD-financed senior housing, the ruling shows step-in rights placed at a holding company outside the HUD-regulated borrower being enforced, because the court read the HUD approval provisions as binding the borrower rather than the holding company. Sponsors in similar structures should not expect approval rules written for the borrower to block an upstream investor's contractual takeover once its triggers are met.
live-285: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg County, through its lawyers at an environmental-law nonprofit, sued in the Seventh Judicial Circuit on July 6, 2026 over how Spartanburg County was permitting a data center campus by Valara Holdings, which the Spartanburg Herald-Journal, in a story republished by South Carolina Lawyers Weekly, describes as a subsidiary of NorthMark Cloud and Compute. The project on South Pine Street, at the site of the former Kohler plant, is reported as a $2.8 billion investment. The group's lawyers, announcing the suit, described about 500,000 square feet of new buildings, a power yard, internal roads and a 450-megawatt gas-fired power plant. The group argued that the county's Unified Land Management Ordinance required the project to be reviewed as a 'major' land development, which goes to the Planning Commission with public notice and comment, rather than as a 'minor' development reviewed by staff. It asked for a declaration that Valara must obtain a major development permit and for an injunction stopping the county from processing the minor application. FOX Carolina reported that the first permit, to redevelop the Kohler building, was approved in August 2025, and that a second application, for four new buildings, the power yard and cooling systems, is still pending. County officials have said the classification depends on the ordinance's specific language rather than a project's size alone, according to the Herald-Journal. Judge Cole dismissed the case on October 6 without deciding whether the classification was correct. According to FOX Carolina, he found the group's concerns about noise, dust, traffic, health and transparency too general to show the special damage South Carolina law requires of neighbors, and he said the group should have appealed to the county Board of Zoning Appeals within 10 days before going to court. He called the challenge to the second permit premature because the county has not acted on it. The dismissal also ended the group's request to pause construction, which had been heard on September 17. A senior attorney for the group told FOX Carolina the ruling conflicts with controlling South Carolina Supreme Court precedent and that residents could not have used the zoning-appeal route because they were told at the time that the project was not a data center; she said the group's lawyers expected to file a notice of appeal within days. The same lawyers are also pursuing a case, now before the South Carolina Court of Appeals, over whether Valara needed Public Service Commission approval, and has asked state regulators to reopen public comment on the project's air permit, issued September 18, over formaldehyde emissions from its planned gas turbines. Valara representatives have said the companies followed all state and local permitting requirements, and a county council member called the suit 'frivolous,' the Herald-Journal reported. FOX Carolina also reported that the county's one-year pause on new data center applications, adopted in June, does not reach Valara's project.
live-286: Hetley Associates owns Hetley Plaza, a strip shopping center in Lemoyne Borough, Cumberland County, zoned Commercial General. It also owns three nearby residential lots in the borough's Urban Residential District, one of them a rented house. The center operates as a lawful nonconforming use with fewer parking spaces than the ordinance now requires. The owner argued that changing conditions around the plaza had made the shortage worse, and that a vacant space once occupied by a restaurant was hard to re-lease without more parking. In January 2025 the owner asked the borough Zoning Hearing Board for a use variance to demolish the three houses and pave a parking lot in their place. After a hearing, the Board denied the request on March 27, 2025. Among other reasons, it found that the owner's own decision to lease to a restaurant had added to the parking problem. The Court of Common Pleas of Cumberland County affirmed on September 4, 2025, after argument in August. It found that the residential lots could keep being used as rentals, for which there is demand, and that the hardship the owner described related to the plaza rather than to the lots in question. On appeal, the owner challenged each of the Board's findings: that the variance would change the character of the neighborhood, that the hardship was self-created, that following the ordinance was practical, and that the request was not the minimum variance needed. In a memorandum opinion filed October 9, 2026, the Commonwealth Court affirmed on a single ground and did not reach the others. Both the borough ordinance and the Municipalities Planning Code require unnecessary hardship arising from physical conditions unique to the property for which relief is sought. Relying on its earlier decision in Bawa Muhaiyaddeen Fellowship, the court explained that the hardship must belong to the property, not to the person who owns it. Applying that rule, the court found that the owner was really claiming a hardship to its commercial plaza: it could not expand that use without taking over the neighboring residential land. Because the residential lots stay usable and valuable for their permitted residential use, there was no unnecessary hardship tied to them. The court noted that the owner cited no authority allowing a variance on one property based on hardship to another. In a footnote, the court also rejected the owner's suggestion that the minimum-variance requirement does not apply to use variances, pointing to its own decisions holding that it does. The court added that, although one owner holds both the plaza and the residential lots, they remain separate parcels, and nothing in the record showed an attempt to combine them. It expressly declined to say whether a reverse subdivision would have been proper or would change the result. The opinion is labeled non-precedential, so it can be cited as persuasive authority but is not binding in Pennsylvania. For retail landlords, the practical lesson is that parking shortfalls at older centers usually cannot be solved by buying adjoining residential lots and asking for a use variance. Better options include a rezoning or text amendment, a parking-reduction or shared-parking provision, an off-site parking agreement on commercially zoned land, or, where the ordinance allows, combining parcels before applying, though the court left that last route open rather than endorsing it. Owners should also expect a zoning board to count leasing decisions, such as bringing in a parking-heavy restaurant tenant, as a self-created hardship. Buyers and lenders evaluating a nonconforming center should treat any planned parking expansion that depends on a variance as uncertain.
live-287: San Francisco Care Center, L.P. borrowed up to $23,108,000 in 2002 from Pacific Commonwealth Mortgage Company to build a senior health care facility in San Francisco. It began operating the property as an assisted-living facility for elderly and memory-care residents in 2004. The loan was assigned to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in May 2006, and HUD sold it to Lenox Mortgage IX LLC that December. The bankruptcy court later called the loan documents "terribly outdated and nothing like what is routinely seen today." The borrower first defaulted around 2006 or 2007. After Lenox recorded a notice of default in January 2008, the borrower paid the $252,470.56 cure amount, which included no attorneys' fees. It then sued Lenox in state court to force the release of more construction funds, and later dismissed that suit voluntarily. Years later, legal costs from a suit brought by the City of San Francisco over building code violations, which the operator won in 2023, combined with the pandemic to strain its finances. It stopped making loan payments in early 2024. Lenox recorded a notice of default in September 2024 and set a foreclosure sale for January 14, 2025. The operator filed Chapter 11 that same day. Lenox filed a proof of claim for $19,189,226.25. In May 2025 the bankruptcy court approved a section 363 sale of the property for $27,750,000 in cash. Under the sale order, any challenged part of a payoff demand was held in escrow. Lenox's demand was $19,822,204.53, plus per diem interest, $1,910,657.89 in unpaid interest and $419,266.94 in attorneys' fees. Lenox broke the fees down as $187,324.54 for the first default, $139,035.94 for the state-court suit, $56,073.32 for the second default and $87,162 for the bankruptcy and payoff litigation. Judge Dennis Montali disallowed all of the fees. In a December 1, 2025 order he also granted the debtor its own fees and costs under California Civil Code section 1717. The case was converted to Chapter 7 in April 2026. The panel read the note, deed of trust and security agreement closely. The note allowed only fees that a court adjudged reasonable in an action on the note, and no court ever did that. The deed of trust covered actions affecting Lenox's security, but the construction-funds suit did not threaten the lien. The nonjudicial notices of default were also not court proceedings. The security agreement allowed fees only out of foreclosure-sale proceeds, and the property was sold through the bankruptcy court rather than at foreclosure. The panel ruled the other way on the bankruptcy-related fees. Lenox had appeared in the case to protect its lien, through the cash-collateral order, its proof of claim and its objections to the sale order. The panel also held that the payoff litigation could not be an action on the contract for the borrower's section 1717 fee claim and yet not an action for Lenox's own fee recovery. It reversed on those fees and sent the case back for a reasonableness determination. It also vacated the borrower's fee award so the bankruptcy court can decide whether the borrower is still the prevailing party. The decision is a nonprecedential memorandum. For lenders holding seasoned or agency-originated loans, it shows that narrow fee clauses tied to court awards or foreclosure proceeds may not reach legal costs accrued over years if the collateral is sold in bankruptcy, and that contesting a payoff can bring a reciprocal fee claim under section 1717. The amount of Lenox's bankruptcy-related fees, and who prevailed, remain for the bankruptcy court on remand.
live-288: Enterprise Bank and Trust held the first deed of trust on ten Laguna Beach, California parcels. Each parcel was owned by its own single-asset real estate entity, including Laguna Festival Center, LLC, Laguna Art District Complex, LLC, 891 Laguna Canyon Road, LLC, 694 NCH Apartments, LLC and Duplex at Sleepy Hollow, LLC. The properties had a collective book value of about $95 million, and Enterprise was owed roughly $80 million. Each parcel carried at least three deeds of trust. The owners had stopped paying property taxes and regular loan payments. Enterprise sent a default notice in November 2024 and recorded notices of default in February 2025. The defaults came against the backdrop of a long-running dispute between two investors over control of the ownership entities. Within three weeks of the default notices, the owners and twelve affiliates filed voluntary Chapter 11 cases in Delaware, jointly administered under MOM CA Investco LLC. Enterprise obtained unopposed stay relief on July 15, 2025, and the Delaware cases were dismissed in August 2025. Enterprise then sued in California state court, which appointed a receiver over the properties on October 7, 2025. Enterprise also noticed nonjudicial foreclosure sales for 3:00 p.m. on October 15, 2025. On the afternoon of the sales, between 2:28 and 3:02 p.m., involuntary Chapter 11 petitions were filed against all ten owners in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Central District of California. The petitioning creditors included Vierergruppe Management, Inc., which the panel described as connected to one of the investors. Neither Enterprise nor the foreclosure trustee knew. The sales ran from 3:13 to 3:52 p.m. About twenty unrelated parties attended, but only one outside bid was placed, on the 694 NCH property. That sale was later canceled and the money returned. Enterprise took the other nine properties by credit bid. The owners opposed stay relief by offering a $102 million purchase agreement with Special Assets Laguna, LLC; the panel noted it was signed for both the sellers and the buyer by the same person, an officer of Vierergruppe. Bankruptcy Judge Scott C. Clarkson found the involuntary cases were filed in bad faith. At a December 12, 2025 hearing he granted Enterprise prospective and in rem relief and retroactively annulled the stay as to the nine properties without outside bids, which validated those sales; the orders were entered December 15, 2025. He also ordered the petitioning creditors to post a $1 million bond. They did not, and the ten cases were dismissed on March 18, 2026. The owners dropped their own appeals in June 2026, which left only the appeal of a prospective bidder. That bidder said he held back because he had heard of the filings, and argued that the petitions chilled the bidding; the panel noted he reached the sale site only after the property he most wanted had been sold. The panel first held that the appeal was not moot and that the bidder had standing, because he had changed his conduct in reliance on the stay. On the merits, it held that the equities analysis under the Fjeldsted factors properly looked at the debtors' bad faith, the lender's lack of notice, its earlier stay relief and how quickly it moved, and not only at the bidder's position. It noted that the bidder had not alerted the trustee or placed a bid. It also found nothing inconsistent in treating the rescinded 694 NCH sale differently, because that property is the subject of a separate appeal. The decision is a nonprecedential memorandum. It shows how the panel weighed the equities of a last-minute involuntary filing: the debtors' bad faith, the lender's lack of notice and prior stay relief, and its prompt motion all favored annulment, while a bidder who knew of the filings and stayed silent had little room to claim harm.
live-289: Braemar Hotels & Resorts Inc., a NYSE-listed REIT based in Dallas that owns luxury hotels and resorts, has settled a wide-ranging dispute with its largest stockholder, Al Shams Investments Limited, a Bermuda company. The Cooperation and Settlement Agreement is dated October 6, 2026. Its other signatories are Ashford Hospitality Trust, Inc. and Ashford Inc., and the beneficial owner of Al Shams signed for limited purposes. Braemar filed the agreement as an exhibit to a Form 8-K on October 8, 2026. A company press release that day announced it alongside a portfolio update and the pending $372 million sale of the Four Seasons Resort Scottsdale. The agreement's recitals set out what was being resolved. Al Shams had sent Braemar a notice nominating a slate of director candidates for the 2026 annual meeting. It had also asserted or threatened direct claims against the company group, including defamation and libel claims, claims under the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and claims similar to those earlier brought by another investor and Morning View Hotels BH1, LLC. Separately, it had asserted or threatened derivative claims on Braemar's behalf alleging fiduciary breaches by the board and management. Al Shams was also pursuing a verified petition under Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 202 to depose two former Braemar directors before filing suit. The company group denies wrongdoing, and no party admits liability. The money terms are substantial. Braemar agreed to pay Al Shams $25 million for the settlement and releases, plus $15 million to reimburse expenses Al Shams incurred in the conflict. That is $40 million in total, payable as $20 million on signing and $10 million each at four and eight months. Each installment depends on Al Shams continuing to comply. Disputes over a claimed breach go to expedited JAMS arbitration in Dallas, and a final finding of material breach triggers a clawback of everything paid. If cash is short, Braemar may pay up to $4 million of the later installments in common stock, and the board must grant an exception to the REIT's 9.8% ownership limit if that issuance would push Al Shams over the cap. Al Shams also gave up a great deal. It withdrew its nominations and the Rule 202 petition and agreed to a 10-year standstill. Under the standstill it may not run proxy contests, join groups, buy more shares, comment on extraordinary transactions, short the stock, or bring any litigation or pre-suit discovery against the companies or their current and former directors and officers, except to enforce the agreement. It must vote with the board's recommendations, and it waived any right to share in other stockholders' derivative or class recoveries. In return, Al Shams may consult with Braemar's director search firm on candidates for one board seat, but the board keeps sole discretion over the choice. Both sides exchanged general releases and agreed not to disparage each other. Braemar's 8-K describes the headline figure as $25 million plus expenses. The company expects its own net contribution to be only $4 million to $6 million after insurance proceeds and Ashford's share. Under a separate Allocation Agreement, Braemar and Ashford each bear half of the payments net of insurance, which both are pursuing, although Braemar cautions that the insurance recovery is not assured. The company says the settlement likely costs less than the litigation it avoided. The 2026 annual meeting is set for December 21, 2026, and the press release says the separation from Ashford should be finished by mid-November. There are several lessons here for REIT boards, external advisors and their D&O carriers. First, Texas Rule 202 petitions can be used as leverage before any suit is filed, and a REIT based in Texas should expect activists to use them to depose former directors. Second, once an activist with a large stake combines a proxy contest with securities, derivative and defamation claims, the case can be settled at a figure far above ordinary expense reimbursement. Paying in installments with a clawback, as here, protects the company if the activist later breaks its promises. Third, splitting costs with the external advisor and leaning on insurance can bring the REIT's net cost far below the gross number. Investors should watch whether the second and third installments are paid in cash or stock, and whether the insurers actually pay.
live-290: Schell Road, LLC bought 80 acres on Schell Road in Grant Township in 2022, planning to develop and operate a gravel mine. It submitted a special use permit application on September 20, 2022, with site plans from a civil engineer; it was the first mining application the township had received since 2003. Township officials, advised by counsel, questioned whether the ordinance's mining rules, unchanged since 1998, accounted for a 2011 amendment to state law. The company submitted supplemental information in December 2022 and January 2023 to address deficiencies, and officials told it they intended to delay consideration until the ordinance was amended. After an exchange of letters in which the company's counsel accused the township of delaying review to defeat the application, Schell Road filed a complaint on February 17, 2023, seeking a writ of mandamus to compel a public hearing. Following a planning commission recommendation, the township adopted amendments to the ordinance on March 23, 2023, effective March 30. Schell Road amended its complaint to allege the amendments were enacted in bad faith to stop its mine and exceeded the township's authority under MCL 125.3205, and added due process, injunctive and declaratory claims. The trial court granted the township summary disposition, finding the application incomplete, finding no bad faith, and holding the amended ordinance complied with the statute. A panel of Judges Korobkin, Rick and Maldonado affirmed on all three issues. On mandamus, it held the trial court could decide completeness on the documentary record at summary disposition, and agreed the application was incomplete: among other gaps, the reclamation plan lacked required information on phasing and timing, and the record did not show the plan had been submitted to the county extension office and soil and water conservation district as the ordinance required. On bad faith, it agreed the record did not support the claim: the township had not received a mining application since 2003, acted on counsel's advice, told the company in December 2022 that amendments were under way, and adopted amendments that apply to any mining application. The court said the application was "a catalyst" for the amendments but that this did not establish bad faith. On validity, the court rejected the company's arguments that MCL 125.3205 sets only a standard for courts on appeal and that the amended ordinance's requirements on market need and on property-value effects along the haul route go beyond the statute, finding those requirements track the statute's need and "very serious consequences" factors. The opinion is unpublished.
live-291: C&B Development, LLC is the equitable owner, under a 2022 purchase agreement, of a 75.5-acre tract in Maxatawny Township, Berks County. The site now holds a restaurant, a mobile home park and an airport. The tract is split among three zoning districts: Commercial (C-1), Light Industrial (L-I) and Agricultural Preservation (AP-1). Its only street frontage is on Kutztown Road. The developer planned to clear the site and build a commercial building plus a 709,000-square-foot warehouse on the L-I portion. That portion can be reached only by a new private drive, called Road A in the record, running from Kutztown Road through the commercial district. The problem was an October 2022 ordinance amendment. It made warehouses and distribution facilities a conditional use in the L-I district, rather than a use permitted by right, and added Section 593(c). That section requires warehouse buildings and all related impervious surfaces to sit at least 500 feet from any building occupied by an existing residential, institutional or educational use. In August 2023 the township's zoning officer found that Road A was an impervious surface serving the warehouse. Because the road could not be routed 500 feet away from nearby homes, it did not comply. He told the developer to get a variance before its conditional use hearing could go forward. The developer appealed to the Zoning Hearing Board. It argued that the road was not covered by the buffer rule and, in the alternative, asked for a dimensional variance. After three hearings ending in January 2024, the board sided with the zoning officer and denied the variance. The board found that the property could support many other permitted uses that do not carry the 500-foot buffer. It also found that routing truck traffic onto Kutztown Road would harm a largely residential area that Kutztown University students use. The Berks County Court of Common Pleas affirmed on July 14, 2025, and the developer appealed. In a memorandum opinion by Judge Patricia A. McCullough, the Commonwealth Court rejected all three of the developer's arguments. First, the zoning officer did not testify, but that was no ground for reversal. The board has its own authority to interpret the ordinance, and the developer had the chance to subpoena him and dropped it. Second, the conditional use provision and the buffer rule do not conflict, so the rule in the Municipalities Planning Code that resolves doubtful ordinance language in the owner's favor did not apply. Third, the board applied the correct variance test. The developer's own brief admitted that the light-industrial lot could be used for things other than a warehouse, so its hardship was self-imposed and not caused by the property. The panel also noted that the developer never filed a formal challenge to the ordinance's validity, which is the proper route for an argument that the zoning leaves no reasonable use. The opinion notes that the developer has a separate inverse condemnation suit pending against the township in the Berks County court. In that suit it alleges a coordinated effort to block the project. The appellate court refused to consider any of that record in the land use appeal. The decision is unreported and non-precedential. It ends this zoning route unless the developer seeks further review, but it does not resolve the separate takings claim. The practical lesson is that local warehouse ordinances increasingly measure setbacks from all related paving, not just from the building, and access drives count. A buyer should map every required road, drive and loading area against residential and institutional buffers during due diligence, especially on sites with one frontage. A variance request based on the inability to build one preferred use is unlikely to succeed when the district allows other uses. A developer who believes an ordinance leaves no reasonable use of the land must bring a formal validity challenge under the Municipalities Planning Code. That argument cannot be raised for the first time in a variance appeal.
live-292: 865 East 49th Street Associates LLC, a commercial landlord, sued its tenant Valdo Auto Sales Corp. and others in Miami-Dade County Circuit Court (Lower Tribunal No. 22-17871-CA-01). The trial court, Judge Valerie R. Manno Schurr presiding, entered summary judgment orders on liability and damages in the landlord's favor. Liability was resolved by an order titled "Agreed Summary Final Judgment as to Liability," which covered all of the landlord's claims, including fraud and unjust enrichment. The only money awarded, however, was $76,199.37 in past-due rent for breach of the commercial lease. The landlord appealed, arguing that once liability was established on the fraud and unjust enrichment counts, the trial court could not award zero dollars on them. The tenant did not appear in the appeal. A panel of Judges Fernandez, Gordo and Rebull decided the appeal, and Judge Gordo wrote the opinion affirming the trial court. The court started from the rule against double recovery. A plaintiff who wins a contract award must show that its fraud or unjust enrichment damages are separate and distinct from that award, and not just the same loss counted again. Fraud requires actual damages as an essential element, and a liability finding alone does not establish them. Unjust enrichment requires competent, quantified evidence of the value of the benefit conferred. The panel cited Florida cases holding that a plaintiff can win liability and still recover nothing. Procedure also decided the appeal. The trial court resolved liability, damages and rehearing only after full in-court hearings, but the landlord did not supply a transcript of any of them or an approved statement of the evidence. Because the liability judgment was an agreed order, nothing in the record showed what the parties had agreed to. In particular, the record did not show whether the landlord kept or gave up any claim to separate damages. The panel would not assume that the agreed judgment decided more than the liability it recites. It agreed with the trial court that the landlord had failed to raise a genuine issue of material fact as to any compensable, non-duplicative damages, and affirmed. The opinion is not final until any timely rehearing motion is resolved. There are several lessons for commercial landlords and their lawyers. First, fraud and unjust enrichment counts in a rent case need their own damages proof, with a dollar figure tied to a loss the lease award does not already cover. Second, an agreed liability judgment should say expressly whether damages on each claim are reserved for later decision. Third, if a summary judgment or damages hearing may be appealed, have a court reporter there; as the court noted, the lack of a transcript is usually fatal to an appellant.
live-293: Valley Post is a four-building dining development off Dunnavant Valley Road in Chelsea, Alabama, in Shelby County south of Birmingham. A Birmingham developer built it, and its only operator was a Pihakis Restaurant Group affiliate. It housed four concepts: Hero Diner, Luca & Lucy, Little Donkey and Rodney Scott BBQ. According to court documents described by AL.com, the development opened in December 2025, and no rent was paid from that month on. In April 2026 the Pihakis Restaurant Group began closing restaurants, and all four Valley Post restaurants shut. That month the landlord side filed liens on several properties leased to the group and its affiliates. WBRC reported that the amended Valley Post lien, filed April 27, claimed $7,166,296.20 plus attorney fees and other expenses for rent due under the leases. In June, the landlord entity, Dunnavant Valley Dining LLC, sued in Shelby County Circuit Court. It alleged that PRG Valley Post had defaulted on a long-term lease of the four buildings, with charges totaling about $7.35 million. The tenant never answered, and the court entered a default judgment for $7.19 million in unpaid rent, attorney fees and court costs, as AL.com reported on October 7, 2026. Waldo's Chicken and Beer opened a Valley Post location on September 29, and Saw's BBQ is expected to open there later this fall.
live-294: The Massachusetts Appeals Court reversed a Land Court judgment on October 14, 2026 that had declared CRG Acquisition, LLC's proposed 800,000-square-foot warehouse and distribution facility in Holliston a use permitted as of right, meaning no special permit was required. The panel's ruling effectively reinstates the position of the town and its planning board, which had already denied CRG a special permit for the project in 2021 after eleven public hearings. Because that discretionary denial was never disturbed, the Appeals Court's decision leaves the project without a zoning path forward in its current form. CRG is the buyer under a pending purchase and sale agreement for roughly seventy-two acres of land from New Hopping Brook Realty Trust, sited in Holliston's industrial zoning district. In 2019, CRG applied to the planning board for site plan approval to build the warehouse and distribution facility, a project that would include 423 trailer truck spaces, 170 loading docks and 129 passenger vehicle parking spaces. The planning board approved the site plan in March 2020 with thirty-one conditions, though the town's building inspector flagged a concern at the time that the use might ultimately require a special permit for general industrial uses rather than qualifying under the bylaw's warehouse category. That concern proved prescient. In June 2020, CRG applied for a special permit while maintaining that none was actually required, and separately sought approval of a modified site plan with fewer trailer spaces and loading docks. After eleven public hearings, the planning board denied both the special permit and the modified site plan in July 2021, citing concerns about traffic, noise and the project's impact on the town's historical and agricultural character. CRG responded by suing in the Land Court on two tracks: a direct appeal of the board's denials under G. L. c. 40A, Section 17, and a separate declaratory judgment claim under G. L. c. 240, Section 14A, arguing that its warehouse was a use permitted by right under the bylaw's Section III.G.1, covering 'wholesale office or showroom, including warehouse facilities,' so that no special permit was needed in the first place. A Land Court judge agreed with CRG on the declaratory judgment count, reasoning that the bylaw's specific use of the word 'warehouse' in Section III.G.1, and nowhere else in its table of uses, meant the principal use of a property as a warehouse was allowed as of right in the industrial district. A judgment entered declaring that CRG needed no special permit and remanding the separate site-plan dispute to the planning board for further review. The town and planning board appealed, and the Appeals Court reversed. The panel agreed with CRG that no deference was owed to the board's interpretation of the use tables for purposes of the declaratory judgment claim, since that statute does not involve review of an existing board decision, unlike a direct zoning appeal. But reviewing the bylaw independently, the panel agreed with the town on the merits: given the scale of CRG's proposed facility, the project falls under the bylaw's separate category for general industrial uses exceeding 15,000 square feet of floor area, not the as-of-right warehouse category CRG had invoked, so a special permit is required after all. The practical upshot for logistics and warehouse developers is that a zoning bylaw's use table cannot be read by matching a keyword like 'warehouse' to a permitted-as-of-right category without accounting for separate, size-based use categories the same bylaw may impose on larger facilities. A roughly 800,000-square-foot distribution center with hundreds of trailer spaces and loading docks can fall outside a town's ordinary warehouse use classification even when that classification exists elsewhere in the same bylaw, pushing the project into a discretionary special-permit process that neighbors and local officials can use to raise traffic, noise and character objections. Developers assembling large industrial sites should confirm, before signing a purchase agreement, whether local bylaws tie use classification to project size or intensity, and should not assume that a favorable declaratory judgment on that question at the trial level will survive an appeal once the underlying discretionary permit denial is already final.
live-295: All American was the framing, drywall, insulation and acoustical ceiling tile subcontractor on a five-story hotel project. After the original general contractor was terminated, GSD was hired as the replacement general contractor. The subcontract let GSD terminate for convenience, in which case All American could recover payment for work performed through termination plus demobilization costs, but nothing for work not performed. A separate clause required ten percent of each partial payment to be held back until ninety days after final completion of the project. When GSD took over, All American had completed about 93.9% of its work and was owed a $71,582.98 retainage; the rest of its work was waiting on other trades. The project then developed significant mold from water intrusion, and All American refused to finish until the mold was properly remediated for its workers' safety. GSD said it had done enough by removing some drywall and doing limited mold testing; All American said that was insufficient because GSD never hired an industrial hygienist or prepared a formal remediation plan. GSD terminated All American and never paid the retainage. All American sued in Broward County circuit court for the retainage, and its owner testified at trial that it was not seeking the $45,300 for unperformed work. The trial court, Judge John B. Bowman, found GSD breached by not paying for work performed and by not properly remediating the mold, and awarded $116,882.98: the retainage plus $45,300. In an opinion by Judge Spencer D. Levine, joined by Judges Klingensmith and Lott, the Fourth District held the subcontract's plain language supported the retainage award: the project was completed in 2023, the ninety-day period had long expired, and the subcontract had no termination-for-cause clause or other provision letting GSD keep the retainage after a termination. The court noted its analysis "could be different" if the contract had a for-cause provision. Having affirmed on that ground, it did not decide whether GSD also breached by failing to remediate the mold. It reversed the $45,300 because the complaint sought only the retainage, All American conceded the point, and the subcontract barred payment for work not performed. The opinion is not final until any timely rehearing motion is resolved.
live-297: On October 14, 2026, the Appellate Division, Second Department, affirmed an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Justice Cassandra A. Johnson), that denied CG & J Realty, LLC's motion to vacate a lien bond and to dismiss CFS Enterprises, Inc.'s cause of action to foreclose a mechanic's lien against it. The panel was Justices Francesca E. Connolly, Valerie Brathwaite Nelson, Barry E. Warhit and James P. McCormack. According to the decision, CFS Enterprises filed a notice of mechanic's lien on November 7, 2022 against real property in Queens owned by CG & J Realty, and sued to foreclose the lien in February 2023. In April 2023, CG & J Realty posted a bond under Lien Law §19 to discharge the lien. The trial court denied the motion on October 24, 2024. On appeal, the Second Department noted that mechanic's liens are purely statutory and that strict compliance is required. Section 59 requires that notice be served on the lienor personally or left at the lienor's last known place of residence with a person of suitable age. The court found that CG & J Realty had only filed the order to show cause on NYSCEF, so its motion was properly denied. The court declined CFS Enterprises' request for the attorneys' fees and expenses of the appeal under New York's frivolous-conduct rule, finding CFS had not shown that CG & J Realty's appeal was frivolous. live-298: The building on the property operated as a bowling alley until 2019. The property had been listed at $525,000 in June 2021. In December 2022 Zecorra leased it to Dolgencorp, LLC (Dollar General), agreeing to complete construction by April 1, 2023, and Dollar General took possession in May 2023. Zecorra challenged the township's 2023 assessment, which turned on value as of December 31, 2022. Its appraiser valued the property at $180,000 after a renovation allowance of about $57,000. The township's appraiser valued it at $570,000, calling the $200,000 price a significant outlier and deducting $525,000 from a stabilized income value for renovation costs and lost rent over a four-month holding period. After a three-day hearing, the tribunal on May 27, 2025, gave the owner's deduction no weight, found the owner's photographs of the property's condition inconsistent and incomplete, and made its own determination: $529,000 by sales comparison and $521,000 by income capitalization after adopting the township's deduction, reconciled to $525,000. Judges Borrello, Bazzi and Lievense affirmed in an unpublished per curiam opinion. They held the tribunal's adoption of the township's deduction was supported by substantial evidence, because that figure was a market-based calculation of what an investor would pay on tax day rather than a measure of actual construction costs, and evidence showed some work had been done in 2022. They also held the tribunal properly valued the property for its undisputed highest and best use, a repurposed commercial use, rather than as a vacant bowling alley, and was not required to accept the sale price, noting the $525,000 value matched the property's 2021 listing price.
live-299: Orchard BJK and Pocono Mountains Industries own commercially and industrially zoned properties in Coolbaugh Township, Monroe County. In April 2023 the township's Board of Supervisors approved their subdivision of one tract into a 35.5-acre Lot 1 and a 73.16-acre Lot 2 and conditionally approved a land development plan for an approximately 333,000-square-foot warehouse on Lot 1 under the ordinances then in effect.
