Before the hearing, the county said it was confident the suit would be dismissed, the Daily Signal reported, and County Administrator Jeremy Raley told WTVR that the overlay added buffers, setbacks and noise limits to protect residents.
live-336: Michelmann Steel Construction Company, an Illinois corporation, owns a lot on 24th Street in Quincy, Illinois, that it has leased for billboard advertising since a 1956 agreement with Quincy Outdoor Advertising Co. Leases from 1968 on used a preprinted form with a one-year original term and automatic year-to-year renewals for up to five years unless a party gave 30 days' written notice. The lease at issue, signed May 1, 1987 with Outdoor Graphics, Inc., leased "the existing structures" on the lot for $400 a year with 10% annual increases, and said structures the tenant placed there would remain its property, removable up to a reasonable time after the lease ended. Link Media Midwest, LLC, which admitted it was Outdoor Graphics' assignee, had the billboard structures dismantled and removed on April 19, 2019. Michelmann sued in Adams County circuit court for conversion, tortious interference with prospective business relationships and breach of contract for unpaid rent. After a bench trial on documentary evidence only, Judge Scott Douglas Larson ruled on December 18, 2024 that Michelmann had not proved it owned the billboards, but awarded it $19,907.97 in past-due rent. Link Media appealed the rent award and Michelmann cross-appealed. Justice Peter C. Cavanagh delivered the judgment, with Justices DeArmond and Grischow concurring. Reviewing the record de novo, the court held that the structures, fixtures that had stood on Michelmann's land for over half a century, were presumed to be Michelmann's, that Link Media did not rebut the presumption, and that removing them was a conversion. Michelmann's damages evidence went to the $68,931.17 cost of building replacement billboards and a claimed 10% loss in value from a required setback. It cited no authority for that measure, and with no proof of fair market value it was entitled only to nominal damages. Its tortious-interference claim was forfeited for lack of a reasoned argument. On rent, the court held that Michelmann had elected to treat Link Media as a holdover tenant, creating a new tenancy on the 1987 lease's terms, including its automatic renewals, and that no written termination notice was proven. Link Media argued its liability ended when it removed the structures in April 2019; the court found it owed rent through April 2024 and held its request for equitable relief forfeited for lack of supporting authority. The case was remanded with directions to enter judgment for Michelmann on conversion and award nominal damages.
live-337: Alexandria Real Estate Equities, Inc., the nation's largest publicly traded owner of life-science laboratory space, disclosed in its third-quarter 2026 SEC filings that it remains locked in litigation with two New York City agencies over its right to incorporate an adjacent land parcel into its flagship Manhattan life-science campus, a dispute that has escalated from a 2024 breach-of-contract suit into a 2026 emergency bid to stop the city from terminating the underlying lease altogether. ARE-East River Science Park, LLC, a subsidiary of Alexandria Real Estate Equities, holds an option granted in 2006 to incorporate a parcel of land adjacent to and north of the Alexandria Center for Life Science megacampus into its existing ground lease, which would clear the way for an additional life-science building on the site. According to Alexandria's quarterly report filed October 26, 2026, the company's investment in pre-construction costs tied to the option had reached $185.9 million as of September 30, 2026, a substantial sunk cost riding on the option's continued validity. On August 6, 2024, ARE sued the New York City Health + Hospitals Corporation and the New York City Economic Development Corporation in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, challenging the agencies' handling of the ground lease and option arrangements governing the parcel. ARE amended its complaint on January 24, 2025, adding claims for fraudulent inducement, breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and a request for a declaratory judgment confirming the option remains valid. The dispute sharpened in 2026 when the city agencies issued a notice of default, asserting that a failure to cure the alleged defaults within a 30-day cure period would trigger escalating daily charges starting at $1,000 a day and rising to $2,000 a day. Alexandria disputes the notice's underlying allegations and says it intends to defend against them vigorously. Rather than wait out the cure period in the federal case, ARE went to the Commercial Division of the New York State Supreme Court on May 12, 2026, filing a second action against the two agencies seeking a Yellowstone injunction, a New York-specific procedural device that tolls a commercial tenant's cure period and preserves the status quo, along with a preliminary injunction and temporary restraining order to stop the agencies from issuing a notice of termination while the parties' underlying rights are litigated. The case is a timely study in the particular risks of long-horizon options and ground leases involving government counterparties. Alexandria's $185.9 million pre-construction exposure shows how far a sophisticated developer can commit capital toward a future building before the underlying right to build is finally resolved, and how quickly a government landlord's default notice can convert a contract dispute into a threat to a years-long capital plan. The Yellowstone injunction mechanism at the center of the state court fight is itself a tool every commercial tenant facing a landlord's default notice in New York should know: filed promptly, it can freeze cure-period deadlines and prevent a landlord from terminating the underlying lease or option while the merits are decided, buying the tenant time it would otherwise lose simply by litigating the contract claims on a slower track. Commercial tenants holding options or expansion rights under a ground lease with a government or institutional landlord should track default-notice cure periods closely and know, before a dispute arises, whether a Yellowstone injunction or similar device is available in their jurisdiction to freeze those deadlines while litigation proceeds. Owners contemplating significant pre-construction spending on an option-dependent expansion should weigh how much capital to commit before the underlying right is judicially confirmed, since a dispute over an option's validity can surface years after it was granted, and both sides of a long-term ground lease with layered option and development rights should build in clear, unambiguous default and cure mechanics up front, since the kind of ambiguity that invites a fraudulent-inducement claim on one side and an emergency injunction fight on the other is exactly what years of litigation cost the most to resolve.
live-338: Thor Equities, LLC, joined by Urbana Owner LLC, Urbana Owner I LLC, Urbana Owner II LLC and Highland55 Investments LLC, filed a civil rights complaint under 42 U.S.C. 1983 on June 19, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio against the City of Urbana, the Urbana City Council and the city's Building and Zoning Appeals Board, according to the federal docket. The case, No. 3:26-cv-00196, is assigned to U.S. District Judge Michael J. Newman. According to DatacenterDynamics, Thor says it worked with city officials for more than a year, assembled about 230 acres and submitted a complete site plan in February 2026 for a $1 billion, 460,000-square-foot data center that would use closed-loop cooling, and that it spent $19.6 million of its own funds on preliminary work. The city passed a 12-month "emergency moratorium" in March and in June rezoned Thor's land as unsuitable for data centers. "Our plans were rejected on grounds that don't match the city's own zoning code, and the council passed an emergency moratorium to pause data centers," Thor global COO Melissa Gliatta said in a statement on the project website. Thor also said the moratorium came amid what it called exaggerated claims about water use, noise and health effects, and that it hopes to resolve the matter fairly. DCD did not report a response from the city. The city filed an answer on July 14, 2026, and the court referred the case to mediation before a magistrate judge, with sessions set for September. On September 18, a group of nearby residents and two local companies moved to intervene; Thor opposed the motion and the city filed a response on October 9, and on October 16 the proposed intervenors filed a notice objecting to a consent decree.
live-339: Chatham County commissioners adopted a moratorium on new data centers in February 2026 that runs until February 11, 2027, or until new zoning rules are adopted, NC Newsline reported. Eco TIP West plans a 750-megawatt data center at the Triangle Innovation Point West business park near Moncure. It sued the county in Chatham County Superior Court in April, arguing the project was already in progress when the moratorium passed and should be exempt. The company said it had spent $11 million on the project and that the site's zoning allowed a data center, and the North State Journal reported that the county had issued a zoning permit in late October 2025 confirming the use was permitted by right once water and sewer service were available. The county argued, according to the Carolina Journal, that Eco TIP had no vested right because it never obtained a development approval for a data center, that it did not submit a complete application before the moratorium took effect, and that summary judgment was premature without discovery. After an August 31 hearing, Judge John Morris found 'no genuine issue as to any material fact' and ruled for the developer. The Carolina Journal reported that he awarded attorney's fees and reserved the determination of damages for further proceedings; NC Newsline reported that the county must pay damages for trying to slow the project. Neither outlet reported whether the county will appeal. NC Newsline said it is unclear how the ruling will affect the other moratoria adopted across the state.
live-340: Six creditors filed an involuntary Chapter 7 petition against Jon Peter Venetos, founder of Dallas-based multifamily firm Lurin Capital, on September 17, 2026, in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas (Case No. 26-36934), according to the court docket. The docket lists the petitioning creditors as Vista Bank, a division of NBH Bank; NREF Center Point, LLC; SCF II Group Holdings; Really High Places LLC; Sespe Investment Group Fund I, LP; and Red Elephant Design + Architectural Signage. The case is assigned to Judge Eduardo V. Rodriguez. The Real Deal reported on September 30 that the petition cites $33.7 million in judgments against Venetos personally. According to the article, the three largest are held by lenders: Silver Point Finance has a $22.7 million judgment for breach of a promissory note, and Vista Bank ($3.1 million) and NexPoint Real Estate Finance ($5 million) have judgments based on his personal guaranties, about $30.8 million combined. The rest are a $1.2 million judgment held by a Vail investor, a $1.5 million judgment held by Sespe Investment Group and a $218,000 judgment held by Red Elephant Design, a Dallas vendor. The article said the judgments came from lender suits over loans on Lurin's Sun Belt apartment portfolio, and that a separate $19 million judgment owed to Acore Capital Mortgage, also tied to personal guaranties, is not part of the petition. Venetos did not respond to The Real Deal's request for comment. Greg Corbin, president of bankruptcy firm Northgate Real Estate Group, told the publication that an involuntary filing against an individual is "one of the rarest moves in bankruptcy." A Chapter 7 case aims to find and sell a debtor's remaining assets; the article said it is unclear what Venetos still owns after Morgan Stanley foreclosed on his Aspen home at the end of 2025. It also reported that the FBI has opened an investigation into Lurin Capital, and that KeyBank and Vista Bank have each accused Venetos of fraud in their own claims. Those accusations are allegations. Lurin's own Chapter 11 case covers 20 filings by single-asset entities plus Lurin Advisors, the company's controlling entity. The Real Deal reported that in a September 22 filing the trustee in that case asked the court to convert it to Chapter 7 or dismiss it, because Lurin had not filed an operating report since April.
live-341: Renaissance Midtown West LLC sued its former tenant, Lividini & Company, LLC, and the tenant's principal in New York County Supreme Court in November 2024, seeking rent for the balance of the lease term, enforcement of a guaranty and an order piercing the corporate veil. According to the decision, the tenant's counsel gave notice in August 2020 that the tenant was vacating, the tenant returned the keys without objection, and the landlord later signed a lease with a new tenant; the landlord acknowledged there was no further communication between the parties until it sued. Justice Lyle E. Frank granted the defendants' motion to dismiss the amended complaint in an order entered July 24, 2025. A First Department panel of Justices Webber, Kapnick, Shulman, Pitt-Burke and Hagler unanimously affirmed on October 27, 2026. Paragraph 17(1) of the lease is a conditional limitation that lets the landlord end the lease for defaults other than nonpayment, including if the premises become "vacant or deserted," by serving a five-day notice to cure and then a three-day notice of cancellation. Citing Holy Properties v. Cole Products, the court held that the tenant's vacatur triggered its right to that notice before reentry and reletting. It rejected the landlord's argument that it meant only to collect rent, not to terminate, because taking back the keys and reletting the space were at odds with a continuing landlord-tenant relationship. The court also held that lease paragraph 17(2) and rider paragraph 66, which the landlord invoked for unpaid amounts, apply only while the tenant remains in possession. It distinguished 622 Third Ave. Co. LLC v. Hyatt Leader Ltd., where the landlord had told the tenant that accepting the surrender was without prejudice to a claim for unpaid rent; no such allegation was made here. The guaranty claim failed under General Obligations Law § 5-701(a)(2) because the standard-form guaranty attached to the lease was blank and unexecuted, and the landlord alleged no facts warranting leave to replead. On veil piercing, the court, citing Cortlandt Street Recovery Corp. v. Bonderman, said the doctrine is not a separate cause of action, and a bare allegation that the principal did not keep a bank account separate from the tenant's did not show domination and control used to commit a wrong against the landlord.
live-342: GRE Downtowner LLC operates Addison on Fourth, a low-income apartment complex near downtown Seattle. According to the opinion, the company bought the property in 2012 for $12.5 million and invested another $26.5 million to qualify it for the federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program, with bond financing from the Washington State Housing and Finance Commission. The complex has 254 studio and one-bedroom apartments for residents earning 60 percent of the area median income, along with 46 artist studios and four commercial spaces, and HUD sets its maximum rents. The company alleges that ordinances and a resolution adopted by the Seattle City Council starting in 2018 made the property impossible to run sustainably: the Fair Chance Housing Ordinance, the 2019 Roommate Ordinance, the 2020 Winter Eviction Ban, a COVID-19 eviction moratorium in effect from March 2020 to February 2022, a 2021 ordinance extending the notice period for rent increases from 60 to 180 days, and the 2021 Economic Displacement Relocation Assistance ordinance. As the court summarized the complaint, the share of maximum rental income collected fell from about 90 to 94 percent in 2015 through 2018 to 44.1 percent in 2023, and the property lost $683,353 in 2020, $980,043 in 2021, $1.8 million in 2022 and $2.7 million in 2023. GRE Downtowner alleges the complex is now functionally valueless on an income-approach appraisal. GRE Downtowner sued in King County Superior Court on October 22, 2024, alleging partial and per se regulatory takings under article I, section 16 of the Washington Constitution. The trial court granted the City's motion to dismiss under CR 12(b)(6) in February 2025, and a Washington Supreme Court commissioner later denied the City's motion to transfer the appeal to that court. Division One reversed. Applying Washington's CR 12(b)(6) standard, which is more lenient than the federal one, the court held the complaint pleaded enough on each of the three Penn Central factors to support a partial takings claim. It rejected the City's arguments that the losses flowed from the tax-credit restrictions and that an owner in a highly regulated field cannot have reasonable investment-backed expectations. Rejecting the City's call for a three-year limit, it adopted the six-year period in RCW 4.16.040(3) for partial regulatory takings claims, so that claim was timely. It also held that the Roommate Ordinance, by giving occupancy rights to uninvited third parties who are not tenants, supports a per se takings claim under Cedar Point Nursery v. Hassid, over the City's argument that a landlord-tenant regulation cannot effect a per se taking.
live-343: A commercial property owner that skipped its own eminent domain trial has lost its bid on appeal to recover more than the government's pre-trial deposit for the taking. In BFT Rental, LLC v. City of Fayetteville, the Arkansas Court of Appeals affirmed a Washington County Circuit Court order granting the City of Fayetteville a directed verdict after BFT Rental, LLC failed to appear for the jury trial set to determine how much compensation it was owed for a condemned easement. The ruling leaves BFT's recovery capped at the $112,180 the City had already deposited with the court, underscoring that a condemnee's right to a jury's independent assessment of just compensation can be forfeited by default just as surely as any other civil claim. The City filed its condemnation action against BFT on November 8, 2023, seeking to acquire an easement across BFT-owned property in Fayetteville for construction of a water-transmission main. Acting under Arkansas's quick-take statute, Ark. Code Ann. section 18-15-303, the City deposited $112,180 into the court registry and obtained an order of immediate possession on November 16, 2023, allowing it to take possession and begin the public works project while the ultimate compensation question was litigated. BFT moved to withdraw the deposited funds, which the court granted, and the case proceeded toward a jury trial on the amount of just compensation. What followed was a run of attorney transitions that proved consequential. BFT's original counsel withdrew in the spring of 2024, and replacement counsel entered an appearance that July. The circuit court set a one-day jury trial for April 30, 2025. On January 31, 2025, roughly three months before trial, that attorney also moved to withdraw. The City objected to any resulting continuance, noting the case had already been pending for well over a year, its witnesses were prepared to proceed, and this was BFT's second attorney to seek withdrawal during the litigation. The circuit court granted the withdrawal on February 27, 2025, but denied the continuance. BFT did not retain new counsel until after the trial date had passed and never objected to the February 27 ruling at the time; instead, BFT simply did not appear for the April 30 jury trial. With no appearance, no witness list, and no exhibit list from the defense, the City moved for a directed verdict, which the circuit court granted, affirming the City's ownership of the easement and fixing just compensation at the $112,180 already on deposit. The court explained in its written order that, absent any evidence from BFT, a reasonable jury would not have had a sufficient evidentiary basis to award BFT just compensation beyond that amount. On appeal, BFT argued that the circuit court abused its discretion by allowing its attorney to withdraw while denying a continuance, and that the error tainted both the directed verdict and the later denial of its motion for a new trial. The Court of Appeals never reached the merits of that argument. Citing Tate-Smith v. Cupples and Nash v. Nash, the panel held that under Arkansas's preservation doctrine, an objection raised for the first time in a motion for new trial is not timely and cannot be considered on appeal, a rule designed to prevent a litigant from waiting to see whether a gamble pays off before raising an available objection. Because BFT voiced no complaint about the February 27 ruling until two months later, after it had already lost at trial, the panel held the issue was unpreserved, and it rejected BFT's separate challenge to the denial of its new-trial motion on the same ground, also noting that BFT's briefing never argued why the directed verdict itself was substantively wrong. Eminent domain compensation disputes are almost always about the numbers, but this case is a reminder that appraisal and valuation evidence is worthless if it never reaches the jury. For commercial landlords, developers, and other property owners facing condemnation, the lesson is that a government's statutory deposit, once left undisputed by competent evidence at trial, can become the ceiling on recovery as a matter of law, and that any scheduling dispute or counsel transition close to trial needs an immediate, on-the-record objection and a formal continuance motion rather than a wait-and-see approach raised only after an adverse verdict.

live-345: On October 19, 2026, 111 West 57th Investment LLC, suing on its own behalf and derivatively for 111 West 57th Partners LLC and 111 West 57th Mezz 1 LLC, filed a Summons with Notice in the Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County, against ACREFI Mortgage LLC and its indirect parent, Apollo Commercial Real Estate Finance, Inc. The filing, docketed under Index No. 655919/2026, alleges that ACREFI improperly transferred funds to Apollo Commercial Real Estate Finance for no consideration or equivalent value. The claim surfaced publicly through AmBase Corporation's quarterly report filed October 28, 2026; AmBase is the ultimate corporate parent of the plaintiff entities and has carried this litigation on its books since its equity investment in the underlying project was impaired in 2017. The new claim is the latest front in a legal battle that has pitted AmBase's investment vehicles against Apollo-affiliated lenders and the project sponsors for nearly a decade over the 111 West 57th Street condominium tower, known to New Yorkers as the Steinway Tower. The dispute traces to a $25 million junior mezzanine loan secured by the plaintiffs' equity interest in the development. In 2017, ACREFI sold that loan to Spruce Capital Partners LLC at par value, notwithstanding internal valuations that reportedly put the underlying equity at roughly $600 million. Two days after acquiring the loan, Spruce initiated a UCC Article 9 strict foreclosure, seizing the pledged collateral and wiping out the plaintiffs' equity position in the project entirely. AmBase's vehicles sued Spruce and the project sponsor that same year in what has become known as the Lender Action, seeking to unwind the foreclosure and recover damages. That earlier fight reached the New York Court of Appeals, which ruled on May 28, 2026 that Apollo's contractual right to assign the mezzanine loan at its sole discretion did not, standing alone, shield the lender from a claim that the discretion was exercised in bad faith as part of a scheme to strip the plaintiffs' equity. The Court of Appeals reinstated the plaintiffs' implied-covenant-of-good-faith claim and sent the case back to the trial court, while leaving dismissal of related tortious-interference claims in place. That litigation remains pending in Supreme Court, New York County. The newly filed action is a distinct case rather than a continuation of the Lender Action: it names ACREFI and Apollo Commercial Real Estate Finance, rather than Spruce or the sponsor, as defendants, and it asserts a different theory, that ACREFI moved money up to its parent without consideration. AmBase's disclosure does not specify the amount allegedly transferred, nor does it identify a presiding judge, consistent with the filing being an initial Summons with Notice rather than a verified complaint. A Summons with Notice is a procedural device under New York practice that commences an action and preserves a plaintiff's filing date while a fuller complaint is prepared or demanded by the defendant. This is not AmBase's first collateral attack on the Apollo lending relationship. In 2024, the same plaintiff entities sued the law firm Kasowitz Benson Torres LLP and attorney Douglas B. Heitner, alleging the firm represented the 111 West 57th entities in the development's financing while simultaneously representing parties with adverse interests, including the project's principals Michael Stern and Kevin Maloney and entities they control. For commercial mortgage lenders and mezzanine investors, the new filing is a reminder that winning a strict foreclosure does not necessarily close the book on a sponsor or equity investor's claims: collateral attacks on intercompany transfers, assignment practices, and professional representation can surface years after the underlying default. Lenders structuring mezzanine debt in New York should expect continued scrutiny of sole-discretion assignment language following the Court of Appeals' May 2026 ruling, and should be prepared to document the business rationale for intercompany fund movements between a special-purpose lending subsidiary and its parent, particularly where those movements follow or coincide with a foreclosure that wipes out a junior equity holder. For sponsors and joint-venture partners who have lost equity in a strict foreclosure, this filing illustrates that fraudulent-transfer and no-consideration theories remain an available avenue even after a Lender Action has run its course, provided the facts support them.

live-347: More than three decades ago, Hidden Valley Corporation bought two neighboring properties in Miami. It leased one to BellSouth Mobility and later gave BellSouth and its successors an easement to use part of the other for telecommunications. The easement agreement's "Remedies for Breach" section entitles the prevailing party in a suit to enforce it to reasonable attorney's fees and costs. Both properties later changed hands; when this dispute arose, RJ's International Trading, LLC (RJI) owned the burdened parcel, and Crown Castle South, LLC subleased the neighboring property from BellSouth and held the easement rights. In 2020, Crown Castle excavated parts of RJI's land beyond the easement and installed underground fiber-optic cable. RJI sued in federal court. The district court granted RJI partial summary judgment on trespass and breach of the easement, and after a six-day trial a jury awarded $1 for the breach and $40,000 for trespass; Crown Castle did not appeal. The district court then denied RJI's motion for attorney's fees under the easement, agreeing with Crown Castle that the provision did not touch and concern the land. On RJI's appeal, the Eleventh Circuit rejected RJI's argument that it was a party to the agreement and certified the covenant question to the Florida Supreme Court. Justice Jamie Grosshans wrote for the court. A covenant runs with the land only if the original parties intended to bind successors, successors had notice, and the covenant touches and concerns the land; the court decided the case on the third element. Tracing the doctrine from Spencer's Case (1583) through Florida decisions, it held that courts should ask whether the obligation is sufficiently connected to how the land is used, occupied or enjoyed. The fee provision does not restrict how RJI's land can be used or who can use it, and it applies only after a dispute is resolved, serving "solely to allocate litigation costs between the parties," the court wrote. It distinguished Hayslip v. U.S. Home Corp., which held that a deed's arbitration clause ran with the land, and noted that most courts outside Florida to address fee provisions agree. Chief Justice Couriel and Justices Labarga, Muñiz and Francis concurred. Justices Barrios and Tanenbaum concurred in result only: Justice Barrios would require a direct effect on the physical use of the property and called Hayslip an outlier, and Justice Tanenbaum wrote that a prevailing-party fee provision can never be a real covenant.
live-348: Cobleskill Enterprise, LLP owned a hotel and restaurant complex in the Town of Cobleskill, Schoharie County, with a bowling alley, banquet room, kitchen and pool. After a fire there in December 2018, it sought coverage under its commercial property policy. Seneca Insurance Company Inc. denied the claim on several grounds, including misrepresentations in the application and the claim and breach of the policy's protective safeguards endorsement, or PSE, and sued for fraud and declarations that the policy was void and that it owed no coverage. Cobleskill Enterprise counterclaimed and brought a third-party action against Links Insurance Services, LLC, the retail broker that placed the policy. Seneca later added fraud and negligent-misrepresentation claims against Links, alleging Links filed the claim knowing a third party had cancelled the policy before the fire. In an order entered March 4, 2025, Supreme Court (Justice James Ferreira) denied Links' motion to dismiss and Seneca's cross-motion for summary judgment on the PSE, finding Seneca's own submissions raised fact issues. Seneca's evidence included an October 2018 Village of Cobleskill citation for inadequate carbon monoxide detectors and testimony from a technician with the fire-equipment firm hired about a month later. He testified that there were no smoke detectors in the pool area, bowling alley, basement or dining room ceiling, only heat detectors in the banquet room and kitchen, and a few nonfunctional "dummy detectors." He also said the reporting panel for the restaurant, kitchen, banquet room and bowling alley could not communicate with the main panel, so a fire in those areas would not set off the building's alarms. Writing for the panel, Justice Stan L. Pritzker held that Seneca established breach and materiality as a matter of law. Giving "operational" its ordinary meaning, detectors that might light up but would not sound an alarm were in effect nonoperational, and some areas had none at all; the bowling alley, a public space, was clearly a common area. The lack of operational detectors in a public space was material to the risk of fire loss, and the property suffered fire and smoke losses, including in areas without them. Cobleskill Enterprise offered no substantive opposition. The court also dismissed Seneca's claims against Links. The fraud claim rested on concealment and required a fiduciary duty that an arm's-length broker relationship did not supply, and Seneca's reliance was not reasonable because, as a sophisticated insurer, it could have checked whether the policy was in force. The owner's third-party claims against Links were dismissed because they were limited to denials based on cancellation or application misrepresentations, not the PSE breach on which coverage was denied.
live-349: In October 2024, the City of South Bend, acting at the direction of its mayor, filed a complaint to condemn real property owned by Argos 316, LLC in a redevelopment project area established by the South Bend Redevelopment Commission. Portage Township of St. Joseph County had already contracted to buy the property and completed the purchase shortly after the City filed. The Township and 350 Columbia Street, LLC, which held easements on the property, intervened and objected that the action was not authorized by the South Bend Common Council, as Indiana Code section 36-7-14-20(a) contemplates. The Marshall Circuit Court, Judge Janette E. Surrisi presiding, overruled the objection, concluding that Council authorization is one way, not the only way, for the City to condemn property in a redevelopment project area. The Court of Appeals reversed in an opinion by Judge Nancy H. Vaidik, joined by Judge May. The City argued that the statute only sets a procedure for when the legislative body chooses to act and leaves other officials' broad condemnation power under Indiana Code section 36-1-4-5(a) intact; the objectors argued it confines the power to the legislative body. Finding both readings reasonable on the text alone, the court looked to the surrounding chapter, which sets out how a redevelopment commission is created, how a project area is designated with plan commission and legislative body approval, and how the commission must first try to negotiate purchases. Read as a whole, the redevelopment scheme "makes clear that the power lies with the unit's legislative body," the court wrote. Because the Common Council never authorized the action, the court held the trial court erred in overruling the objection, and it did not reach the objectors' other arguments. Chief Judge Tavitas concurred in the result, noting that neither party had argued the statute was ambiguous.
live-350: In December 2004, The Weitz Company, LLC, general contractor on a multi-building retirement community in Shelby County, Tennessee, and Commercial Painting Company, Inc. entered into a drywall subcontract for $3,222,400, later raised by change orders to $3,315,189. Weitz paid 12 of Commercial Painting's 17 pay applications and refused the other five, saying they were untimely and contained improper change order requests. Commercial Painting sued Weitz and its sureties, Federal Insurance Company and St. Paul Fire & Marine Insurance Company, in Shelby County Chancery Court in August 2006, and Weitz counterclaimed for delay and defective work. Commercial Painting later added fraud and misrepresentation claims, alleging Weitz concealed a six-month extension it had negotiated with the project owner, which carried a bonus of $8,597 a day for up to 45 days of early completion, and then compressed the schedule, supplemented the drywall work and charged Commercial Painting for it. In October 2018, a jury found for Commercial Painting on breach of contract, unjust enrichment, intentional misrepresentation and the payment bond, and the award totaled $8,359,863.83: $1,272,952.46 in compensatory damages, $2,083,362.16 in prejudgment interest, $1,103,549 in attorney's fees and $3.9 million in punitive damages. The trial court upheld the punitive award, finding that Weitz knew before signing that the project was about eight months behind, planned to compress the schedule and supplement the drywall work without telling Commercial Painting, and misrepresented the extension it later obtained. In 2022 the Court of Appeals reversed the punitive award under the economic loss doctrine. The Tennessee Supreme Court reversed that ruling in 2023 and, after a further appeal, directed the Court of Appeals in June 2025 to decide whether Commercial Painting had contractually waived punitive damages on its misrepresentation claim. Judge Jeffrey Usman, joined by Judges J. Steven Stafford and Carma Dennis McGee, held that it had not. Section 11.6 of the subcontract bars anticipatory profit and indirect, special or consequential damages and waives "any other measure of damages" beyond those the subcontract provides, but it does not specifically waive damages for fraud or misrepresentation and appears to address contract remedies rather than tort. Under either the traditional view, reflected in Tennessee cases holding that "fraud vitiates all that it touches," or an approach that enforces only clear and specific waivers, the court concluded the clause does not bar the punitive award. It treated the jury's misrepresentation finding as the law of the case and held Weitz's ratification argument waived.
live-351: PMC Property Group, Inc. filed a new federal lawsuit against Apogee Enterprises, Inc. on Oct. 27, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, USGlass magazine reported. live-352: Accord, LLC acquired a parcel in the Hamlet of Accord, Town of Rochester, Ulster County, that is the site of a historic granary and seed mill complex, and asked the Town Board to rezone it into an Economic Enterprise Overlay (EEO) district and approve its conceptual development plan. After a SEQRA review ended in a negative declaration, the Town Board adopted Local Law No. 10 of 2023, granting the rezoning and approving a plan to convert the buildings into a restaurant, a bike shop, an artist gallery, a coworking space, worker housing and an inn. It agreed the project needed 63 parking spaces: 57 on site, 25 of them for the restaurant, and six off site. During site plan review, Accord's architect told the Planning Board in May 2024 that the artist gallery would be dropped, the coworking space reduced by 421 square feet and the six off-site spaces eliminated. On July 8, 2024, the Planning Board granted conditional site plan approval, finding the modified project in substantial conformance with the conceptual plan and adopting the Town Board's on-site parking finding. In August 2024, two individuals with property near the site filed an Article 78 petition, arguing among other things that the restaurant needed 78 spaces under the code's one-space-per-50-square-feet standard applied to its listed 3,914.65 square feet. Accord's engineer responded that he had used an alternative one-space-per-three-seats calculation, presented to the Town Board, because the code does not say whether gross or net floor area applies. Supreme Court, Ulster County (Justice David Gandin) dismissed the petition in a judgment entered April 11, 2025. Writing for a unanimous panel, Justice Christine M. Clark held the approval was not arbitrary or capricious. The EEO rules allow approval of a site plan in "substantial conformance" with the conceptual plan, and the changes here reduced the project's scope without adding a new use or changing on-site parking. The petitioners never asked the Planning Board to seek a code interpretation from the zoning board or code enforcement officer, and in any event the Planning Board did not interpret the code: the Town Board had accepted Accord's parking calculation in Local Law 10, and in EEO districts the code's parking standards are guidelines rather than strict requirements. The court also upheld dropping the six off-site spaces, which tracked the removal of the gallery and the smaller coworking space, and rejected an argument about an "unconditioned event space" because the Planning Board expressly declined to approve events as a use.
live-353: The Kentucky Court of Appeals on October 30, 2026 affirmed summary judgment against Lampton Securities Partnership, LLP in its reverse condemnation suit against Louisville-Jefferson County Metro Government and the Louisville and Jefferson County Metropolitan Sewer District, holding the claim was not ripe. In an opinion by Judge Lisa Payne Jones, joined by Judges Combs and Easton, the court found that Lampton never sought the variance the Sewer District's Floodplain Board may grant, so there was no final decision on how the property could be used. In the early 1990s, the owners of a roughly four-acre Ohio River tract received the Sewer District's approval for a two-phase condominium plan. Phase One was built on about two acres; on the remaining two acres, the Tract, only an electrical equipment building and utility lines were installed. In 1997, in response to catastrophic flooding, Metro Government enacted floodplain ordinances that bar most new construction in the conveyance zone, which includes the Tract. The ordinances allow construction already begun to continue and let landowners seek a variance from the Floodplain Board, and the record shows the Board has granted variances to other landowners. Lampton bought the Tract for $800,000 in 1998, after the ordinances took effect. Around 2019 it marketed the Tract as commercially developable, and at a later meeting the Sewer District's counsel told Lampton the ordinances prevented development. Lampton neither sought a variance nor tried to start Phase Two and instead sued in Jefferson Circuit Court in May 2020, alleging it had lost all economically beneficial use. In July 2025, Judge Jessica E. Green granted summary judgment to the defendants, finding Lampton had not exhausted administrative remedies and had not filed on time. The Court of Appeals affirmed on a different ground, ripeness. Relying on U.S. Supreme Court decisions including Palazzolo v. Rhode Island, MacDonald, Sommer & Frates v. Yolo County, Suitum v. Tahoe Regional Planning Agency and Pakdel v. City and County of San Francisco, and on the Kentucky Supreme Court's 2002 decision in Spanish Cove Sanitation, Inc. v. Louisville-Jefferson County Metropolitan Sewer District, it held there was no final decision on the Tract's permitted uses. It rejected Lampton's futility argument: counsel's opinion did not bind the Board, the record showed variances granted to others, and the Sewer District's designated representative testified that no similar variance had been requested. The court noted the trial court's statement that Lampton may bring a future takings claim once it is ripe.
live-354: The District of Columbia's Office of the Attorney General announced on September 14, 2026 that it had reached consent judgments with JBG Smith and Mid-America Apartment Communities, Inc. (MAA), resolving the District's claims that both landlords used RealPage's revenue-management software to coordinate rents in violation of antitrust law. JBG Smith, through its JBG Associates, L.L.C. entity, agreed to pay $8.1 million, and MAA agreed to pay $1.2 million, for a combined $9.3 million, in a case captioned District of Columbia v. RealPage, Inc., et al., No. 2023-CAB-006762, pending in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia. The District's suit is one node of a much larger legal reckoning facing RealPage and the landlords that used its pricing products. Since 2022 and 2023, the Department of Justice, dozens of state attorneys general, and a sprawling multidistrict class action in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee have all pursued claims that RealPage's revenue-management software functioned as a vehicle for horizontal price coordination: landlords fed RealPage non-public, competitively sensitive data on asking rents, lease terms, and occupancy, which RealPage's algorithm then used to recommend pricing informed by the pooled data of competitors. Regulators have characterized this as a hub-and-spoke conspiracy, with RealPage as the hub and participating landlords as the spokes. The District's complaint named RealPage along with a roster of landlords operating in the District, including JBG Smith and MAA. According to the consent judgments, JBG Smith used RealPage's revenue-management software to help set rents across multiple District properties, while MAA's use was tied to a single District property. Neither company admitted liability as part of the settlements, which is standard in these resolutions, and both agreed to prospective restrictions on their future use of shared-data pricing software -- commitments running eight years in MAA's case -- along with the possibility of an independent compliance monitor, at the settling company's expense, if the OAG later has reason to believe the terms are not being followed. The District's deals with JBG Smith and MAA followed earlier District settlements with other large operators, including a $1.4 million resolution with Avenue5 Residential and Bell Partners reached in June 2026, and track a parallel wave of settlements Kentucky's Attorney General has reached in its own, separately filed RealPage suit, including with Greystar Management Services in July 2026. In the Tennessee MDL, dozens of landlord defendants have resolved their exposure, with the presiding court approving roughly $360 million in aggregate settlements as of mid-October 2026, while RealPage and a shrinking number of holdout defendants continue to litigate. MAA disclosed the $1.2 million payment and the accompanying consent judgment in its Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, noting the amount was accrued during the third quarter and that the company continues to defend a separate, still-pending suit brought by Kentucky's Attorney General against RealPage and a number of the state's largest landlords, including MAA itself. For multifamily owners and managers still facing RealPage-related exposure, the District of Columbia settlements confirm that enforcement authorities are treating even a single property's use of shared-data pricing software as sufficient grounds for antitrust liability, with the scale of use affecting only the settlement amount. In-house teams should treat a RealPage-related consent judgment as an ongoing compliance obligation rather than a one-time payment, and build monitoring of revenue-management software practices into their regular legal and operational review going forward.
live-355: The Appellate Division of the Superior Court of New Jersey on October 30, 2026, affirmed a Law Division order dismissing with prejudice a neighboring owner's challenge to approvals for the renovation of the Gottlieb Building, a two-story building erected in 1906 at 641 Arnold Avenue in Point Pleasant Beach's downtown commercial district. live-356: Monarch Casino & Resort, Inc. (NASDAQ: MCRI) disclosed in its quarterly report filed October 30, 2026 that the judge presiding over a long-running mechanics' lien foreclosure action in Gilpin County, Colorado lifted a litigation stay effective September 16, 2026, and set a case management conference for January 22, 2027. Separately, PCL filed a mechanics' lien foreclosure action in March 2021 in the District Court for Gilpin County, the county where the Black Hawk property sits, seeking to foreclose liens against the casino property itself rather than pursue a straight breach-of-contract judgment. That case, captioned PCL Construction Services, Inc. v. Monarch Growth Inc., et al., No. 2021CV30006, named Monarch and its Colorado subsidiaries as defendants, with PCL's own asserted lien amounting to roughly $45.5 million and additional subcontractor liens pushing the total claimed closer to $50 million. The Gilpin case had been stayed, likely pending resolution of the overlapping Denver litigation, until the September 2026 order lifting it at the request of one of the lien claimants. Monarch, for its part, filed a third action, the Second Denver Lawsuit, No. 2023CV30458, against PCL in February 2023, continuing to press its own claims arising from the same expansion. Monarch's 10-Q states the company is currently unable to determine the probability of the outcome or reasonably estimate the loss or gain, if any, from the newly reactivated Gilpin lien case, even though a related judgment already running into the tens of millions of dollars has been entered against the company in a companion proceeding over the identical construction work. That disclosure underscores how a lien foreclosure against the real property itself remains a live threat to an owner's title and operations even after a money judgment has been entered in a parallel suit, since a lien claimant can pursue both remedies until one is formally resolved or released. The case also illustrates the layered risk construction lien law creates for large hospitality and gaming developments. A general contractor's mechanics' lien attaches directly to the real property, giving the contractor leverage independent of whatever happens in a contract-damages lawsuit, and in Colorado, as in most states, a stayed lien case can be revived years later at a lien claimant's request, as happened here. Owners of large hospitality, gaming, and mixed-use developments should track mechanics' lien foreclosure actions separately from any parallel breach-of-contract litigation over the same project, recognize that a money judgment in a companion contract case does not extinguish a contractor's or subcontractor's separate lien rights against the property itself, and budget for the possibility of both a damages award and a lien foreclosure arising from the same dispute, since expansion and renovation projects at operating hospitality properties can carry lien exposure that resurfaces years after substantial completion, particularly where litigation has gone dormant under a stay rather than being dismissed or settled.

live-359: A Texas appellate court has affirmed summary judgment for a commercial landlord accused of overcharging a dental-practice tenant by misrepresenting the size of its leased space, holding that the tenant's breach-of-contract, fraud, and consumer-protection claims were filed years too late, and that the landlord in question had sold the shopping center, and been released from the lease, long before the tenant ever complained. The Thirteenth Court of Appeals' October 29, 2026 decision in Veena Dental PA v. Brixmor GA Apollo II TX LP is a reminder to both commercial landlords and tenants that a lease's assignment-and-release provisions, combined with ordinary limitations rules, can foreclose a claim no matter how sympathetic the underlying factual dispute looks. In March 2013, Veena Dental PA leased roughly 1,863 square feet of retail space at 1548 Wildcat Drive in Portland, Texas, part of the Northshore Plaza shopping center, from Brixmor GA Apollo II TX LP, intending to build out and operate a dental office. The parties negotiated a per-square-foot rental rate and extended the lease by amendment in September 2018. That same year, Brixmor sold Northshore Plaza to a successor entity, Northshore Plaza LP, assigning Veena's lease and triggering a provision under which Brixmor was released from all further liability and obligations once the buyer assumed them. Five years later, in 2023, Veena measured its space and says it discovered the true square footage was closer to 1,500 square feet, matching the dimensions shown on the dental office's own 2013 construction plans, rather than the 1,863 square feet stated in the lease. Veena demanded reimbursement for what it characterized as years of rent overpayments tied to the inflated square footage, and when Brixmor refused, filed suit on May 22, 2024, asserting breach of contract (more accurately, the court later noted, fraudulent inducement), common-law fraud, and violations of the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Brixmor moved for summary judgment on limitations grounds, and the trial court in San Patricio County granted the motion in September 2025. Writing for a unanimous panel, Justice Ysmael D. Fonseca held that the record conclusively established the limitations defense. Texas gives a plaintiff four years to sue for breach of contract or fraud and two years for a DTPA violation, but a fraud or DTPA claim's clock does not start until the plaintiff discovers, or in the exercise of reasonable diligence should have discovered, the wrongful act under the discovery rule. The court found that rule couldn't rescue Veena's claims: in discovery, Veena had admitted that its own 2013 construction plans, prepared before it ever opened for business, reflected the space's true, smaller dimensions, so the actual square footage was reasonably discoverable well before 2023 regardless of when Veena actually got around to measuring the space. With the accrual date pinned to the March 2013 lease signing, every claim was untimely, and the court affirmed summary judgment in full. The decision illustrates two risks that recur across commercial leasing disputes: a tenant cannot rely on the discovery rule to excuse years of inattention to information already in its own files, and a seller-landlord's standard assignment-and-release clause can extinguish liability for a transferring landlord's own alleged pre-sale misconduct once a successor assumes the lease. For commercial tenants, the practical lesson is to verify stated square footage against their own architectural drawings or a physical measurement at signing rather than relying on the landlord's figures, since a later claim will be measured against what the tenant's own contemporaneous records show was knowable; landlords selling a leased property should likewise confirm that assignment-and-release language is drafted to survive exactly this kind of after-the-fact dispute, and both sides should treat the limitations clock for a lease-related misrepresentation claim as running from signing rather than from whenever the harm happens to be noticed.

live-362: NFI Apartment Management's policy with Third Coast Insurance Company, issued March 15, 2020, covered several NFI properties, including an apartment complex in San Antonio, and barred suits not brought within two years and one day after the cause of action accrued. In February 2022 NFI's counsel sent a pre-suit notice demanding that Third Coast reverse its denial and pay about $1 million. live-363: In 2018, Sinmier, LLC loaned Vintro Hotels and Resorts seven million dollars to buy the Maui Sands Resort and Waterpark on Lake Erie in Sandusky, Ohio, recording a mortgage on September 7, 2018. Policies from Berkley and Everest Indemnity Insurance Company were cancelled when the closing was delayed, and Everest's reissued policy, effective October 19, 2018, listed Sinmier only as an additional insured under the general liability coverage, not as a mortgagee. Sutton held that a mortgagee's insurable interest extends only to the amount of the debt and ends when the debt does, citing Ohio cases going back to the 1840s and decisions from other states. By fully releasing Vintro's mortgage debt, Sinmier ended that interest, and all of its claims depended on it. The panel rejected Sinmier's argument that the deed's no-merger language conflicted with the settlement, finding it forfeited and, in any event, consistent with the release. It held that the settlement's reservation of how insurance proceeds would be divided did not preserve the debt, that the $627,375 obligation was secured by the consent judgment rather than the mortgage, and that the policy clause protecting a mortgagee that has started foreclosure did not apply because the deed ended the action. Sinmier's claims that Bankers negligently failed to tell it about a cancellation or to secure mortgagee coverage were forfeited, and the second also failed on the merits.
live-364: In January 2023, Bartow County approved conceptual site plans from Norhaven Partners, LLC for a 97-unit townhome community, the Overlook on Pettit, on residentially zoned land, and by October 2023 it had fully approved the development plans and a land disturbance permit. live-369: A Maricopa County Superior Court judge has ruled that the City of Phoenix must prove its data-center zoning ordinance is necessary to guard public health or face a lawsuit seeking more than $54 million, KJZZ reported on Oct. 28, 2026. live-370: The American Dream Mall's owner has secured a second consecutive legal win over its property tax bill, as a New Jersey Tax Court judge ruled on October 30, 2026 that the mall's sharply reduced 2025 assessment must carry forward unchanged into 2026 and 2027, rejecting arguments from both the Borough of East Rutherford and the trustee for the mega-mall's own bondholders that the reduction should not apply. The decision, in Ameream LLC v. Borough of East Rutherford, is a significant win for the mall's developer and a setback for the municipality's effort to recapture roughly $250 million in annual assessed value it had added back for the 2026 tax year. The dispute traces to a July 2025 trial in which the Tax Court cut the mall's cumulative assessment by roughly $850 million, from about $2.5 billion to $1,653,960,000. For tax year 2026, the Borough responded by raising the cumulative assessment back up to $1,899,992,100, prompting Ameream to invoke New Jersey's Freeze Act, a 1946 statute that makes a Tax Court judgment binding on the assessor and the taxing district for the judgment year and the two years that follow, subject to narrow exceptions. Because American Dream operates under a payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreement rather than paying conventional property taxes directly, the Borough and amicus curiae US Bank and Trust Company, serving as trustee for the bondholders whose bonds financed the mega-mall's development and are repaid largely from PILOT revenue, argued the Freeze Act should not apply at all, since Ameream is not a conventional taxpayer. Judge Michael J. Gilmore rejected that argument, holding that the PILOT agreement itself requires the Borough to assess the property as if it were subject to conventional taxation and expressly preserves Ameream's right to contest those assessments, so the Freeze Act's protections travel with the assessment regardless of how the resulting payment is labeled. Having cleared that threshold question, the court turned to whether any statutory exception defeated the freeze. US Bank offered testimony and news coverage describing reopened storefronts, tenant improvements, an improving economy and falling capitalization rates as evidence of a change in value, one of the Act's enumerated exceptions. The court found none of that evidence quantified an actual increase in the property's value, and held that general market improvement and higher occupancy, without more, cannot defeat the freeze. The court likewise rejected the argument that the Borough's annual municipal-wide reassessment program qualified as a complete reassessment exception, reasoning that the exception exists to prevent a frozen judgment from leaving one property out of step with a genuine district-wide revaluation, not to let a municipality's routine yearly updating override a specific judgment it dislikes. The ruling is the latest round in an increasingly adversarial relationship between East Rutherford, the mall's owner, and the mall's own creditors. US Bank, as bondholder trustee, has separately sued alleging the Borough and the mall's ownership effectively engineered the 2025 valuation reduction to each side's mutual benefit at bondholders' expense, while the Borough has pursued its own suit over roughly $183 million in PILOT payments Ameream claims it overpaid. The Freeze Act ruling does not resolve either of those fights, but it removes one significant lever, a higher 2026 assessment, that the Borough might otherwise have used to generate additional PILOT revenue while the broader disputes play out. For developers and owners operating under PILOT or similar payment-substitute arrangements, the ruling confirms that a favorable Tax Court valuation judgment is not automatically vulnerable just because the property does not pay conventional property taxes; if the underlying PILOT agreement ties payments to assessed value as if conventionally taxed, Freeze Act protection likely follows. Municipalities seeking to defeat a freeze need to come forward with quantified appraisal-grade evidence of a genuine change in value, not general market narrative or anecdotal leasing improvement, and bondholders and trustees relying on PILOT-backed debt should recognize that a borrower's successful tax appeal can bind the municipality's hands for up to three tax years, making early engagement in the underlying valuation litigation, not collateral challenges to the freeze itself, the more effective point of intervention.
live-371: Clipper Realty Inc., a New York Stock Exchange-listed owner of Brooklyn and Manhattan apartment and office properties, disclosed in a November 4, 2026 SEC filing that it remains in foreclosure litigation over its 250 Livingston Street office building in Downtown Brooklyn, more than seven months after a court-appointed receiver took over the property. The dispute is a case study in how a single large government lease can anchor, and then sink, a commercial mortgage. The trouble began on August 23, 2025, when New York City government agencies that had occupied all 342,496 rentable square feet of commercial space at the 12-story building terminated their lease and vacated. Those leases had accounted for roughly 18% to 22% of Clipper's annual revenue in the two preceding years. Facing a building with no paying commercial tenant, Clipper notified its lender that it would no longer support the property's operations, and the $125 million note secured by the building, held in the 2019 GS Mortgage Securities Trust 2019-GC40 commercial mortgage-backed securities pool, soon fell into default. On March 25, 2026, Wilmington Trust, National Association, acting as trustee for the trust's certificate holders, filed a foreclosure complaint in Kings County Supreme Court against the building's ownership entity, 250 Livingston Owner LLC, along with Clipper Realty Inc. and its operating subsidiary, Clipper Realty L.P., both of which guarantee certain obligations under the loan. The complaint asked the court to appoint a receiver to manage the property and to order the building sold, with proceeds applied against the outstanding debt. The court granted that request on April 29, 2026, installing a temporary receiver over the building's leasing and operations. Clipper's latest disclosure makes clear the case is far from resolved. The loan documents gave the lender a defined marketing period before it could move to an outright foreclosure sale or accept a deed in lieu of foreclosure, and separately gave Clipper the right to submit its own offer to purchase the loan. As of November 4, 2026, Clipper says the lender has not yet exercised its foreclosure or deed-in-lieu rights, leaving the parties in an extended standoff. The company has flagged the matter as an ongoing risk factor, warning that a foreclosure or deed-in-lieu transfer would have a material adverse effect on its financial condition, and that even a successful buyback would leave it needing to re-lease nearly 343,000 square feet with no comparable government anchor in sight. The 250 Livingston Street case has run on a different track than Clipper's dispute over its sister property at 141 Livingston Street, where a lender serviced on behalf of Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. sought similar receivership relief in 2025. There, a court denied the receiver motion in May 2025, and Clipper has since reported that it substantially settled that lender's claims by the end of 2025. The diverging outcomes underscore how fact-specific CMBS special-servicing fights can be, with results turning on the specific loan documents and each special servicer's own posture rather than on how similar the underlying buildings look from the street. For CRE owners and lenders alike, the matter is a reminder that loan covenants tied to a single large lease, government or otherwise, concentrate default risk in a way that can move faster than a borrower can arrange a replacement tenant, and that a receivership fight on one asset in a multi-property lender relationship does not predict the outcome on a similarly situated sister property.
live-372: The Hartford Business Journal reported on May 1, 2026 that JZ Investments, Inc., a Connecticut investment company, had sued a former business partner and several Greenwich real estate entities over the loss of its ownership stake in a proposed 262-unit housing development at 497-501 Middle Turnpike in Mansfield, near UConn's main campus. live-373: On November 5, 2026, the Tenth District Court of Appeals of Ohio reversed a Franklin County Court of Common Pleas judgment in an eminent domain case brought by the City of Columbus, holding that the trial court was wrong to bar a mortgage lender, Wiltshire Capital Partners, LP, from claiming an interest in the property. Judge Dingus wrote the decision, and Judges Edelstein and Leland concurred. In August 2021 the city petitioned to appropriate a fee simple interest and a temporary easement on a 0.082-acre parcel, and a temporary construction easement on a 0.016-acre parcel, for the Hudson Street Sidewalks Project. In July 2023 the trial court ruled that res judicata barred Wiltshire's claim and that Wiltshire lacked standing. Wiltshire's first appeal was dismissed in 2024 for lack of a final, appealable order, although the appellate court noted that the issue was not really one of standing, since the city itself had named Wiltshire as a respondent. In May 2025 the trial court approved the city's settlement with Ohio Wholesale Auto Sales over Wiltshire's objection and vested title in the city upon a $4,014 payment to the owner. It also agreed with the owner that Wiltshire had failed to set forth an interest in the property, citing an apparent assignment of the note underlying the mortgage. On the second appeal, the panel noted that Ohio Civil Rule 41(B)(3) generally treats a dismissal for failure to prosecute as an adjudication on the merits unless the court says otherwise. But under the Ohio Supreme Court's decision in Thomas v. Freeman, when a plaintiff has not obtained service on the defendant, a dismissal under either Civil Rule 41(B)(1) or Civil Rule 4(E) is otherwise than on the merits. Wiltshire had served only the county treasurer in the 2017 case, not the owner, so that dismissal was without prejudice and could not bar its claim. The court said it made no finding on whether Wiltshire holds a valid and enforceable mortgage, and directed that Wiltshire be allowed to assert its claim and argue those issues on remand. live-377: The Intermediate Court of Appeals of West Virginia, in an opinion by Judge Ryan White filed November 6, 2026, affirmed the dismissal of a breach-of-contract suit brought by Fountain Place, LLC against the City of Logan and the now-defunct City of Logan Development Authority over a decades-old economic development agreement that had once paid the shopping center's owner more than half of the municipal business taxes collected from its tenants. The ruling closes off, at least for now, a revenue stream the center's ownership had relied on since the late 1990s, and offers a cautionary lesson for developers who structure long-term incentive deals around a municipal authority's continued existence. The dispute traces to 1997, when the City of Logan and the Development Authority it had created entered into a Development Agreement with Monterra, the predecessor-in-interest to what is now Fountain Place, LLC, to facilitate construction of a shopping center in an unincorporated part of Logan County. In exchange for Monterra's agreement not to object to the City annexing the property, the City and Development Authority agreed to remit 57% of the business and occupancy taxes collected from businesses operating at the completed shopping center to Monterra and its successors for an initial 20-year term, with an option to renew for an additional ten years. The agreement also exempted the developer from paying its own business and occupancy taxes on construction, rental, and leasing activity at the property, an exemption from which neither Monterra nor Fountain Place has ever deviated. Monterra built the shopping center, which still operates as the Fountain Place mall, but filed for bankruptcy in 1999; a federal bankruptcy court assigned the Development Agreement's rights, including the tax-rebate payments, to Fountain Place, LLC without objection. The City kept making the 57% payments for years, even after the Development Authority itself dissolved around 2013, with Fountain Place collecting directly from the City instead. In 2016, Fountain Place formally exercised its option to renew the agreement through 2027, and the City did not object, continuing to pay until May 2021, when it abruptly concluded it was no longer legally obligated to do so. Fountain Place sued for breach of contract and declaratory judgment in the Circuit Court of Logan County in August 2023. The City and Development Authority moved to dismiss, and the circuit court granted that motion in July 2025 on three independent grounds: that the Development Agreement created an unconstitutional municipal indebtedness under Article X, Section 8 of the West Virginia Constitution because it was never submitted to a public vote; that the City was statutorily immune from any liabilities of the Development Authority, which had dissolved years earlier; and that the City was not estopped from challenging the agreement's lawfulness despite having honored it for more than two decades. On appeal, the Intermediate Court of Appeals affirmed, but notably declined to resolve the constitutional debt-limit question the circuit court had reached first. Instead, Judge White's opinion rested the affirmance on narrower grounds: the dissolution of the Development Authority under West Virginia's statutory scheme governing such authorities, and the court's estoppel jurisprudence, which the panel found dispositive without need to decide whether the original arrangement amounted to unconstitutional municipal debt. The West Virginia Attorney General's office filed an amicus brief supporting the City and Development Authority. Shopping center affiliates Fountain Place Realty, LLC and Namdar DG Realty, LLC were also named as respondents below and on appeal, reflecting the property's ties to Namdar Realty Group, a frequent acquirer of regional malls nationally. For developers who negotiate long-term municipal incentive payments tied to a dedicated development authority, the case is a reminder to build in contingencies for what happens if that authority dissolves, since courts may treat a municipality's post-dissolution statutory immunity as controlling even where the city kept paying for years afterward. It also shows that a municipality's years of voluntary compliance will not necessarily estop it from later challenging an agreement's validity, that reliance-based estoppel arguments carry less weight against government defendants than against private counterparties, and that appellate courts will often resolve a case on the narrowest available ground, leaving a live constitutional question unresolved for a future dispute. Owners negotiating annexation-linked tax-sharing deals should assume judicial scrutiny may eventually turn on whether the agreement was ever submitted to voters, particularly in states with constitutional debt-limitation provisions requiring public approval for municipal indebtedness above a statutory threshold.
live-378: For decades General Iron Industries ran a metal scrap recycling business in Chicago's Lincoln Park neighborhood. By July 2018 it had agreed to sell assets to Reserve Management Group, and in a September 2019 term sheet with the city, General Iron and RMG agreed to end the Lincoln Park operations, with RMG stating it intended to transition to a new operation at the Burley site, a 175-acre property where RMG affiliates already ran four recycling facilities. The city agreed to reasonably cooperate on permitting while reserving its authority to enforce its ordinances to protect public health. General III obtained a special use approval from the Zoning Board of Appeals in April 2019, an Illinois EPA construction permit in June 2020 and a city air pollution control permit in September 2020, and built the facility from September 2020 to March 2021 at a cost it puts at about $80 million. General III applied for the city's large recycling facility permit in November 2020. After HUD opened an investigation of a civil rights complaint about the move and U.S. EPA Administrator Michael S. Regan wrote in May 2021 suggesting the city first study cumulative health effects, the department suspended its review and, with U.S. EPA assistance, prepared a health impact assessment that recommended denial. On February 18, 2022, the department denied the permit, relying mainly on that assessment and also on compliance issues at affiliated facilities on the site. After a January 2023 hearing, an administrative law judge vacated the denial on June 1, 2023, finding the assessment beyond the commissioner's authority and the compliance-history rule inconsistent with the code. In August 2024 the circuit court, Judge Allen P. Walker, reversed and reinstated the denial. In an opinion by Justice Pucinski, joined by Justices Hyman and Evans, the First District affirmed. It treated the administrative law judge's decision as the final decision under review but held that the health department, not the hearings department, is owed deference in interpreting the code. It held that the commissioner's code powers to protect public health, conduct studies and cooperate with federal agencies authorized use of the assessment, that the zoning board's approval did not limit the health department's separate review, and that the delegation of authority was constitutional. It also held that the department's rule allowing review of an applicant's compliance history does not conflict with the code provision on prior permit revocations and is not limited to adjudicated violations. The court rejected General III's argument that its spending in reliance on earlier approvals gave it a vested right to the permit, noting that the doctrine has been applied to zoning classifications and that the record showed no pattern of official assurances that this permit would issue. Southeast Side community groups filed an amicus brief supporting the department; business and manufacturing groups filed one supporting General III.
