live-380: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit on November 6, 2026, affirmed the dismissal of a suit by AB Realty, LLC, owner of the Yale Park Apartment Complex in Omaha, Nebraska, over the city's 2018 closure of the property. Judge Jonathan A. Kobes wrote for a panel that included Chief Judge Colloton and Judge Gruender. According to the facts alleged in the complaint and its exhibits, two housing advocates began talking with Yale Park tenants in the summer of 2018, documented conditions and passed complaints to the city, which began planning the closure. Chief Housing Inspector Scott Lane obtained an inspection warrant relying mostly on their information. His application cited suspected health and safety violations in 84 of the complex's 100 units, and the court noted it contained factual errors, including a false statement that an individual plaintiff had refused Lane's request to enter. The city executed the warrant on September 20, 2018, tenants were relocated, and the city ordered that Yale Park could not reopen until the violations were cured. The city later sent notices of about 2,000 violations and prosecuted an individual plaintiff for misdemeanor code violations; a jury convicted on a few counts and acquitted on most. AB Realty and two individuals filed suit in federal court in March 2019 under 42 U.S.C. Section 1983, according to the CourtListener docket, and AB Realty reopened the complex in the spring of 2021 after repairs. The district court dismissed part of the case, stayed the rest until the criminal case ended, and then dismissed the remaining claims. On appeal, AB Realty argued the warrant was invalid under Franks v. Delaware because the application falsely said entry had been refused and that police had been called, that inspections had occurred, that threats were made against tenants and that a gas leak caused an explosion. The panel held that even excluding the disputed information, the application established probable cause under the standard for administrative warrants, citing complaints about 84 of 100 units, holes in the roof, untreated natural gas leaks and an admission that maintenance requests had been handled in a "lackadaisical" way. A Nebraska statute requiring a refusal of consent before an inspection warrant issues did not help, the court said, because a violation of state law alone does not state a Section 1983 claim. The due-process claims failed because the complaint did not identify which protected interests were at stake or who violated them. On takings, the court found no per se taking because AB Realty still owns the property, and no regulatory taking because the plaintiffs did not argue one under the Penn Central test.
live-381: Bethlehem Landfill Company owns and operates a municipal solid waste landfill at 2335 Applebutter Road in Lower Saucon Township, Pennsylvania. To expand it, the company asked the township to rezone 275.7 acres from Rural Agricultural to Light Industrial and to release two 1994 recorded instruments in the township's favor that would bar development on parts of the land. On August 14, 2023, a group of neighboring residents sued the township and the company, arguing the land was subject to Pennsylvania's Donated or Dedicated Property Act and could not be rezoned or released without Orphans' Court approval. On August 30, 2023, the township council voted to release the 1994 instruments in exchange for new conservation easements on about 193 acres, adopted the rezoning ordinance by a 3-2 vote, and approved an amended host community agreement. In December 2023 it conditionally approved the company's preliminary land development plan. After the November 2023 election changed the council's makeup, the township stopped defending the neighbors' suit alongside the company. On April 15, 2024, the township solicitor filed a brief joining the neighbors' position, and two council members said at public meetings that the council had never voted on that change. On May 1, 2024, the council voted 3-2 to ratify the filing, over the company's objections that the motion was not on the agenda and that one council member should recuse herself. The company sued on May 15, 2024, alleging Sunshine Act violations, seeking a declaration that the solicitor's brief was void, seeking to bar the council member from voting on expansion matters, and asserting promissory estoppel based on the township's earlier promise to release the 1994 instruments. The township defendants argued, among other things, that the public ratification vote cured any violation. On May 14, 2025, in an order amended the next day, the trial court dismissed the Sunshine Act and declaratory counts with prejudice as moot because the company had not appealed the ratification vote, dismissed the conflict-of-interest counts without prejudice and with leave to amend, and let the promissory estoppel count go forward against the township defendants. The company did not amend, discontinued the promissory estoppel count, and appealed. In an opinion by Judge Anne E. Covey, for a panel that included Judge Stacy Wallace and Senior Judge Mary Hannah Leavitt, the Commonwealth Court held it lacked jurisdiction. An order sustaining preliminary objections with leave to amend is interlocutory, the court said, and the company had neither filed a praecipe asking the trial court to dismiss its complaint nor sought a determination of finality. The court also rejected the argument that the order was immediately appealable because it denied injunctive and declaratory relief, since the company could still pursue that relief on the counts it was allowed to amend. The court did not reach the merits.
live-382: The Appellate Court of Illinois' First District ruled on November 9, 2026, that a commercial landlord can assign its claim to collect a tenant's already-accrued, unpaid rent to a third party, reversing a Cook County circuit court dismissal and reviving a rent-collection lawsuit against a Chicago commercial tenant. The decision resolves, as a matter of first impression under modern Illinois law, whether a chose in action for back rent -- as opposed to the right to future rent, which runs with the property -- can be freely assigned away from the landlord who holds it. The dispute traces to a long-term lease of commercial space on North Clark Street in Chicago. The tenant, Affordable Portables, Inc., doing business as Philips Interiors, signed a 20-year lease in 2002 obligating it to pay base rent plus a share of the property's real estate taxes and utilities. The property changed hands several times during the lease term, and by 2021 the landlord was 2600 N. Clark Street, LLC. The complaint alleges that while 2600 N. Clark Street, LLC held the lease, the tenant fell behind on rent, tax, and utility charges owed under the lease. In 2024, the landlord assigned its right to collect that unpaid balance to a third party, who filed a verified complaint in Cook County in January 2025 seeking to collect the arrears as an assignee rather than as the current landlord. The tenant moved to dismiss, arguing the assignee lacked standing because a claim for rent that accrued to a previous landlord does not travel with an assignment made independently of the property itself. The circuit court agreed, dismissing the suit solely on standing grounds. In doing so, it relied on the Illinois Supreme Court's 1872 decision in Kennedy v. Kennedy and a 2018 First District opinion, 1002 E. 87th Street, LLC v. Midway Broadcasting Corp., both of which had been read to treat a landlord's accrued-rent claim as a type of interest that does not pass to a stranger to the lease. The appellate panel, in an opinion by Presiding Justice Ellis, reversed. The court distinguished between the right to future rent, which runs with the property and automatically transfers to a new owner under settled Illinois law, and a claim for rent already due and unpaid, which it characterized as a distinct chose in action held personally by the landlord to whom it was owed. Surveying Illinois Supreme Court precedent on the assignability of claims generally, the panel concluded that nothing in modern law bars a landlord from assigning that chose in action to anyone it chooses, including a party with no other connection to the lease or the property. The court held the lower court's reliance on Kennedy and Midway Broadcasting was inconsistent with that modern view and remanded the case for further proceedings on the merits of the unpaid-rent claim itself, without deciding how much, if anything, the tenant actually owes. For commercial landlords and the lenders and buyers who deal with them, the ruling is a reminder that uncollected rent is its own asset, separable from the building that generated it: a landlord exiting a troubled lease or selling a property can sell or assign the right to chase down back rent to a collections specialist, an affiliate, or anyone else, and still expect a court to recognize that assignee's standing to sue. It cuts the other way for buyers of leased commercial property, who should not assume a purchase automatically brings with it the right to collect rent that was already in arrears before closing; if that receivable matters to the deal, the purchase agreement needs to say so explicitly, because Illinois law treats it as the outgoing landlord's asset to keep, sell, or walk away from. Tenants facing a stale rent demand from an unfamiliar plaintiff, meanwhile, should not assume a standing challenge will succeed just because the plaintiff never served as their landlord; after this decision, Illinois courts will look at whether the claim was properly assigned, not just who originally held it.
live-383: Lineage, the cold-storage warehouse REIT, has sued Altus Power, the company that operated a solar array on the roof of its Boyle Heights warehouse in Los Angeles, alleging Altus' negligence caused the fire that burned there for about a week in June 2026, Bisnow reported on September 11, 2026. live-384: GSL Holdings, LLC, a Michigan real estate developer, owns a roughly six-acre parcel in an industrial complex in Lyon Township. In December 2020 it leased the site to Moba Americas, Inc., a machinery manufacturer for the egg industry, agreeing to use its best reasonable efforts to have a new facility ready for occupancy by October 1, 2021. The parcel had no public sewer access, so GSL needed a septic permit from the Oakland County Health Division. The county had denied a 2018 application for the same property and said it would not issue a permit unless GSL combined the parcel with an adjacent lot. The township preliminarily approved GSL's site plan, which called for an on-site septic field, in January 2021, but its ordinance requires permits from other agencies before construction starts. On March 8, 2021, a GSL representative emailed the township's entire board of trustees about the pace of review. The township's attorney called that inappropriate and later said it risked a violation of Michigan's Open Meetings Act. The same day, GSL signed a hold-harmless agreement so the township would go ahead with building-plan review. GSL applied for the septic permit on March 9, and on March 22 the county again said it would not consider the application until the lots were combined; GSL then applied to combine them. GSL says a township coordinator told it in late March that foundation and shell permits were ready, but it did not pick them up. On April 5 the township said that, at Supervisor Dolan's direction, no building permit would issue until after a utility pre-construction meeting, which required the septic permit. On May 3 the township proposed a second hold-harmless agreement that would have let GSL build without the septic permit if GSL agreed to extend the public sanitary sewer at its own cost should the permit not be obtained. GSL considered the terms atypical and unduly burdensome, and the agreement was never signed. The facility was not ready by October, and GSL and Moba negotiated an end to the lease. GSL sued the township and Dolan in the Eastern District of Michigan. Judge Matthew F. Leitman granted summary judgment to the defendants on all claims except a later First Amendment retaliation claim over the township's denial of a speculative-building designation and a Michigan Freedom of Information Act claim, which the parties settled shortly before trial. The Sixth Circuit panel of Judges White, Thapar and Mathis affirmed. On equal protection, GSL pointed to a neighboring owner that received a building permit around 2017 before it had a septic permit. Assuming that owner was similarly situated, the court held the township's sewage-related reasons were rational and that it was conceivable the earlier permit was a mistake; the township conceded the former coordinator who issued it had breached township policy. Irritation by the township's outside counsel and engineering consultant at GSL's email did not show animus by a final decisionmaker. On procedural due process, the court held that even if permits had issued, GSL did no substantial construction under them, so under Michigan law it had no vested property interest. The substantive due-process claim failed because the township followed its ordinance, and the township rationally denied the speculative-building designation because its tax-abatement guidelines bar applicants with pending suits against it. The First Amendment claim failed because the request not to email the whole board at once was content neutral, narrowly tailored to the township's interest in complying with the Open Meetings Act, and left other channels open.
live-385: According to the trial court's summary quoted in the opinion, SA Living Fund LLC borrowed $3,850,000 in July 2022 for 18 months under a loan secured by mortgaged premises at 827 Spring Garden Street in Philadelphia. Two individuals guaranteed it. The note, the loan agreement and the guaranty each contained confession-of-judgment provisions. First Citizens Community Bank is the successor by merger to Huntingdon Valley Bank, the original lender. In March 2024 the borrower extended the maturity by one month for a $9,625 extension fee and a $750 legal fee. In November 2024 a second modification called for a payment of $103,433.33 to bring the loan current, plus a prepayment of interest for the coming year, and extended maturity to October 2029 unless the bank called the loan sooner. Both modifications contained confession-of-judgment provisions. A January 2025 letter from the bank said the borrower still owed $18,463.33 on the modification payments and $30,010.55 for a principal and interest payment due January 1, 2025, and gave it 15 days to cure. The bank filed a complaint in confession of judgment in March 2025, and the prothonotary entered judgment. The borrower and guarantors petitioned to strike or open the judgment, arguing that the complaint alleged default only in conclusory terms and that the bank's figures were wrong. At the July 9, 2025 hearing the bank agreed its calculations were incorrect, and the trial court denied the petition while directing the bank to file a motion to reassess damages. That motion has been deferred until the appeal is resolved. Writing for a panel with Judges Bowes and Olson, Judge McLaughlin held that the trial court should not have relied on the later-submitted letter and testimony in deciding the motion to strike, because that review is limited to the record when judgment was entered. The error was harmless: the complaint itself averred the default that Pennsylvania Rule of Civil Procedure 2952(a)(6) requires, and the loan documents provided for acceleration on default. On the petition to open, the court noted that the borrower did not claim it was not in default; an error in the amount is not a meritorious defense, and the corrected figure will be set on the motion to reassess damages. The borrower's argument that the bank breached the duty of good faith by pressing it to refinance or sell and by demanding a year of prepaid interest was waived because the petition did not raise it, and the court said it would fail anyway, because an unwillingness to renegotiate is not bad faith, particularly where the bank had agreed to two modifications.
live-386: On November 9, 2026, the Supreme Court denied certiorari in Rubicon Real Estate Holdings, LLC v. City of Pontiac, Michigan, closing out a dispute that began in January 2023 and traced back to a derelict, roughly 26.5-acre parcel on Glenwood Avenue that Rubicon had planned to redevelop into a medical marijuana cultivation and processing hub. The denial leaves intact a published June 18, 2026 opinion from a three-judge Sixth Circuit panel affirming summary judgment for the city, which in turn left standing a federal district court's earlier dismissal of Rubicon's entire case. Rubicon's plan centered on converting the long-vacant site into licensed cannabis cultivation and processing facilities, a use Michigan law allows municipalities to permit but does not require them to fast-track. According to Rubicon's complaint, the Pontiac Planning Commission and City Council initially cooperated, approving a rezoning request for the property. But Rubicon alleged that over the following years, the city and its clerk dragged the permitting and licensing process out for nearly four years, and that the delay caused its construction lender to walk away from a committed $45 million loan needed to build out the facilities. Rubicon also alleged a retaliation angle: that city officials targeted its principal after he won an earlier, unrelated ruling against the city in 2021, including by pressuring a contractor to terminate a roughly $9.3 million contract connected to his design firm. Rubicon and an affiliated design firm sued the City of Pontiac and its clerk in January 2023, first in Oakland County Circuit Court and then in federal court in the Eastern District of Michigan, seeking roughly $60 million in damages and fees. The complaint asserted that the city's conduct violated the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment, along with First Amendment retaliation and Fifth Amendment claims, framing years of permitting delay as intentional, targeted government action rather than ordinary municipal slowness. The federal district court rejected that framing, granting the city's motion for summary judgment on the ground that the record did not establish a triable issue that the project's collapse resulted from a constitutional violation rather than discretionary, if slow-moving, bureaucratic process. The Sixth Circuit's June 2026 opinion affirmed that result, holding that without evidence a city singled out a specific applicant for different treatment than similarly situated developers, or that officials acted for a constitutionally impermissible reason, a slow or frustrating approval process is not itself a due process or equal protection violation, even when the financial consequences for the developer are severe. Rubicon's September 2026 petition asking the Supreme Court to take up the case did not persuade the justices to intervene, and the November 9 order denying certiorari makes the Sixth Circuit's holding the final word in the litigation. For developers and lenders financing cannabis, cultivation, or other use-restricted commercial redevelopment projects that depend on discretionary municipal sign-off, the case is a reminder of how structurally difficult it is to convert a costly permitting delay into a federal constitutional claim, and a prompt to price that permitting-timeline risk into loan structures and term sheets up front, document any specific instances of disparate treatment contemporaneously, and consider financing patient enough to tolerate delay on politically contested land uses rather than counting on a court to later redistribute that risk back onto the municipality.
live-387: Weis Markets, Inc. operates a grocery store under a lease at Bangor Plaza, a 20.3-acre planned development in Washington Township's Commercial District in Northampton County, Pennsylvania. In an application dated June 17, 2022, Weis sought a special exception to add a Gas-N-Go fuel station with six fueling positions at three pumps under a canopy, replacing a previously approved bank use that was vacant. Its geologist testified that water flows from the plaza toward its spring and that the station's oil-water separator would discharge into a stormwater basin that forms part of Greenwalk Creek. Its petroleum-systems expert cited state Department of Environmental Protection records showing storage-tank violation notices at about half of Weis's Gas-N-Go locations in Pennsylvania. Weis's hydrologist testified that the aquifer is confined and not susceptible to contamination from surface spills or tank releases. The zoning hearing board granted the special exception with conditions in February 2023. Common pleas remanded in January 2024, holding the board had to review and approve a site plan. On remand the board approved the site plan in May 2024, but in April 2025 a different common pleas judge reversed, holding the site plan did not meet the ordinance and that the board could not approve it based on future compliance. Weis appealed. The Commonwealth Court rejected Weis's argument that no special exception was needed because a fuel station is permitted by right: because Weis had not appealed the zoning officer's determination within 30 days, that determination was binding. But the court agreed with Weis that the ordinance's provisions on site-plan review for a special-exception use that is also a land development are ambiguous, resolved that doubt in Weis's favor, and held no site plan was required at this time. Because common pleas had not addressed whether Weis met its burden for the special exception or whether the board adequately considered Bluetriton's evidence of harm, the court remanded for common pleas to decide those issues in a new opinion within 60 days.
live-389: On November 10, 2026, the Mississippi Court of Appeals, sitting en banc, affirmed a Hinds County Circuit Court judgment upholding the Hinds County Board of Supervisors' approval of two conditional use permits for Soul City Storage LLC and Soul City Energy LLC (together, Soul City). live-391: Two Sunrise Realty Trust, Inc. (NASDAQ: SUNS) stockholders sued the commercial real estate finance REIT and its board of directors in New York state court in late September 2026, alleging that the proxy statement prepared for its merger with Southern Realty Trust Inc. omitted material information stockholders needed to cast an informed vote. The merger closed anyway on November 5, 2026, after Sunrise filed supplemental disclosures that it says were meant to moot the claims rather than concede they had merit. The first suit, Miller v. Sunrise Realty Trust, Inc., et al., was filed September 23, 2026 in the Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County, under Index No. 655415/2026. A second, similar complaint, Smith v. Sunrise Realty Trust, Inc., et al., followed a day later under Index No. 655426/2026. Both name Sunrise and its board as defendants and assert disclosure-based claims under New York common law. Sunrise disclosed both suits, along with pre-suit demand letters raising similar objections, in the "Merger Litigation" section of its Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, filed with the SEC on November 10. The deal required stockholder approval at both companies, including a SUNS vote to approve issuing roughly 8.46 million merger shares. Sunrise has said it believes the claims lack merit but chose to supplement its proxy disclosures anyway, stating in its 10-Q that doing so was intended to moot certain plaintiffs' disclosure claims and avoid the risk that the litigation would delay or otherwise affect the merger. Both companies held special stockholder meetings on October 23, 2026; at Sunrise's meeting roughly 59.5% of outstanding shares were voted, with about 91.6% of votes cast in favor of the share issuance, and SRT stockholders approved the merger the same day. The deal closed November 5, 2026, with Sunrise issuing approximately 8,464,977 new shares as merger consideration. Sunrise's 10-Q does not disclose that either suit has been dismissed, withdrawn, or settled, so both remain pending even though the transaction they targeted has already closed. For REIT boards, external managers, and the counsel who shepherd merger proxies through SEC review, the sequence is a reminder that a conventional, board-approved stock-for-stock merger will often draw at least one disclosure-based stockholder suit almost reflexively regardless of the deal's actual risk profile, that supplementing proxy disclosures promptly is typically far cheaper than absorbing a delay to the stockholder vote, and that a deal closing on schedule does not mean the litigation behind it has been resolved -- boards should expect this kind of suit to persist past closing and track it separately from the transaction timeline.
live-392: The Alabama Court of Civil Appeals on November 6, 2026 voided a circuit court judgment in a Montgomery commercial-property dispute, ruling that the case had no business being in circuit court in the first place. The decision in Devosky Hood v. Barbara L. Smith erased more than a year of litigation over a disputed commercial lot and sent the matter back to where it started, underscoring how jurisdictionally rigid Alabama's summary unlawful-detainer remedy really is. Barbara L. Smith commenced an unlawful-detainer action against Devosky Hood in the Montgomery District Court in December 2025, alleging the two had entered into a commercial lease in July 2022 and that Hood owed roughly $53,500 in unpaid rent. Hood answered that he was not Smith's tenant at all, producing what he described as a purchase agreement for the same property, plus a 2024 addendum under which he would receive a deed once he finished paying Smith $53,000 in installments. Mid-trial, the district court concluded the dispute had strayed into territory beyond its authority and transferred the case to the Montgomery Circuit Court, where Hood counterclaimed that the matter was a contract dispute over the alleged sale, not a landlord-tenant case. The circuit court held its own trial in April 2026 and entered judgment in May 2026 finding Smith held legal title and Hood had defaulted under the lease, while expressly declining to decide whether the alleged purchase agreement was valid. Hood appealed, and the Court of Civil Appeals raised a jurisdictional problem neither party had argued: Alabama law gives district courts exclusive original jurisdiction over unlawful-detainer actions, and a circuit court can only acquire jurisdiction over one after the district court has actually adjudicated it and a party has appealed that adjudication, not through a mid-case transfer ordered by the district court itself. Because the district court never ruled on Smith's unlawful-detainer claim before transferring it, the panel held the circuit court never acquired jurisdiction, making its May 2026 judgment void from the start. The court dismissed Hood's appeal but ordered the circuit court to vacate its void judgment and transfer the action back to the district court where it began, also noting that Smith's $53,000 claim exceeds the district court's $20,000 jurisdictional damages cap, meaning she will have to waive the excess or file a separate circuit court action to recover the balance. For commercial landlords relying on Alabama's unlawful-detainer statute, the case is a reminder to treat the remedy as a narrow, summary one that a trial court cannot broaden by moving a complicated case somewhere more comfortable once the facts get tangled with a competing sale theory, and that any landlord whose claim could plausibly exceed the district court's statutory damages ceiling should weigh filing in circuit court directly or be prepared to cap the claim, rather than risk a judgment that later proves to have been entered without jurisdiction at all.
live-393: On November 12, 2026, Florida's Fourth District Court of Appeal affirmed in part and reversed in part a final default summary judgment entered for landlord Congress Ave Boynton, LLC against tenant First Care Therapy, LLC and the individual who guaranteed its lease. Judge Alan O. Forst wrote the opinion, joined by Judges Shepherd and Shaw. The tenant had leased commercial premises in Boynton Beach from SNH Medical Office Properties Trust in September 2021; Congress Ave Boynton bought the property in May 2024 and took an assignment of the lease and guaranty. The landlord sued on February 21, 2025, for nonpayment of rent without pleading a sum certain, attaching a lease ledger showing $34,337.91 in unpaid charges. Neither defendant responded, and the clerk entered defaults in March 2025. The landlord then moved for summary judgment on an affidavit of indebtedness from its managing agent totaling $85,782.80: $48,480 in rent, $4,222 in legal fees to draft and negotiate a new lease, a $10,557 reletting commission and $22,523 in tenant improvements for reletting. At a July 2025 hearing the guarantor appeared without a lawyer and no attorney appeared for the tenant. The court heard argument and entered judgment for the full amount requested, plus interest, and found the landlord entitled to attorney's fees. The panel rejected the tenant's and guarantor's arguments that the judgment was void. The circuit court had subject-matter jurisdiction, and any objection to its authority in this particular case was waived. The landlord did not have to attach the written assignment, and by defaulting the defendants admitted the allegation that the lease and guaranty had been assigned to it. A company cannot appear in court without counsel, and the tenant's failure to retain one was not a due-process violation. The damages award was another matter. Following its August 2026 decision in Affinity Health Partners, LLC v. Hayes Locums, LLC, the court held that a clerk's default supports only liquidated damages, and that these damages were unliquidated because the complaint pleaded no sum certain, the ledger showed less than half the award, and the final figure could be reached only by weighing the affidavit. The prejudgment interest and costs were likewise unliquidated. Because the July 2025 hearing was a non-evidentiary summary judgment proceeding rather than a damages trial noticed under Rule 1.440(d), the court reversed the award and remanded for such a trial, leaving the liability ruling in place. The opinion is not final until any timely motion for rehearing is resolved.

live-395: A long-running infrastructure-cost dispute tied to a 2014 West Maui land sale has turned into an active foreclosure fight, according to a Form 10-Q that publicly traded land company Kaanapali Land, LLC filed with the SEC on November 12, 2026. The filing discloses that the company's subsidiary, Kaanapali Land Management Corp., known as KLMC, initiated foreclosure proceedings in Maui on September 29, 2026 against Newport Hospital Corporation, known as NHC, after NHC failed to pay a receivable owed under a shared infrastructure agreement. NHC responded by moving to stay or dismiss the foreclosure proceeding on November 5, 2026, and the company says there is no assurance KLMC will ultimately prevail or collect what it is owed. The underlying transaction dates to 2014, when KLMC sold NHC approximately 14.9 acres of land in West Maui under a Property and Option Purchase Agreement. As part of that deal, the parties entered into an Infrastructure Improvement Agreement, later amended, under which KLMC committed to fund a share of off-site infrastructure work, including roads, sewer, and electrical improvements, serving the broader area, with the company's exposure capped at up to $0.6 million depending on several variables. The agreement in turn created reciprocal contribution obligations, and it is NHC's side of that bargain that is now at the center of the dispute: according to the 10-Q, NHC owes KLMC a receivable tied to the infrastructure work, secured by what the filing calls the NHC Contribution Lien against NHC's land. The company's filing states that after NHC failed and refused to pay the receivable, KLMC gave NHC written notice of default under the Infrastructure Improvement Agreement on September 4, 2026, along with a demand for payment. When NHC did not cure the default, KLMC exercised its contractual right to foreclose on the Contribution Lien and filed a foreclosure complaint in Maui on September 29, 2026. NHC did not simply let the foreclosure proceed; on November 5, 2026, it filed a motion seeking to stay or dismiss the proceeding, which remains pending. Kaanapali Land's filing cautions that there is no assurance the company will prevail in the foreclosure proceeding or that a win would actually result in collecting the receivable and accrued interest. The dispute is not an isolated commercial transaction for Kaanapali Land. The company's filing notes that it retains certain approval rights over the uses and design of the NHC parcel under the Infrastructure Improvement Agreement, intended to keep development on the site consistent with Kaanapali's broader master-planned development for the surrounding region; the company says it is in the planning stages for a 295-acre parcel mauka of, or upslope from, its Kaanapali Coffee Farms community. A lien foreclosure against a parcel embedded inside a larger master development gives the landowner-plaintiff leverage beyond simply recovering a receivable, since an unresolved dispute over the NHC parcel's infrastructure contributions and permitted uses could complicate planning and permitting decisions across the adjoining acreage. Developers who structure a land sale around a shared infrastructure-cost agreement, rather than requiring the buyer's contribution up front, should recognize that enforcing that obligation years later, after the roads, sewer, and electrical work are already built, can mean litigating a contested foreclosure rather than simply collecting a bill, particularly once the buyer disputes the underlying default. A contribution lien is only as useful as the foreclosure remedy behind it, and a motion to stay or dismiss can extend the collection timeline well past the original notice-and-cure period contemplated in the agreement; for master-plan developers retaining design and use-approval rights over parcels already sold off, an unresolved infrastructure-cost dispute with one buyer is worth flagging early in connection with planning and entitlement work on adjacent, still-undeveloped acreage.
live-396: The owners of a building on West Burnside in Portland had for decades leased its large west wall to advertising companies that sold space for signs. In 2009 they leased the wall to Onsite Advertising Services, LLC under a revenue-sharing arrangement, and in 2010 Onsite assigned the lease to OnDisplay Advertising. A 2014 addendum extended the lease to June 30, 2019, with automatic five-year renewal unless either side gave notice. After the state designated that stretch of West Burnside a state highway in 2012, ODOT began requiring a permit for the sign as of June 30, 2015. The owners agreed to give OnDisplay a consent letter for ODOT on the condition that they would own the permit when the lease ended, and the letter stated the permit "shall be in the name of" OnDisplay and the owners. ODOT issued the permit only to OnDisplay. OnDisplay sold its assets, including the lease, to Lamar in a deal that closed June 16, 2015, and ODOT reissued the permit in Lamar's name alone. The owners were not told. The owners gave notice that they would not renew, and in February 2019 Lamar said that if the lease ended it would remove the lighting and cabling and relinquish the permit, which the court said was the owners' first notice that the permit was in Lamar's name. Lamar declined to sell the permit, telling the owners through counsel that doing so would not serve its interest because it would "allow a competing advertising agency to saturate the market even further." On July 18, 2019, despite the owners' written instruction not to surrender it, Lamar used the permit to obtain a relocation credit from ODOT, and no location was available where that credit could be used. ODOT refused to issue a new permit to the owners, whose separate challenges against ODOT were later rejected. The owners sued OnDisplay and Lamar, settled with OnDisplay, and went to trial against Lamar in Multnomah County. The jury found for the owners on the good-faith claim but not on conversion, and the judgment, including costs, was $1,237,191.92. In an opinion by Presiding Judge Darleen Ortega, joined by Judges Joyce and Hellman, the Court of Appeals held two of Lamar's nine assignments of error unreviewable and rejected the rest. It held that, as a matter of law, the parties could have held the expectations the owners claimed, grounded in the lease's limited term and its renewal and termination provisions, including that Lamar would not act to prevent the owners from leasing the wall to others once the lease ended. Whether the parties actually held those expectations and whether Lamar's conduct breached them were questions for the jury. The court also found the future-damages evidence sufficient and no error in the jury instructions.

live-399: On February 8, 2023, Ms. Audrey's Crafting Emporium, LLC signed a 62-month lease for retail space with Ghasem Properties, Inc., and an individual guaranteed it up to $155,124.60. Rent and common-area maintenance totaled $2,585.41 a month starting in the third month. The tenant paid through December 2023 and then stopped. The landlord said it mailed a default notice on January 6, 2024, and a forcible-detainer action was dismissed in April 2024 after the tenant vacated. The landlord sued in Jefferson Circuit Court on April 8, 2024. The tenant and guarantor admitted signing the lease, defaulting and not paying rent from January 2024 on, but denied responsibility for damages. The landlord moved for summary judgment on an affidavit from its president stating that rent for the rest of the term would have totaled $131,855.91 and that a listing agreement had not produced a new tenant. The defendants did not respond, and on September 30, 2024 the court signed the landlord's tendered judgment for $131,855.91 with 8% prejudgment interest from January 1, 2024, 6% post-judgment interest, and fees and costs. The court later denied the defendants' motion to vacate, saying their arguments should have been made before judgment, and entered a supplemental award of $8,299.30 in fees and costs. The Court of Appeals, in an opinion joined by Judges Caldwell and Taylor, held that the defendants could not wait until after judgment to challenge the affidavit, and that their own admissions established liability. It found the interest issue properly raised, however, because the 8% rate first appeared in the landlord's tendered order. With no rate in the lease, the statutory rate for a judgment, including prejudgment interest, is 6% under KRS 360.040. On future rent, the court acknowledged the defendants never raised the point but addressed it to avoid applying the wrong law: under Kentucky precedent, without an acceleration clause, rent that has not yet accrued cannot be awarded in advance. Only nine months of rent had accrued at judgment, while the award covered the remaining 42 months, which the court called a windfall. The landlord may seek supplemental judgments for rent as it comes due if it cannot relet the space before the term ends in March 2028. The court affirmed the 6% post-judgment interest.

live-401: The special servicer on 1440 Broadway, a 745,000-square-foot office building near Times Square, has gone to court to foreclose. live-402: New York Supreme Court Justice Francis Kahn on November 11, 2026 denied summary judgment to 109Co in its $44 million foreclosure against Fortuna Realty's Hotel Hayden, finding that the note and mortgage had not been properly attached to each other, The Real Deal reported. The ruling sends the case to trial. The 122-room hotel is at 127 West 28th Street in Manhattan. Fortuna bought it in 1999 and refinanced it with Morgan Stanley Private Bank in 2018. Morgan Stanley started the foreclosure in April 2025 and, in February 2026, sold the loan for an undisclosed price to 109Co, a firm formed in 2023. Default is not in dispute: according to the report, the owner's principal signed a forbearance agreement admitting it. The dispute is over standing. A foreclosing lender has to show how and when it came to hold the note along with the mortgage, and courts have required the papers to be "so firmly affixed thereto as to become a part thereof." The Real Deal reported that Morgan Stanley filed the note and mortgage separately when it refinanced the hotel, and Justice Kahn found the requirement was not met. The rule protects borrowers from a second party later claiming the same debt and trying to foreclose again. These challenges became common in the foreclosures after the 2007 housing crash, and they usually come up after a loan has changed hands. "No staple, no case," the borrower's attorney told The Real Deal. He said 109Co must now try to prove its standing at trial or go back and fix the attachment problem, which could be hard if it means finding people involved in the 2018 loan, and that he expects more such challenges as banks sell off bad loans. Representatives of 109Co and Fortuna could not immediately be reached. The ruling gives the hotel owner more leverage in any settlement talks.

In 2016 they formed HC Government Realty Trust, Inc., a Maryland REIT, and its operating partnership, HC Government Realty Holdings, L.P., and signed a management agreement under which their own company, Holmwood Capital Advisors, LLC, would run the REIT for an asset management fee of 1.5% of stockholders' equity, a 1% acquisition fee and a leasing fee. A related entity, Holmwood Capital, LLC, contributed seven single-property entities to the operating partnership in a May 2017 exchange for 1,078,416 partnership units valued at $10,784,161. The management agreement promised the manager a termination fee of three times the fees earned over the prior 24 months if the REIT ended the arrangement without cause, and a November 2017 side letter scaled that fee to how much equity the REIT managed to build: waived below $15 million, halved between $15 million and $35 million, and paid in full above $35 million. In March 2019, over the objection of one founder-director, the REIT's board approved a recapitalization with a new outside investor that included up to $20.5 million of preferred stock, $3 million of common stock and a secured loan of up to $20.5 million. At the same meeting the board voted not to renew the management agreement, which ended March 31, 2020. On that date the REIT told the manager the termination fee was $1,645,453, paid as $1,275,000 in cash and the balance in common stock at $7.17 a share. That figure used the halved, 1.5x multiplier, because the REIT's new finance chief had begun booking a $1.75 million estimate of the termination fee itself as an accrued liability, which pulled reported stockholders' equity just under $35 million. The manager sued in May 2020, and the REIT counterclaimed. Vice Chancellor Bonnie W. David sided with the manager on the central question. The agreement's definition of stockholders' equity excludes non-cash items that have affected equity as reported in the financial statements, and an accrued but unpaid termination fee is such an item, so it had to be added back. The court also read the side letter's reference to the REIT 'building' equity to $35 million as a high-water mark rather than a snapshot on the termination date, so the full 3.0x multiplier applies. The REIT's late arguments that equity had been overstated all along, because dividends were never deducted from retained earnings and because the contributed properties were overvalued by about $3.2 million, were rejected. The court found the REIT waived both points by using the same method in its own March 2020 fee notice, and found the appraisal evidence unpersuasive in any event. The manager did not win everything. The court held that accrued acquisition fees were paid in stock on the termination date and so do not get added to the fee base, and that no acquisition fee is owed on three properties the REIT bought in October 2019 in Fort Lauderdale, Lawrence, Kansas and Oklahoma City, because the manager did no work on those deals. Applying contra proferentem against the founders, who controlled every party when the agreement was written and then marketed the REIT to outside investors, the court held the REIT could choose to pay the termination and acquisition fees in common stock, and that the manager must bear organization and offering expenses above 15% of the $8,871,660 raised, an excess of $723,932. The $408,514 that Holmwood advanced to cover operating shortfalls was not proven to be an interest-bearing demand loan, but the court found it must be repaid on terms the parties are to propose. On the counterclaims, the REIT failed to prove $76,322 in allegedly duplicative property management fees, and its unjust enrichment claim fell with the valuation argument. It did prevail on the contribution agreement. Three of the contributed properties secured a CMBS loan that barred any transfer of direct or indirect interests without lender consent. Holmwood transferred the economic interest in those properties without telling the lender, the servicer issued a notice of default in November 2022, and the REIT spent $517,463.35 obtaining a consent and loan modification in March 2023. The court held that Holmwood's representation that the deal would not cause a default under any contract was false, and awarded that amount as damages. The practical lessons are plain. A termination fee tied to an equity measure should say whether the accrual of the fee itself counts, and whether thresholds are tested once or continuously; here silence on timing cost the REIT half the multiplier. A company that pays under one calculation method will struggle to attack that method years later. Sponsors who sit on both sides of a management agreement should expect ambiguities to be read against them once outside investors are in the capital stack. And a cost-allocation clause for obtaining lender consents before closing does not protect a contributor who never sought consent at all. The final dollar amount of the fee remains open until the parties submit a revised calculation.
live-405: The landlord, HCJV 115 & 135 Hoyt Avenue Owner, LLC, leased a commercial unit in Mamaroneck, in Westchester County, to Project Veritas in 2020. The lease ran five years, from November 1, 2020 through October 31, 2025. Rent was due on the first of each month, payments more than 10 days late drew additional interest, and section 20 of the lease provided that any change or modification had to be in writing and signed by the party against whom it would be enforced. In December 2023, with almost two years left on the term, the tenant told the landlord it would need to terminate the lease that month and would be vacating. The landlord responded by sending a lease termination agreement. According to the decision, the tenant never signed it and never sent it back. The landlord sued in January 2024 for breach of the lease. The tenant answered with affirmative defenses that included estoppel, taking the position that the parties had in substance agreed to end the lease and that it had performed its side of that bargain. Supreme Court, Westchester County (Justice William J. Giacomo) granted the landlord summary judgment on the complaint in a December 20, 2024 order and, after an inquest on damages, entered judgment on March 6, 2025 in the principal sum of $114,098.96. The tenant appealed. The Second Department affirmed, with costs. It began with General Obligations Law section 15-301(1), under which a contract that requires written modifications cannot be changed orally. New York recognizes an exception where a party has partly performed the alleged oral modification, but only when the conduct is unequivocally referable to that modification, meaning it cannot be explained any other way. The tenant pointed to three things: a 'termination payment' covering rent due to date, forfeiture of its security deposit to cover the landlord's losses, and its abandonment of desks, chairs and other office equipment. The court found none of them sufficient. Paying rent through the date of departure and losing the deposit on default were exactly what the existing lease called for, so they were fully consistent with the lease remaining in force. As for the furniture, the tenant's claim that it was worth thousands of dollars was unsubstantiated, and leaving it behind was not conduct that could only be explained by a termination deal. The same reasoning disposed of the estoppel defense. The landlord, for its part, had made out each element of a breach claim: a valid lease, its own performance, the tenant's breach and resulting damages. Having resolved the appeal on those grounds, the panel did not reach the parties' remaining arguments. The takeaways are practical. For landlords, a no-oral-modification clause continues to do real work in New York, and sending a draft surrender agreement that the tenant ignores does not waive the right to collect rent for the balance of the term. Keeping a record that the document was sent and never returned was enough here to win on summary judgment. For tenants looking to exit early, the order of operations matters: get the termination agreement fully signed before handing back the keys, and do not assume that money already owed under the lease, or property left in the space, will later be credited as consideration for a release. Where a tenant does give something beyond what the lease requires in exchange for a surrender, it should be documented and valued at the time, because unsupported assertions about its worth will not create an issue of fact.
live-406: H&R Block Eastern Enterprises, Inc. had leased space at the Hallwood Plaza shopping center in Flint, Michigan since 1998, under a lease signed with the predecessor of the current owner, Hallwood Plaza LLC. Just after midnight on August 8, 2023, an intoxicated driver with no known connection to the tenant drove into the center, struck the H&R Block unit and started a fire that left the space unusable. In November 2023 the landlord moved the tenant into temporary space elsewhere in the center. Each side then waited for the other to repair the original unit. According to the opinion, the landlord billed full rent on both the fire-damaged unit and the temporary space while the stalemate continued, and warned that nonpayment of either would be a default. H&R Block sued on July 30, 2024, alleging breach of the lease and seeking a declaration that the landlord's refusal to rebuild amounted to constructive eviction. In October 2024, after roughly a year of paying rent on two spaces, it moved to a new permanent location. Hallwood Plaza counterclaimed, alleging that the tenant failed to maintain the sprinkler system, failed to make repairs, failed to indemnify the landlord and failed to carry required insurance. It sought repair costs, lost rent and legal fees. Both sides moved for partial summary judgment. The central question was which lease provision controls after a fire. The landlord relied on the general repair sections, under which it maintains the foundation, roof, exterior walls and common areas while the tenant maintains the interior. The tenant relied on Section 13, titled "Fire or Other Casualty." That section gives the landlord a choice after serious fire damage: terminate the lease, or keep it in force with a fair and proportionate rent abatement. If the lease continues, the section says the landlord shall rebuild the premises to the condition in which they were originally delivered, after which the tenant restores its own property and reopens. Applying the Michigan rule that a specific contract provision controls over a general one, and that section headings help identify the applicable provision, the court held that Section 13 governs and is unambiguous. The court also pointed to a sentence in the tenant-repair clause making the tenant responsible for fire-damaged HVAC equipment "notwithstanding Article 13," which would be unnecessary if the tenant already bore all interior fire repairs. On rent, the court read the lease to give the landlord three paths after a fire: terminate, continue with abated rent, or continue while providing temporary space that is treated as if it were the leased premises. None of those paths, the court said, allowed full rent on both the untenantable unit and the temporary space. The court also declined to grant the landlord summary judgment on constructive eviction, noting that the temporary space had become effectively permanent because the landlord refused to restore the original unit. Photographs in the record showed the unit in much the same condition in April 2026 as shortly after the fire. The landlord's counterclaims fared worse. The sprinkler claim failed for lack of evidence; the landlord's own representative testified that he had no records or facts indicating the system was not maintained or did not work. The repair counterclaim failed because the tenant's limited restoration duties were conditioned on the landlord rebuilding first. The indemnification counterclaim failed because the clause addresses third-party claims and because the landlord had limited its counterclaims in discovery to the sprinkler and insurance theories. The insurance counterclaim failed because the record showed the tenant carried the required general liability policy naming the landlord as an additional insured. With those four claims resolved, the court dismissed the landlord's remaining declaratory counterclaim as presenting no live controversy. The landlord's only win was the dismissal of the tenant's request for legal fees, since no statute or lease provision authorized them. For owners and tenants of multi-tenant retail property, the practical points are concrete. A casualty clause that says the landlord shall rebuild will be enforced as written even where everyday repair clauses put the interior on the tenant. A landlord that elects to continue a lease after a fire should decide promptly whether it is abating rent or providing temporary space, and should not charge for both. A landlord that wants the tenant to clear fixtures and debris before rebuilding should give the notice the lease calls for. And positions taken in discovery about the scope of a counterclaim can foreclose broader theories at summary judgment. The tenant's breach-of-contract and declaratory claims remain pending.
live-407: A second lawsuit over the Project Delta data center site was filed in Stokes County Superior Court on November 12, 2026, according to an announcement by the plaintiffs' lawyers; the complaint posted on their case page carries file number 26CV0000976-840. The plaintiffs are four organizations, the National Hairston Clan, CleanAIRE NC, the Dan River Basin Association and 7 Directions of Service, joined by 16 county residents, some of whom own land next to the site. They challenge the Stokes County Board of Commissioners' 3-2 vote on September 14, 2026, to rezone about 1,850 acres of farmland and forest along the Dan River near Walnut Cove for a data center campus, which the plaintiffs' lawyers call speculative and one of the largest AI data center campuses in the country. Public radio station WFDD identifies the developer as Engineered Land Solutions. This is the second rezoning of the same land and the second suit. Commissioners first approved a rezoning in January 2026, by the same 3-2 margin, WFDD reported. The same lawyers sued on March 12, 2026, challenging the decision's process, and in April the county voided that rezoning. In August the parties filed a joint motion for a consent judgment and the court formally voided the January rezoning. Engineered Land Solutions then reapplied, and the plaintiffs say the commissioners approved the new request against the county Planning Board's recommendation and heavy public opposition. The new complaint, as described by the plaintiffs' counsel, shifts from process to the substance of the county's decision. The plaintiffs allege the supporting analysis was rushed and deficient and appears to have been generated by AI without independent verification. They say the approval came during a drought, without a confirmed water source, without limits on on-site power generation and without a complete survey of graves and archaeological sites on the land, which they say include Saura village sites and a mapped cemetery of about 65 graves. For its part, the developer revised its proposal several times after January, in part to add stricter standards on noise, energy generation and water use, which its CEO said responded to community concerns, WFDD reported in September. Timing matters. The plaintiffs' counsel says the commissioners are set to vote on November 23 on a 15-year development agreement for Project Delta. According to the lawsuit as described by counsel, that agreement would lock in the rezoning's shortcomings, exempt the property from any future data center moratorium and commit the county to help defend the developer's interests against challenges from residents. The plaintiffs ask the court to declare the rezoning void and to block the county from relying on or implementing it. No hearing date or assigned judge has been reported, and the allegations have not been tested. A second approval after a procedural defect is now being tested on the strength of its record, and a development agreement signed while the rezoning is challenged protects only as much as the rezoning itself.
live-408: The case arises from the long-running effort to rebuild the Hill Top House Hotel in Harpers Ferry. According to the opinion, SWaN Hill Top House, LLC bought the century-old, derelict hotel in 2007 intending to reconstruct it as a luxury property. The project sat for more than a decade, and when the developer began moving forward in 2019, friction developed with town residents. Harpers Ferry had 269 residents in the 2020 Census. In 2020 the Legislature adopted the Tourism Development District Act. The law allows the state's commerce and economic development officials to create a district around a qualifying tourism project. Inside a district, the project is not subject to municipal zoning, historic preservation, noise, viewshed, lighting or land use ordinances, municipal regulation of alcohol sales, municipal building permitting and code enforcement, municipal licensing, or most municipal taxes and fees, and the town may not adopt rules that impede the project. State regulators oversee building code and land use matters instead. Three limits define who can use the law: the project must be in a municipality of 2,000 people or fewer, it must carry projected costs of at least $25 million, and no more than five districts may be approved statewide. The Hill Top House project is the only applicant and the only district designated since the law passed. In January 2022 a group of Harpers Ferry residents and voters sued the two state officials in the Circuit Court of Kanawha County. They argued the Act is a special or local law barred by Article VI, sections 39 and 39a of the West Virginia Constitution, that its classifications are arbitrary and violate equal protection principles under Article III, section 10, and that handing control over land use in their town to a state agency negates their rights to self-government and to vote in municipal elections. The circuit court dismissed the complaint on March 29, 2023. The Intermediate Court of Appeals affirmed in 2024, and the residents appealed again. Writing for the court, Justice Wooton affirmed on every point. On the special-law claim, the court applied its settled presumption that legislative classifications are reasonable and held that the Act does not target particular persons or entities or set up one project to succeed at the expense of others; it offers benefits to up to five large projects that private parties choose to locate in small communities. On equal protection, the court found the population and cost thresholds rationally related to stated legislative goals of encouraging tourism investment in small municipalities and supporting large projects the Legislature considered important to the state's economy. On self-rule, the court found no such right in the state constitution, repeating that municipalities have only the powers the Legislature grants and that those powers can be modified or withdrawn at any time. The Act changes what small towns may regulate, the court said, without affecting anyone's ability to vote. The court declined to decide whether an earlier Jefferson County ruling against a citizens' association barred the claims and resolved the case on the merits. Chief Justice Bunn dissented and reserved the right to file a separate opinion. One justice was disqualified and a circuit judge sat by temporary assignment. The practical lessons run in two directions. Developers and lenders evaluating large hotel or resort projects in West Virginia's small towns now have a high-court ruling that a district designation displaces local zoning, historic review and permitting, which removes a category of entitlement risk from underwriting, though state oversight under the commerce department's rules still applies. The decision also shows the standard of review such laws face: deferential, rational-basis scrutiny in which the fact that only one project has qualified did not make the statute special legislation. Towns and neighboring owners who oppose a designated project should expect that their remaining arguments lie with the state agency and the Legislature, not with municipal boards, and that a challenge built on the breadth of the preemption alone is unlikely to succeed. The forthcoming dissent may indicate where any future challenge would focus.

live-410: F-Star Socorro, L.P. and affiliated companies filed Chapter 11 petitions in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas on November 4, 2025, according to the ElevenFlo case summary and the court docket. The group, which developed a Ritz-Carlton project in Arizona and also owned industrial and commercial property around El Paso, filed amid a liquidity crisis and a dispute with lender Madison Realty Capital. The debtors allege Madison stopped funding construction and manufactured defaults on the Arizona project; Madison had scheduled a foreclosure on the Arizona collateral. The Texas side of the business, which the docket calls the Commercial Property Debtors, is now on its own track. On September 25, 2026, the court authorized the sale of four El Paso County properties to Madison through a $90 million credit bid, subject to closing conditions, and separately approved a $180 million replacement financing facility from Farallon along with the use of cash collateral. On November 13 the court conditionally approved the disclosure statement for the Commercial Property Debtors' plan, which lets voting begin and leaves final approval for a combined hearing with confirmation. Under the plan, the $120 million senior mortgage DIP facility and the $60 million mezzanine DIP facility would become exit loans dollar for dollar, with no cash payment. Allowed general unsecured claims would be paid in full from a claims reserve, without postpetition interest; insider and affiliate claims would receive senior interests in a plan trust, and parent equity would receive junior interests. Funding the reserve and meeting the exit-financing conditions are among the conditions for the plan to take effect. Ballots and confirmation objections are due December 7, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. Central Time, and the combined hearing is set for December 16. A dispute over the clawback guaranty in the September sale order is set for hearing on November 19. live-411: The Pennhurst property covers about 124.6 acres at 1205 Commonwealth Drive in East Vincent Township, Chester County, in the township's Industrial Mixed Use District. The Philadelphia Inquirer described the plan in May as 1.9 million square feet in three two-story buildings, with a power generation and battery storage field. On May 21, 2026, the township's Board of Supervisors unanimously rejected the application. According to MyChesCo, which cited reporting by Spring-Ford Press, the supervisors concluded that the proposal did not qualify as a planned commercial development under the zoning ordinance. Penn Hurst Holdings filed its land use appeal in the Chester County Court of Common Pleas in June, arguing that the supervisors misread the ordinance's provisions on permitted uses, zoning standards and transferable development rights. The developer argued that the farm owners had not formally established party status in the township proceedings and that a group owning no property in the township could not stand in for affected owners.
